01_Geometrical_Vocabulary.json.title: Geometrical Vocabulary
01_Geometrical_Vocabulary.json.subject: Mathematics

objectives.statement: Use and interpret the terms point, line, line segment, vertex, parallel and perpendicular lines, and classify an angle as acute, right, obtuse, reflex or a straight angle.
Name and describe triangles by their sides and angles, name the six special quadrilaterals from their properties, and name polygons with up to ten sides, distinguishing regular from irregular.
Name common 3D solids (cube, cuboid, prism, pyramid, cylinder, cone, sphere) and count their faces, edges and vertices, using Euler's formula $V-E+F=2$ to check the count for a flat-faced solid.
Label the parts of a circle correctly — centre, radius, diameter, chord, tangent, arc, sector and segment — and use them in a simple geometrical argument.

Explain the difference between congruent and similar shapes in terms of the scale factor, and use the Extended-only vocabulary: plane, perpendicular bisector, hemisphere, frustum, major arc and minor arc.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise and name basic 2D shapes (triangle, square, rectangle, circle) and basic 3D solids (cube, sphere) from earlier years.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson sorts those familiar shapes into precise families (by sides, by angles) and adds the exact vocabulary a mark scheme expects; without the shapes already being familiar by sight, the new vocabulary has nothing to attach to.

prerequisites.statement: Add and subtract numbers up to a few hundred, including with a calculator-free method.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Angle facts such as 'interior + exterior = $180^{\circ}$' and 'a full turn is $360^{\circ}$' are used immediately in worked examples and exercises, and every one of them is a simple addition or subtraction.

prerequisites.statement: Understand that a fraction such as $\tfrac12$ or a ratio such as $2:1$ describes 'how many times bigger'.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The scale factor that distinguishes similar shapes from congruent ones is exactly this idea applied to lengths; without it, 'similar' can only be learned as a disconnected new word.

prerequisites.statement: Plot and read coordinates $(x,y)$ on a pair of axes.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The Extended exercise on the perpendicular bisector of a segment $AB$ given by coordinates needs the midpoint and the idea of a vertical or horizontal line as an equation.

diagnostic_items.question: Why is every square a rectangle, but not every rectangle a square?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: A square has four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel, so it meets every requirement of the rectangle definition. A rectangle only needs opposite sides equal (not all four sides equal), so a non-square rectangle such as $3\times5$ satisfies the rectangle definition without satisfying the square definition.

common_wrong_answers.answer: They are different shapes, so neither is the other.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Treats shape names as mutually exclusive labels rather than as nested sets defined by a list of properties; the learner has not yet connected 'properties a shape has' with 'names that shape qualifies for'.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner thinks of quadrilateral names as a hierarchy built from properties (so one name can imply another) rather than as a flat list of mutually exclusive labels, before any of the special-quadrilateral vocabulary is used in exercises.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: List the defining properties of a rectangle and of a square side by side and show that every property on the rectangle's list also appears on the square's list, but not the reverse; repeat with rhombus/square to reinforce the pattern.

diagnostic_items.question: How is a prism different from a pyramid?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: A prism has the same cross-section all the way through its length, with two identical parallel end faces and rectangular (or parallelogram) side faces; a pyramid tapers from a polygon base to a single point, the apex, with triangular side faces.

common_wrong_answers.answer: A pyramid has a point and a prism doesn't, but otherwise they're similar shapes.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Notices the apex as a surface feature but has not connected it to the structural idea of a cross-section that stays constant (prism) versus one that shrinks to a point (pyramid), so the distinction feels arbitrary rather than defining.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that 'prism' and 'pyramid' are understood as structural definitions (constant cross-section vs. tapering to an apex), which is exactly what is needed to count faces/edges/vertices correctly later in the lesson.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Compare a triangular prism and a square-based pyramid side by side, tracing the cross-section of the prism along its length (always the same triangle) against the pyramid's cross-section shrinking towards the apex.

diagnostic_items.question: What is the difference between a chord and a diameter of a circle?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Both are straight lines joining two points on the circumference, but a diameter is the special chord that passes through the centre; every diameter is a chord, but a chord is only a diameter if it goes through the centre, so the diameter is also the longest possible chord.

common_wrong_answers.answer: A diameter is just a longer chord.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Notices the length relationship but misses the defining geometric condition (passing through the centre) that makes the diameter the longest chord, rather than it being an unrelated coincidence.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether circle vocabulary is being learned as a set of related definitions (diameter as a special case of chord) rather than as a list of unconnected words, before the circle-theorem lessons rely on exactly this relationship.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Draw several chords of different lengths in one circle and show that the longest one always passes through the marked centre; name that one the diameter.

diagnostic_items.question: Can a triangle have two obtuse angles? Why or why not?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. Two obtuse angles (each more than $90^{\circ}$) would already add to more than $180^{\circ}$, but the three angles of any triangle must add to exactly $180^{\circ}$, so a triangle can have at most one angle of $90^{\circ}$ or more.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, if the triangle is big enough.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Assumes that making the triangle physically larger changes the angle sum, rather than recognising that the $180^{\circ}$ angle-sum rule depends only on the triangle being a triangle, not on its size.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the $180^{\circ}$ angle-sum fact for triangles is already available as a reasoning tool (stated as self-evident here, formally justified using symmetry/parallel lines in lesson 4.6), since classifying triangles by angle depends on it.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Add $91^{\circ}+91^{\circ}=182^{\circ}$ explicitly and compare it with the fixed total $180^{\circ}$, to make the contradiction concrete rather than abstract.

theory_blocks.title: A name is just a shortcut for a list of properties
theory_blocks.body:
Every shape is described by a small list of properties: how many sides, which sides are equal or parallel, which angles are equal or right angles.

A name such as 'rhombus' is just a *short way of [[blue:quoting that list]]*. In the exam, marks are given for using the exact vocabulary in a reason ('angles on a straight line', 'the triangle is isosceles'),

so this lesson is the dictionary for the whole Geometry unit — learn the list behind each name and the vocabulary will feel logical rather than like memorisation.

theory_blocks.title: Points, lines, parallel and perpendicular
theory_blocks.body:
A **point** marks a position and has no size. A **line** is straight and extends without end in both directions; a piece of it between two points is a **line segment**.

A **vertex** (plural **vertices**) is a point where two lines or edges meet, such as the corner of a shape.

- **Parallel lines** never meet, however far they are extended; they stay the same distance apart. In diagrams they are marked with matching arrows.
- **Perpendicular lines** meet at a right angle ($90^{\circ}$), marked with a small square.
- A **bearing** is a direction, measured as an angle clockwise from north (developed fully in lesson 4.3).

theory_blocks.title: Naming angles by size
theory_blocks.body:
Angles are named by their size: **acute** ($0^{\circ}<x<90^{\circ}$), **right angle** ($x=90^{\circ}$), **obtuse** ($90^{\circ}<x<180^{\circ}$) and **reflex** ($180^{\circ}<x<360^{\circ}$).

An angle of exactly $180^{\circ}$ is a **straight angle** (a straight line) and one of $360^{\circ}$ is a full turn.

assets.caption: The four named angle sizes, each with its range: acute, right, obtuse and reflex.
assets.purpose: Show the four angle categories on one scale so the acute/obtuse/reflex boundaries are visible as ranges, not isolated examples.

theory_blocks.title: Interior and exterior angles at a vertex add to $180^{\circ}$
theory_blocks.body:
An **interior angle** of a shape lies *inside* it at a vertex; an **exterior angle** is formed outside the shape when one side is extended.

At any vertex, the interior angle and the exterior angle lie on a straight line, so they add up to $180^{\circ}$. This single fact is reused constantly, from classifying angles here to the full polygon-angle rules in lesson 4.6.

assets.caption: The interior and exterior angle at one vertex of a pentagon lie on a straight line, so they add to $180^{\circ}$.
assets.purpose: Make the interior+exterior=180 fact visible at a single vertex before it is reused for the whole-polygon rules in lesson 4.6.

theory_blocks.title: Two common sizing and orientation errors
theory_blocks.body:
- Calling any angle bigger than a right angle 'obtuse'. An obtuse angle is between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$ only; [[orange:a larger angle is reflex]].
- Thinking that parallel lines must look horizontal, or that perpendicular lines must be one horizontal and one vertical. Direction does not matter, only the relationship between the lines.

theory_blocks.title: Triangles: by sides and by angle
theory_blocks.body:
Triangles are classified in two ways: by their *sides* and by an *angle*. **Equilateral** (3 equal sides, and all three angles $60^{\circ}$), **isosceles** (2 equal sides, and the angles opposite the equal sides are also equal), **scalene** (no equal sides) and **right-angled** (one $90^{\circ}$ angle).

A triangle can be both right-angled and isosceles (angles $90^{\circ},45^{\circ},45^{\circ}$) or right-angled and scalene. Equal sides carry the same number of small tick marks on a diagram.

assets.caption: The four triangle classifications: equilateral, isosceles, scalene and right-angled.
assets.purpose: Give a single reference figure for all four triangle names, with tick marks matching the convention used throughout the exercises.

theory_blocks.title: The six special quadrilaterals
theory_blocks.body:
A **quadrilateral** has four straight sides. The six special ones, with ticks for equal sides, arrows for parallel sides and squares for right angles:

| Shape | Sides | Angles and diagonals |
|---|---|---|
| Square | 4 equal sides; opposite sides parallel | four $90^{\circ}$ angles; diagonals equal, bisect each other at $90^{\circ}$ |
| Rectangle | opposite sides equal and parallel | four $90^{\circ}$ angles; diagonals equal and bisect each other |
| Parallelogram | opposite sides equal and parallel | opposite angles equal; diagonals bisect each other |
| Rhombus | 4 equal sides; opposite sides parallel | opposite angles equal; diagonals bisect each other at $90^{\circ}$ |
| Kite | two pairs of equal adjacent sides | one pair of equal opposite angles; diagonals meet at $90^{\circ}$ |
| Trapezium | exactly one pair of parallel sides | no special angle or diagonal property |

The shapes are linked: a square is a special rectangle *and* a special rhombus, and both are special parallelograms. So 'a square is a rectangle' is true, but 'a rectangle is a square' is false.

assets.caption: The six special quadrilaterals: ticks mark equal sides, single and double arrows mark the two pairs of parallel sides, and small squares mark right angles. The rhombus is drawn with angles of 60° and 120°, so it is clearly not a tilted square.
assets.purpose: Give a single reference figure for all six special quadrilaterals using a consistent marking convention.

theory_blocks.title: A trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides
theory_blocks.body: Writing that a trapezium has 'two pairs of parallel sides'. In Cambridge IGCSE a trapezium has *exactly one* pair; a shape with two pairs is a parallelogram.

theory_blocks.title: Polygons: regular and irregular
theory_blocks.body:
A **polygon** is a closed shape with straight sides. A **regular** polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal; otherwise it is **irregular**.

The names come from Greek numbers: *penta* (5), *hexa* (6), *octa* (8), *deca* (10). A triangle and a quadrilateral are the polygons with $3$ and $4$ sides.

The name only counts sides, so an irregular hexagon is still a hexagon even though it does not look like the regular one.

assets.caption: Regular pentagon, hexagon, octagon and decagon, plus an irregular hexagon — still a hexagon, just not regular.
assets.purpose: Show the four named regular polygons together with an irregular example of one of them, so the name/regularity distinction is visible side by side.

theory_blocks.title: Solids: faces, edges and vertices
theory_blocks.body:
A **solid** is a three-dimensional shape. Its flat surfaces are **faces**, the lines where two faces meet are **edges**, and the corners are **vertices**. Curved solids also have a curved surface.

A **prism** has the same cross-section all the way through (a triangular prism has triangles at both ends). A **pyramid** has a polygon base and triangular faces meeting at one vertex (the apex).

A cylinder and a cone have a circular base and a curved surface.

assets.caption: Common 3D solids: cube, cuboid, triangular prism, cylinder, square-based pyramid, cone, sphere, hemisphere and frustum. Dashed lines show hidden edges.
assets.purpose: Give a single reference figure for every solid name needed in the lesson, including the two Extended-only solids (hemisphere, frustum).

theory_blocks.title: A check for flat-faced solids: Euler's formula
theory_blocks.body: For any solid with only flat faces, $V-E+F=2$ (Euler's formula, with $V$ vertices, $E$ edges, $F$ faces). Cuboid: $8-12+6=2$. Pentagonal pyramid: $6-10+6=2$. Use it to check your counts of faces, edges and vertices before moving on.

theory_blocks.title: The vocabulary of a circle
theory_blocks.body:
- **Circumference**: the distance round the circle (also the name of the curve itself).
- **Radius** (plural **radii**): a line from the centre to the circumference. **Diameter**: a chord through the centre; it equals two radii.
- **Chord**: a straight line joining two points on the circumference. **Tangent**: a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point.
- **Arc**: part of the circumference. **Sector**: the region between two radii and an arc. **Segment**: the region between a chord and an arc. **Semicircle**: half a circle, cut by a diameter.

assets.caption: Circle vocabulary: radius, diameter, chord, tangent and circumference (left); sector, segment and arc (right).
assets.purpose: Give one reference figure covering every circle term needed in this lesson and reused throughout the circle-theorem lessons 4.7-4.8.

theory_blocks.title: A strategy for identifying an unknown shape
theory_blocks.body:
To identify an unknown shape, ask in this order: **1.** How many sides? **2.** Are all sides equal, or in equal pairs? **3.** Which sides are parallel? **4.** Are there right angles?

Each answer removes candidates from the list, the same way the worked example 'Name the quadrilateral' narrows from 'four equal sides' down to 'rhombus, not square'.

theory_blocks.title: Plane and perpendicular bisector
theory_blocks.body:
A **plane** is a flat surface that extends without end in all directions, like an infinite sheet of paper; each face of a cuboid lies in a plane.

The **perpendicular bisector** of a line segment $AB$ is the line that cuts $AB$ in half (it *bisects* it) and meets it at a right angle. Every point on this line is the same distance from $A$ as from $B$.

You do not need to construct this line with compasses (the syllabus does not require that construction), but Extended candidates must recognise and use the term.

assets.caption: $AM=MB$ (equal tick marks) and the angle at $M$ is $90^{\circ}$: the red line is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
assets.purpose: Show both defining properties of a perpendicular bisector (bisects, meets at 90 degrees) in a single labelled figure.

theory_blocks.title: Major and minor arc
theory_blocks.body:
A chord divides the circumference into two arcs: the shorter is the **minor arc** and the longer is the **major arc** (a diameter gives two equal semicircular arcs).

Core papers just use the word 'arc'; Extended candidates must distinguish major from minor, since later circle-theorem work (lesson 4.7) depends on knowing which arc an angle is subtended by.

theory_blocks.title: Congruent and similar shapes
theory_blocks.body: **Congruent** shapes are identical copies (they may be turned over or rotated): same shape, same size. **Similar** shapes are enlargements of each other: all angles are equal and all lengths are multiplied by the same number, the **scale factor**. If a rectangle $3\times5$ is enlarged to $6\times10$, the scale factor is $2$. You are never asked to *prove* congruence in this course, but you must use the words correctly; similarity (including the scale factor's effect on area and volume, and proving triangles similar) is developed fully in lesson 4.4.

assets.caption: Congruent shapes (same shape, same size) versus similar shapes (same shape, scale factor $2$ in this example).
assets.purpose: Contrast congruent and similar shapes side by side, directly supporting the related idea.

keywords.definition: A point where two lines, edges or sides meet (plural: vertices).
Lines that never meet and stay the same distance apart, however far extended.
Lines that meet at exactly $90^{\circ}$.
An angle strictly between $180^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$.
A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides.
A quadrilateral with two pairs of equal adjacent sides and diagonals that meet at $90^{\circ}$.
A polygon with all sides equal and all angles equal.
For any flat-faced solid, $V-E+F=2$, where $V$, $E$, $F$ are the numbers of vertices, edges and faces.
A solid with the same cross-section all the way through its length.
A straight line joining two points on the circumference of a circle.
A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point.
The region of a circle between two radii and an arc.
Identical in shape and size (scale factor exactly $1$).
The same shape but a possibly different size, with all lengths multiplied by a fixed scale factor.

worked_examples.statement: Name the quadrilateral. A quadrilateral has four equal sides, opposite sides parallel, no right angles, and its diagonals cross at $90^{\circ}$. Name it and give two facts about its angles.
knowns: Four equal sides, opposite sides parallel
unknowns: The shape's name and two facts about its angles
reasoning: Four equal sides means the shape is a square or a rhombus (the only two special quadrilaterals with all four sides equal).
There are no right angles, so it cannot be a square — that rules out the only other candidate from step 1.
It must be a rhombus, so quote the rhombus angle facts from the table: opposite angles equal, and co-interior angles (between the parallel sides) add to $180^{\circ}$.
worked_examples.solution: It is a **rhombus**. Its opposite angles are equal, and two angles next to each other add up to $180^{\circ}$ (they are co-interior angles between parallel sides).
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the strategy of the related idea in action: each property given in the question removes a candidate name, until only one is left.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Naming it a 'square' because four equal sides is the first property checked, without reading on to the 'no right angles' condition that rules a square out.

worked_examples.statement: Interior and exterior angles. A regular polygon has exterior angles of $45^{\circ}$. Find its interior angle and the number of sides.
unknowns: The interior angle; the number of sides
reasoning: At each vertex the interior and exterior angles lie on a straight line, so interior $=180^{\circ}-45^{\circ}$.
Going once round the polygon turns you through a full turn ($360^{\circ}$ in total), and every turn equals one exterior angle, so the number of sides is $360\div45$.
worked_examples.solution: Interior angle $=180^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=135^{\circ}$. Number of sides $=360\div45=8$: a regular octagon.
worked_examples.interpretation: This 'turning' idea (walking once around the polygon makes one full turn) is only asserted here; it is proved and reused generally for any polygon in lesson 4.6.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing $360^{\circ}$ by the interior angle instead of the exterior angle, which does not correspond to any turning argument and gives a meaningless number of sides.

worked_examples.statement: Faces, edges and vertices. Give the number of faces, edges and vertices of (a) a cuboid, (b) a pentagonal pyramid.
knowns: (b) a pentagonal pyramid has one pentagon base and 5 triangular faces
reasoning: (a) Count the faces directly (6 rectangles). Edges: 4 round the top face, 4 round the bottom face and 4 vertical edges joining them, giving 12. Vertices: 4 on the top and 4 on the bottom, giving 8.
(b) Faces $=1$ base $+5$ triangles $=6$. Edges: 5 around the pentagon base, plus 5 going up to the apex, giving 10. Vertices: 5 base corners plus the apex $=6$.
Check both counts with Euler's formula $V-E+F=2$ before moving on.
worked_examples.interpretation: Counting faces first, then edges in groups (round the base or ends, then the edges joining them or rising to the apex), then vertices, is more reliable than trying to count all three directly from a mental picture of the solid.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting the edges 'going up' from a pyramid's base to its apex, and counting only the base edges — this undercounts $E$ and then fails the Euler's-formula check, which is exactly why the check matters.

worked_examples.statement: Reasoning with radii. $A$ and $B$ are points on a circle with centre $O$ and radius $6$\,cm. The chord $AB$ is also $6$\,cm long. What kind of triangle is $OAB$, and what is angle $AOB$?
unknowns: The type of triangle $OAB$; the size of $\angle AOB$
reasoning: $OA$ and $OB$ are radii of the same circle, so they are automatically equal, and here $AB$ happens to equal that same length too.
All three sides of triangle $OAB$ are equal, which is exactly the definition of equilateral, so all three angles are $60^{\circ}$.
worked_examples.solution: $OAB$ is **equilateral**, and $\angle AOB=60^{\circ}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the first appearance of the 'two radii make an isosceles (here, equilateral) triangle' idea that becomes the single most useful strategy in the circle-theorem lessons 4.7-4.8.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming $\angle AOB=90^{\circ}$ by picturing $A$ and $B$ on a 'typical' diagram, instead of reasoning from the given side lengths.

guided_exercises.statement: A quadrilateral has two pairs of equal adjacent sides and its diagonals meet at $90^{\circ}$, but it has no parallel sides at all. Name it.
hints: Use the four-question strategy: how many sides, which sides are equal, which are parallel, any right angles?
'Two pairs of equal adjacent sides' (not opposite sides) rules out the parallelogram family straight away.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Four sides: a quadrilateral. Equal sides come in two adjacent pairs, not opposite pairs, so it is not a parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus or square (all of those have opposite sides equal). No parallel sides rules out the trapezium. Diagonals meeting at $90^{\circ}$ matches the kite property exactly. It is a kite.
common_errors: Guessing 'rhombus' because both shapes have diagonals meeting at $90^{\circ}$, without checking that a rhombus's equal sides are in opposite pairs, not adjacent pairs.

guided_exercises.statement: A solid has 5 faces (one square and four triangles), 8 edges and 5 vertices. Name the solid and check your faces/edges/vertices count with Euler's formula.
hints: One square base plus four triangular faces meeting at a point is the definition of a particular solid you already know.
Euler's formula is $V-E+F=2$ — substitute the three given numbers in that order.
guided_exercises.answer: A square-based pyramid; $5-8+5=2$, so the count is consistent.
guided_exercises.full_solution: A square base with four triangular faces meeting at one apex is exactly the definition of a square-based pyramid (not a triangular prism, which would have two triangular ends and three rectangular sides instead). Checking: $V-E+F=5-8+5=2$, which matches Euler's formula, so the given counts are internally consistent.
common_errors: Confusing this with a triangular prism because both solids involve triangles — the giveaway is which shape is repeated (one square base here, versus two triangular ends in a prism).

guided_exercises.statement: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $7$\,cm. $P$ and $Q$ are points on the circle with $OP=OQ=PQ$. What is $PQ$, and what kind of triangle is $OPQ$?
hints: $OP$ and $OQ$ are radii, so you already know their length without being told it separately.
If all three sides of a triangle turn out equal, what does that make every angle?
guided_exercises.answer: $PQ=7$\,cm; triangle $OPQ$ is equilateral, with every angle $60^{\circ}$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: $OP$ and $OQ$ are radii of the circle, so $OP=OQ=7$\,cm. The condition $OP=OQ=PQ$ then forces $PQ=7$\,cm as well. All three sides of triangle $OPQ$ are equal, so it is equilateral and every angle (including $\angle POQ$) is $60^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Treating $PQ=7$\,cm as an assumption that needs separate justification, rather than reading it directly off the equation $OP=OQ=PQ$ already given.

exercises.statement: Classify each angle as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex: (a) $35^{\circ}$ (b) $90^{\circ}$ (c) $118^{\circ}$ (d) $180^{\circ}$ (e) $274^{\circ}$.
exercises.full_solution: Compare each value with the four boundaries $0^{\circ},90^{\circ},180^{\circ},360^{\circ}$: (a) $35^{\circ}<90^{\circ}$, acute. (b) exactly $90^{\circ}$, right angle. (c) between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$, obtuse. (d) exactly $180^{\circ}$, straight. (e) between $180^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$, reflex.
common_errors: Calling (e) 'obtuse' because it is a 'big' angle, instead of checking it against the $180^{\circ}$ boundary (see the related idea).

exercises.statement: Name each triangle: (a) sides $6$\,cm, $6$\,cm, $6$\,cm; (b) sides $5$\,cm, $5$\,cm, $7$\,cm; (c) sides $3$\,cm, $4$\,cm, $6$\,cm; (d) angles $90^{\circ}$, $35^{\circ}$, $55^{\circ}$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) all three sides equal: equilateral. (b) exactly two sides equal: isosceles. (c) no two sides equal: scalene. (d) one angle is exactly $90^{\circ}$: right-angled.
common_errors: Trying to classify (d) by its sides when only angles are given — a right-angled triangle is defined by having a $90^{\circ}$ angle, regardless of whether its sides also happen to be equal.

exercises.statement: Name the quadrilateral: (a) four equal sides, no right angles; (b) exactly one pair of parallel sides; (c) two pairs of equal adjacent sides, diagonals meet at $90^{\circ}$; (d) opposite sides equal and parallel, four right angles, not all sides equal.
exercises.full_solution: (a) four equal sides rules in square/rhombus; no right angles rules out the square: rhombus. (b) 'exactly one pair of parallel sides' is the defining property of a trapezium. (c) two pairs of equal *adjacent* sides is the kite property. (d) four right angles with unequal sides rules out the square: rectangle.
common_errors: Answering (b) 'parallelogram', confusing 'exactly one pair' with 'two pairs' of parallel sides (see the related idea).

exercises.statement: How many sides do a pentagon, hexagon, octagon and decagon have?
exercises.full_solution: Pentagon: $5$ sides (penta $=5$). Hexagon: $6$ sides (hexa $=6$). Octagon: $8$ sides (octa $=8$). Decagon: $10$ sides (deca $=10$).
common_errors: Confusing octagon (8 sides) with a shape having 10 sides, by mixing up the Greek prefixes octa- and deca-.

exercises.statement: Name the solid: (a) six square faces; (b) a circular base, a curved surface and one vertex; (c) a square base and four triangular faces; (d) two circular faces and a curved surface.
exercises.full_solution: (a) six identical square faces: cube. (b) one circular base tapering to a single point: cone. (c) a square base with triangular sides meeting at an apex: square-based pyramid. (d) two equal parallel circular ends joined by a curved surface: cylinder.
common_errors: Confusing (b) cone with (d) cylinder by not checking whether the solid tapers to a single vertex (cone) or keeps two equal circular ends (cylinder).

exercises.statement: Write down the number of faces, edges and vertices of (a) a triangular prism; (b) a hexagonal prism. Check each with $V-E+F=2$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Triangular prism: 2 triangular ends $+$ 3 rectangular sides $=5$ faces; 3 edges on each triangular end plus 3 joining edges $=9$ edges; 3 vertices on each end $=6$ vertices. Check: $6-9+5=2$. (b) Hexagonal prism: 2 hexagonal ends $+$ 6 rectangular sides $=8$ faces; $6+6+6=18$ edges; $6+6=12$ vertices. Check: $12-18+8=2$.
common_errors: Forgetting the 'joining' edges between the two end faces of a prism, undercounting $E$ by exactly the number of sides of the cross-section.

exercises.statement: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $9$\,cm. (a) Write down the diameter. (b) What is the length of the longest chord?
exercises.full_solution: (a) Diameter $=2\times$ radius $=2\times9=18$\,cm. (b) The diameter is itself a chord, and it is the longest possible chord in a circle, so the longest chord is also $18$\,cm.
common_errors: Treating 'longest chord' as a separate calculation, rather than recognising it as another name for the diameter already found in part (a).

exercises.statement: A regular polygon has exterior angles of $36^{\circ}$. Find (a) its interior angle; (b) the number of sides.
exercises.full_solution: (a) interior $+$ exterior $=180^{\circ}$ at each vertex, so interior $=180^{\circ}-36^{\circ}=144^{\circ}$. (b) the exterior angles of any polygon add to $360^{\circ}$, so the number of sides is $360\div36=10$.
common_errors: Dividing $360^{\circ}$ by the interior angle ($144^{\circ}$) instead of the exterior angle, which does not correspond to the 'one full turn' argument.

exercises.statement: A tent is a triangular prism. How many faces does it have and how many of them are rectangles?
exercises.answer: $5$ faces; $3$ are rectangles (the $2$ triangular ends are the others).
exercises.full_solution: A triangular prism has 2 triangular end faces and 3 rectangular side faces, giving $2+3=5$ faces in total, of which exactly $3$ are rectangles.
common_errors: Counting the groundsheet of a real tent as a face of the mathematical solid, when the question is only about the prism shape itself.

exercises.statement: Are the rectangles $4\times6$ and $10\times15$ similar? If so give the scale factor.
exercises.full_solution: Compare each pair of corresponding sides as a ratio: $10\div4=2.5$ and $15\div6=2.5$. Both ratios are equal, so all angles (already $90^{\circ}$ in both) and side ratios match: the rectangles are similar with scale factor $2.5$.
common_errors: Checking only one pair of sides and assuming similarity, instead of checking that BOTH ratios agree (see the related idea): for example, $4\times6$ and $8\times10$ give $8\div4=2$ but $10\div6\neq2$, so they are not similar.

exercises.statement: State whether each is true or false, and explain: (a) every square is a rectangle; (b) every rectangle is a rhombus; (c) a trapezium has two pairs of parallel sides.
exercises.full_solution: (a) True: a square has four right angles and opposite sides equal, so it meets every rectangle requirement. (b) False: a $3\times5$ rectangle has unequal adjacent sides, so it fails the rhombus requirement of four equal sides. (c) False: a trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides; two pairs would make it a parallelogram.
common_errors: Answering (c) 'true' by recalling the shape of a trapezium loosely instead of checking the exact definition (see the related idea).

exercises.statement: $A=(1,3)$ and $B=(7,3)$. Write down the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
exercises.full_solution: The midpoint of $AB$ is $\left(\dfrac{1+7}{2},\dfrac{3+3}{2}\right)=(4,3)$. Since $AB$ is horizontal (both points have $y=3$), its perpendicular bisector must be vertical and pass through the midpoint: $x=4$.
common_errors: Writing $y=3$ (the line through $A$ and $B$ itself) instead of the perpendicular line through the midpoint.

exercises.statement: How many flat faces, curved surfaces and edges does (a) a hemisphere have; (b) a frustum of a cone have?
exercises.answer: (a) $1$ flat face, $1$ curved surface, $1$ (circular) edge. (b) $2$ flat faces, $1$ curved surface, $2$ (circular) edges.
exercises.full_solution: (a) A hemisphere is half a sphere cut by a flat plane: it has the one flat circular face from the cut, the curved spherical surface, and one circular edge where they meet. (b) A frustum has its original circular base, plus the smaller circular top left after the cone's point was cut off, so 2 flat faces; the slanted curved surface in between; and 2 circular edges (one at each flat face).
common_errors: Forgetting the smaller top circle of a frustum, counting only the base and the curved surface.

exercises.statement: $A$ and $B$ are on a circle with centre $O$ and $\angle AOB=100^{\circ}$. Which arc $AB$ is the minor arc? What angle at $O$ belongs to the major arc?
exercises.answer: The arc subtending $100^{\circ}$ at $O$ is the minor arc; the angle for the major arc is $260^{\circ}$.
exercises.full_solution: The minor arc is always the shorter of the two arcs, and it is the one 'enclosed' directly by the given angle at the centre, so the $100^{\circ}$ arc is the minor arc. The two arcs together make a full turn at $O$, so the major arc's angle is $360^{\circ}-100^{\circ}=260^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Assuming the major arc's angle at $O$ is simply $180^{\circ}-100^{\circ}=80^{\circ}$ (treating the two arcs as supplementary instead of summing to a full turn).

exercises.statement: A cuboid $ABCDEFGH$ has base $ABCD$ and top $EFGH$, with $E$ above $A$. (a) How many pairs of parallel planes contain its faces? (b) Name the two edges that meet $AB$ at $B$ and are perpendicular to it.
exercises.full_solution: (a) A cuboid has 6 faces in 3 opposite pairs (top/bottom, front/back, left/right), and each pair of opposite faces lies in a pair of parallel planes: 3 pairs. (b) Three edges meet at $B$: $AB$, $BC$ and $BF$. $BC$ is perpendicular to $AB$ because the base $ABCD$ is a rectangle, and $BF$ is perpendicular to $AB$ because the side face $ABFE$ is also a rectangle ($BF$ is vertical and $AB$ is horizontal). So the two edges are $BC$ and $BF$.
common_errors: Naming $AD$ or $AE$, which are perpendicular to $AB$ but meet it at $A$, not at $B$; or naming $CG$ or $DH$, which point in a perpendicular direction but never meet $AB$ (perpendicular lines must meet at $90^{\circ}$).

exercises.statement: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is $156^{\circ}$. Find the number of sides and name the polygon.
exercises.full_solution: Exterior angle $=180^{\circ}-156^{\circ}=24^{\circ}$. Number of sides $=360^{\circ}\div24^{\circ}=15$: a regular pentadecagon.
common_errors: Dividing $360^{\circ}$ by the interior angle ($156^{\circ}$) directly, skipping the conversion to the exterior angle that the 'one full turn' argument actually needs.

exercises.statement: $ABCD$ is a kite with $AB=AD$ and $CB=CD$. $\angle ABC=110^{\circ}$ and $\angle BAD=80^{\circ}$. Find $\angle BCD$, giving a reason.
exercises.full_solution: In a kite with $AB=AD$ and $CB=CD$, the angles at $B$ and $D$ are equal (the pair of 'opposite equal angles' property), so $\angle ADC=\angle ABC=110^{\circ}$. The angles of any quadrilateral add to $360^{\circ}$, so $\angle BCD=360^{\circ}-80^{\circ}-110^{\circ}-110^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Assuming $\angle ADC\ne\angle ABC$ and trying to find it some other way, instead of using the kite's defining 'one pair of equal opposite angles' property directly.

exam_questions.statement:
(a) Name the special quadrilateral that has exactly one pair of equal opposite angles, two pairs of equal adjacent sides and diagonals that meet at $90^{\circ}$. [1]
(b) Write down the number of faces, edges and vertices of a square-based pyramid. [3]
(c) Verify your answer to (b) using Euler's formula. [1]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) The defining properties given (one pair of equal opposite angles, two pairs of equal adjacent sides, diagonals at $90^{\circ}$) match the kite exactly. (b) A square-based pyramid has a square base plus $4$ triangular faces meeting at the apex: $F=1+4=5$; $4$ base edges plus $4$ edges up to the apex: $E=4+4=8$; $4$ base vertices plus the apex: $V=4+1=5$. (c) $V-E+F=5-8+5=2$, which matches Euler's formula, confirming the counts are consistent.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for 'kite'
(b) B1 for $F=5$; B1 for $E=8$; B1 for $V=5$
(c) B1 for correctly substituting into $V-E+F=2$ and confirming the result is $2$
common_errors: In (b), counting only the $4$ base edges and forgetting the $4$ edges running up to the apex, which undercounts $E$ and then fails the check in (c).

exam_questions.statement:
A regular polygon has an exterior angle of $30^{\circ}$.
(a) Find the number of sides of the polygon. [2]
(b) Find the size of each interior angle. [1]
(c) Name the polygon. [1]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) The exterior angles of any polygon add to $360^{\circ}$ and are all equal for a regular polygon, so the number of sides is $360^{\circ}\div30^{\circ}=12$. (b) Interior $+$ exterior $=180^{\circ}$ at each vertex, so interior $=180^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=150^{\circ}$. (c) A $12$-sided polygon is a dodecagon.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for the method $360\div30$; A1 for $12$
(b) B1 for $150^{\circ}$
(c) B1 for 'dodecagon' (accept '12-sided polygon' or '12-gon')
common_errors: In (a), dividing $360^{\circ}$ by the interior angle guessed first instead of by the given exterior angle, producing a non-integer and no valid polygon.

exam_questions.statement:
$A$ and $B$ are points on a circle with centre $O$ and radius $8$\,cm. $OA$, $OB$ and the chord $AB$ are all drawn.
(a) State, with a reason, what kind of triangle $OAB$ must be if $AB=8$\,cm. [2]
(b) $AB$ is now changed so that $AB=11$\,cm instead. State, with a reason, whether $OAB$ is still the same type of triangle. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Equilateral, since $OA=OB=AB=8$\,cm. (b) Isosceles (not equilateral), since $OA=OB=8$\,cm but $AB=11$\,cm is a different length.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $OA$ and $OB$ are radii, so both equal $8$\,cm; if $AB$ is also $8$\,cm, all three sides of triangle $OAB$ are equal, making it equilateral. (b) $OA=OB=8$\,cm still (radii of the same circle never change length), but now $AB=11$\,cm, which is different from the other two sides. Exactly two sides remain equal ($OA=OB$), so the triangle is isosceles but no longer equilateral.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for 'equilateral'; B1 for the reason that all three sides ($OA$, $OB$, $AB$) are equal
(b) B1 for 'isosceles' (not equilateral); B1 for the reason that $OA=OB$ (radii) but $AB$ is a different length
common_errors: In (b), still calling the triangle equilateral because two of the sides (the radii) have not changed, without checking the third side against them.

challenge_questions.statement: Explain why every square is both a rectangle and a rhombus. Which property of a rhombus does a rectangle not always have, and which property of a rectangle does a rhombus not always have?
challenge_questions.answer: A square has four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel (rectangle properties), and four equal sides with opposite sides parallel (rhombus properties). A rectangle does not always have four equal sides; a rhombus does not always have right angles.
challenge_questions.full_solution: A square satisfies the rectangle definition (opposite sides equal and parallel, four right angles) and also the rhombus definition (four equal sides, opposite sides parallel), so it is a special case of both. A general rectangle need not have all four sides equal (the rhombus property it is missing), and a general rhombus need not have any right angles (the rectangle property it is missing). A square is exactly the overlap of the two families.

challenge_questions.statement: A solid has $12$ faces, all pentagons, and $30$ edges. Use Euler's formula to find the number of vertices, and check the number of edges from the faces.
challenge_questions.answer: $V=20$ vertices; the edge count checks out: $12\times5\div2=30$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Euler's formula rearranged: $V=2-F+E=2-12+30=20$. Check from the faces: each of the 12 pentagonal faces has 5 edges, giving $12\times5=60$ edge-sides, but every edge is shared by exactly 2 faces, so the true number of edges is $60\div2=30$, matching the given value. This solid is a (regular) dodecahedron.

challenge_questions.statement: A prism has a regular $n$-sided polygon as its cross-section. Find its numbers of faces, edges and vertices in terms of $n$ and show that Euler's formula always holds.
challenge_questions.answer: $F=n+2$, $E=3n$, $V=2n$; and $V-E+F=2n-3n+(n+2)=2$ for every $n$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Faces: $n$ rectangular side faces plus the $2$ polygon ends, so $F=n+2$. Edges: $n$ edges round each of the two polygon ends ($2n$ total) plus $n$ edges joining corresponding vertices, so $E=2n+n=3n$. Vertices: $n$ on each end, so $V=2n$. Then $V-E+F=2n-3n+(n+2)=(2n-3n+n)+2=0+2=2$, confirming Euler's formula holds for every value of $n$.

challenge_questions.statement: Six chords, each equal in length to the radius, are drawn one after another round a circle of radius $r$, starting at a point $P$ on the circle. Explain why the last chord ends exactly at $P$, and name the polygon formed.
challenge_questions.answer: Each chord subtends $60^{\circ}$ at the centre, and six of them make exactly $360^{\circ}$, so the path closes back at $P$; the figure is a regular hexagon.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Each chord equals the radius, so the triangle it forms with the two radii to its endpoints is equilateral (all three sides $=r$), meaning each chord subtends exactly $60^{\circ}$ at the centre. Six such chords in a row sweep out $6\times60^{\circ}=360^{\circ}$ — a full turn — so the sixth chord's endpoint coincides with the starting point $P$. The resulting closed figure, with six equal sides and (by the same equilateral-triangle argument at every vertex) six equal angles, is a regular hexagon.

challenge_questions.statement: A polygon with $n$ sides has $\tfrac12n(n-3)$ diagonals. Explain where this comes from and find the number of diagonals in a decagon.
challenge_questions.answer: $35$ diagonals in a decagon.
challenge_questions.full_solution: From each vertex you can draw a diagonal to every other vertex except itself and its two neighbours (which are joined by sides, not diagonals): that is $n-3$ diagonals per vertex. Multiplying by all $n$ vertices gives $n(n-3)$, but this counts every diagonal twice (once from each of its two end-vertices), so divide by $2$: $\tfrac12n(n-3)$. For a decagon, $n=10$: $\tfrac12\times10\times7=35$.

challenge_questions.statement: The diagonals of a quadrilateral are equal in length and bisect each other. Show that the quadrilateral must be a rectangle, and explain why it need not be a square.
challenge_questions.answer: Bisecting diagonals force a parallelogram; equal diagonals then force right angles, giving a rectangle, which need not have all sides equal.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Let the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $M$. They bisect each other and are equal in length, so all four halves are equal: $MA=MB=MC=MD$. Triangle $MAB$ is isosceles, so $\angle MAB=\angle MBA=p$; triangle $MBC$ is isosceles, so $\angle MCB=\angle MBC=q$. In triangle $ABC$ the angles are $\angle BAC=p$, $\angle BCA=q$ and $\angle ABC=p+q$, so $p+q+(p+q)=180^{\circ}$, giving $\angle ABC=p+q=90^{\circ}$. The same argument works at every vertex, so all four angles are right angles and the shape is a rectangle. It could still have unequal adjacent sides (for example a $3\times5$ rectangle satisfies both conditions), so it is not necessarily a square — only a rectangle with the EXTRA condition of equal adjacent sides is a square.

mcq.stem: An angle measures $274^{\circ}$. What type of angle is it?

options.text: Obtuse
options.why_wrong: Obtuse only covers $90^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$; $274^{\circ}$ is well past that upper boundary.

options.text: Reflex
Acute
options.why_wrong: Acute means less than $90^{\circ}$; $274^{\circ}$ is far larger than this.

options.text: A straight angle
options.why_wrong: A straight angle is exactly $180^{\circ}$; $274^{\circ}$ is neither equal to this nor close to it conceptually (it is well into the reflex range).

mcq.explanation: $274^{\circ}$ lies between $180^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$, which is exactly the definition of a reflex angle.

mcq.stem: A quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides. What is it called?

options.text: Parallelogram
options.why_wrong: A parallelogram has TWO pairs of parallel sides, not one; this is the opposite of the given condition.

options.text: Kite
options.why_wrong: A kite is defined by two pairs of equal adjacent sides, not by having any parallel sides at all.

options.text: Trapezium
Rhombus
options.why_wrong: A rhombus has two pairs of parallel sides (it is a special parallelogram), not exactly one.

mcq.explanation: 'Exactly one pair of parallel sides' is the defining property of a trapezium in Cambridge IGCSE.

mcq.stem: A solid is claimed to have $7$ faces, $15$ edges and $11$ vertices. According to Euler's formula, is this count possible for a flat-faced solid?

options.text: Yes, because $F+E+V=33$ is a whole number
options.why_wrong: Euler's formula is $V-E+F=2$, not a condition on the SUM $F+E+V$; being a whole number proves nothing about consistency.

options.text: Yes, because every solid satisfies Euler's formula regardless of the numbers given
options.why_wrong: Euler's formula is a genuine check that specific numbers must pass; substituting these three values gives $3$, not $2$, so this particular triple is not realisable.

options.text: No, because the solid must have exactly $6$ faces like a cube
options.why_wrong: There is no rule that every solid has $6$ faces; cubes do, but prisms, pyramids and others have different counts that still satisfy Euler's formula — the real problem here is the substitution, not the face count alone.

options.text: No, because $11-15+7=3$, not $2$

mcq.explanation: Substituting into $V-E+F$ gives $11-15+7=3$, which does not equal $2$, so this combination of faces, edges and vertices cannot belong to a real flat-faced solid.

mcq.stem: $AB$ is a chord of a circle with centre $O$ and radius $5$\,cm, with $AB=5$\,cm. What type of triangle is $OAB$?

options.text: Equilateral
Right-angled
options.why_wrong: Nothing in the given information states a $90^{\circ}$ angle; assuming one ignores that all three sides are actually equal.

options.text: Scalene
options.why_wrong: Scalene means no two sides equal, but here $OA=OB=AB=5$\,cm — all three sides ARE equal.

options.text: Cannot be determined without more information
options.why_wrong: $OA$ and $OB$ are always equal (radii), and here $AB$ is also given as $5$\,cm, so the triangle type is fully determined.

mcq.explanation: $OA=OB=5$\,cm (radii) and $AB=5$\,cm (given), so all three sides of triangle $OAB$ are equal: it is equilateral.

mcq.stem: Shape $P$ is an exact copy of shape $Q$, just rotated. Shape $R$ is shape $Q$ enlarged by scale factor $3$. Which statement is correct?

options.text: $P$ and $Q$ are similar but not congruent; $Q$ and $R$ are congruent
options.why_wrong: This swaps the two relationships: an exact rotated copy ($P$,$Q$) IS congruent (scale factor $1$), while an enlargement by $3$ ($Q$,$R$) is similar but NOT congruent, since the sizes differ.

options.text: $P$ and $Q$ are congruent; $Q$ and $R$ are similar but not congruent
$P$ and $Q$ are neither congruent nor similar; $Q$ and $R$ are congruent
options.why_wrong: An exact rotated copy is always both congruent AND similar (congruent is a special case of similar with scale factor 1), so 'neither' is wrong for $P$ and $Q$.

options.text: $P$, $Q$ and $R$ are all congruent to each other
options.why_wrong: $R$ is three times the size of $Q$, so it cannot be congruent to $Q$ (congruent shapes must be the same size, not just the same shape).

mcq.explanation: A rotated exact copy has scale factor $1$: congruent (and trivially similar too). An enlargement by $3$ changes the size, so it is similar but not congruent.

mcq.stem: Two straight lines are drawn on a page, one tilted at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal and the other tilted at $60^{\circ}$ to the horizontal but on the other side, so that they meet at exactly $90^{\circ}$. What is the relationship between the two lines?

options.text: Not perpendicular, because neither line is horizontal or vertical
options.why_wrong: Perpendicular only requires the two lines to meet at $90^{\circ}$; their orientation relative to the page (horizontal/vertical) is irrelevant.

options.text: Parallel
options.why_wrong: Parallel lines never meet; these two lines are explicitly stated to meet at $90^{\circ}$, so they cannot be parallel.

options.text: Perpendicular
Neither parallel nor perpendicular, since they are both tilted
options.why_wrong: Being tilted (not axis-aligned) does not prevent two lines from being perpendicular; only the $90^{\circ}$ angle between them matters.

mcq.explanation: Two lines meeting at exactly $90^{\circ}$ are perpendicular by definition, regardless of how they are oriented on the page.

flashcards.front: What is an obtuse angle?
flashcards.back: An angle strictly between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$.

flashcards.front: Obtuse vs. reflex — what's the actual boundary?
flashcards.back: Obtuse: between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$. Reflex: between $180^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$. The boundary is $180^{\circ}$, not 'looks big'.

flashcards.front: True or false: perpendicular lines must be one horizontal and one vertical.
flashcards.back: False. Perpendicular only means 'meets at $90^{\circ}$' — the orientation of the pair on the page is irrelevant.

flashcards.front: True or false: a trapezium has two pairs of parallel sides.
flashcards.back: False. A trapezium has exactly ONE pair; two pairs makes it a parallelogram instead.

flashcards.front: Name the six special quadrilaterals.
flashcards.back: Square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, kite, trapezium.

flashcards.front: Euler's formula for a flat-faced solid
flashcards.back: $V-E+F=2$, with $V$ vertices, $E$ edges, $F$ faces.

flashcards.front: Prism vs. pyramid — what's the structural difference?
flashcards.back: Prism: same cross-section all the way through (two identical parallel ends). Pyramid: tapers from a polygon base to a single apex.

flashcards.front: Chord vs. diameter of a circle
flashcards.back: A chord joins any two points on the circumference. A diameter is the special chord that passes through the centre — it is also the longest possible chord.

flashcards.front: Congruent vs. similar — what's the key difference?
flashcards.back: Congruent: same shape AND same size (scale factor $1$). Similar: same shape, scale factor can be anything — congruent is just the special case $k=1$ of similar.

flashcards.front: True or false: congruent and similar mean the same thing.
flashcards.back: False. Every congruent pair is similar (with scale factor $1$), but a similar pair with a scale factor other than $1$ is NOT congruent.

flashcards.front: Two radii and a third side of known length — what triangle type should you check for?
flashcards.back: Isosceles automatically (the two radii are always equal); check whether the third side also matches the radius to see if it's equilateral.

flashcards.front: What does 'regular' mean for a polygon?
flashcards.back: All sides equal AND all angles equal (both conditions are needed).

flashcards.front: You are told a polygon's number of sides $n$. How do you get its exterior and interior angles if it's regular?
flashcards.back: Exterior $=360^{\circ}\div n$; interior $=180^{\circ}-$ exterior.

flashcards.front: Sector vs. segment of a circle
flashcards.back: Sector: region between two radii and an arc. Segment: region between a chord and an arc.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any angle that looks 'big' or is bigger than a right angle is called obtuse, including angles that are actually reflex.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners first meet 'obtuse' as meaning 'bigger than a right angle' and never revisit the upper limit once they move on to angles bigger than $180^{\circ}$, so the category silently expands to cover every large angle.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner labels a $250^{\circ}$ or $274^{\circ}$ angle as 'obtuse' instead of 'reflex', or hesitates to use the word 'reflex' at all.
misconceptions.correct_model: Obtuse means strictly between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$. Once an angle passes $180^{\circ}$ it becomes reflex (between $180^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$); the two categories do not overlap, and there is no 'extra obtuse' category beyond $180^{\circ}$.
misconceptions.remediation: Draw a single angle scale from $0^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$ marked with the four named regions, and classify several angles (including ones close to $180^{\circ}$ and close to $360^{\circ}$) by locating them on the scale rather than by eye.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Parallel lines must be drawn horizontally (or both the same way), and perpendicular lines must be exactly one horizontal and one vertical.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The first examples of parallel and perpendicular lines a learner sees are almost always axis-aligned (ruled paper, graph axes), so the visual orientation gets bundled into the definition instead of being irrelevant to it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner denies that two slanted lines with matching arrow marks are parallel, or denies that two slanted lines meeting at a marked right angle are perpendicular, purely because neither line is horizontal.
misconceptions.correct_model: Parallel means 'never meeting, same distance apart however far extended' and perpendicular means 'meeting at exactly $90^{\circ}$' — both are relationships between the two lines only, completely independent of how the whole pair is rotated on the page.
misconceptions.remediation: Take a confirmed pair of horizontal/vertical perpendicular lines and mentally (or physically) rotate the whole diagram by $30^{\circ}$; ask whether the relationship between the two lines has changed (it hasn't) even though neither line is now axis-aligned.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A trapezium has two pairs of parallel sides, like a parallelogram, just with unequal lengths.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: In everyday language 'trapezoid-shaped' objects are sometimes drawn close to parallelogram-like, and the word 'trapezium' sounds like it should describe a 'wonkier parallelogram' rather than a genuinely different category with only one pair of parallel sides.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a trapezium as having 'two pairs of parallel sides' or cannot tell a trapezium apart from a parallelogram when both are drawn without arrow marks.
misconceptions.correct_model: In Cambridge IGCSE, a trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides; a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides is, by definition, a parallelogram (and every rectangle, rhombus and square is a parallelogram too). 'Exactly one pair' is what makes the trapezium its own category.
misconceptions.remediation: Mark the parallel sides of a trapezium with a single arrow type and show that the other pair of sides, if extended, eventually meet — which a true parallel pair never does — then repeat with a parallelogram where both pairs, when extended, never meet.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Congruent and similar both just mean 'the same shape', so the two words are interchangeable.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both words describe shapes that 'match' in some sense, and everyday English rarely distinguishes between 'identical' and 'the same shape but a different size', so the precise mathematical boundary between the two words is easy to blur.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner calls two shapes 'congruent' when one is clearly an enlargement of the other, or says 'similar' when describing two identical cut-out shapes.
misconceptions.correct_model: Congruent shapes are identical in shape AND size (scale factor exactly $1$, possibly after a rotation, reflection or translation). Similar shapes have the same shape but a different size (scale factor $k\neq1$ in general); every pair of congruent shapes is also similar (with $k=1$), but not every pair of similar shapes is congruent.
misconceptions.remediation: Place a shape, an identical copy of it, and a $\times2$ enlargement of it side by side; sort the three into pairs and name each relationship (congruent for the identical pair, similar — but not congruent — for every pair involving the enlargement).

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling every angle bigger than $90^{\circ}$ 'obtuse', including ones that are actually reflex (past $180^{\circ}$).
common_mistakes.why: Obtuse is the first 'large angle' category learners meet, so it is sometimes applied to any angle that merely looks big.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always check against $180^{\circ}$ before deciding: obtuse stops at $180^{\circ}$, and anything beyond that (up to $360^{\circ}$) is reflex.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the edges that join the two ends of a prism or pyramid when counting $E$.
common_mistakes.why: It is easy to count the edges visible 'around' the two flat ends of a solid and overlook the edges running lengthwise or up to the apex.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Count faces, then edges by tracing systematically round each face boundary, then vertices; finally check the three numbers with $V-E+F=2$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Naming a shape from only the first property checked (e.g. 'four equal sides → square') without checking the remaining properties given.
common_mistakes.why: Several special quadrilaterals share the 'four equal sides' property (square and rhombus), so stopping after one property can pick the wrong one.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Work through all four questions of the identification strategy (sides, equal sides, parallel sides, right angles) before committing to a name.

exam_notes: When a question says 'give a reason', the exact vocabulary word (e.g. 'isosceles', 'perpendicular', 'tangent') IS the reason — a correct calculation with the wrong or missing word loses the reason mark even if the number is right.
'Describe' a shape by quoting its defining properties ('four equal sides, no right angles'), not just its name; 'name' and 'write down' want only the term with no working.

Diagrams in the exam are very often marked 'not drawn accurately' — trust the given marks (ticks, arrows, right-angle squares) and given numbers, never a ruler or protractor held up to the printed page.
When Euler's formula is used to 'check' an answer, show the substitution explicitly (e.g. '$8-12+6=2$') — simply writing 'checks out' with no numbers shown does not earn the check mark.

summary.big_idea: A geometric name is shorthand for a short checklist of properties (number of sides, which sides/angles are equal, which are parallel or right angles); once that checklist is known for each shape, solid and circle part, naming and reasoning about them both become mechanical rather than memorised.
key_points: Angles: acute $<90^{\circ}$, right $=90^{\circ}$, obtuse $90^{\circ}$-$180^{\circ}$, reflex $180^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$; interior $+$ exterior $=180^{\circ}$ at a vertex.
Triangles by sides/angle: equilateral, isosceles, scalene, right-angled. Quadrilaterals: square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, kite, trapezium (exactly one pair of parallel sides).
Solids: $V-E+F=2$ for flat-faced solids; prism (constant cross-section) vs. pyramid (tapers to an apex).
Circle vocabulary: radius, diameter ($=2r$), chord, tangent, arc, sector, segment — reused throughout the circle-theorem lessons 4.7-4.8.
Congruent (same shape AND size) is the special case of similar (same shape, scale factor $k$) where $k=1$.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Identify any shape, solid or circle part by checking its defining properties one at a time (sides, equal/parallel sides, right angles for 2D; faces/edges/vertices and Euler's formula for 3D), rather than by appearance alone — and always state the exact vocabulary word when a reason is asked for.
