options.why_wrong: Like option B, this uses drawn position rather than the actual geometric correspondence (matching angles), which is unreliable once a shape is rotated or reflected.

options.text: By comparing the two longest sides, whichever triangle they belong to
options.why_wrong: The longest side of one triangle does correspond to the longest side of a similar triangle, but 'longest side' is really just a special case of the angle-opposite rule (the side opposite the LARGEST angle) — stated this way it misses the general rule for any pair of sides, not just the longest.

mcq.explanation: Corresponding sides are always the ones opposite matching (equal) angles, regardless of how the shape has been rotated, reflected or redrawn on the page.

mcq.stem: Two similar solids have a length scale factor $k=5$. The smaller solid has volume $10$\,cm$^3$. What is the volume of the larger solid?

options.why_wrong: This multiplies the volume by $k=5$ directly, treating volume as if it scaled like a length rather than like $k^3$.
This multiplies by $k^2=25$ (the AREA scale factor) instead of $k^3=125$ (the volume scale factor).
This adds $k=5$ to the volume ($10+5$) rather than using $k$ as a multiplying factor at all.

mcq.explanation: Volume scales by $k^3=5^3=125$, so the larger volume is $10\times125=1250$\,cm$^3$.

mcq.stem: In a 'show that two triangles are similar' exam answer, which response would earn full marks for the angle-equality step $\angle ADE=\angle ABC$?

options.text: $\angle ADE=\angle ABC$ (they look the same size in the diagram)
options.why_wrong: A visual impression from a diagram is not a valid geometric reason; diagrams in exam questions may not even be drawn to scale.

options.text: $\angle ADE=\angle ABC$ (no reason given)
options.why_wrong: Stating the equality without its geometric reason loses the reasoning mark, even though the equality itself is correct.

options.text: $\angle ADE=\angle ABC$ (corresponding angles, $DE\parallel BC$)
$\angle ADE=\angle ABC$ (both triangles are similar)
options.why_wrong: This reverses the logic: similarity is the CONCLUSION that follows once the angle equalities are established, not a reason that can be used to justify one of those equalities.

mcq.explanation: A valid 'show that' step always states the equality together with its specific geometric reason — here, 'corresponding angles, $DE\parallel BC$'.

mcq.stem: Which pair of shapes is definitely congruent, not just similar?

options.text: Two triangles with the same three angles but different side lengths
options.why_wrong: Same angles but different side lengths means the triangles are similar (scale factor $k\neq1$) but NOT congruent — congruent requires identical size as well as shape.

options.text: Two rectangles with the same area
options.why_wrong: Equal area does not mean equal shape or equal side lengths (e.g. a $2\times8$ and a $4\times4$ rectangle both have area $16$ but are not the same shape at all).

options.text: Two circles with different radii
options.why_wrong: Circles with different radii are similar (all circles are similar) but not congruent, since congruent requires the same size too.

options.text: Two triangles with scale factor $k=1$ between them

mcq.explanation: A scale factor of exactly $k=1$ means every corresponding length is identical, so the two shapes are congruent — identical in shape AND size.

flashcards.front: What does it mean for two shapes to be similar?
flashcards.back: Corresponding angles are equal, AND corresponding sides are all in the same ratio (the scale factor $k$).

flashcards.front: True or false: for ANY two shapes, equal corresponding angles is enough to prove they are similar.
flashcards.back: False. This shortcut only works for TRIANGLES; for any shape with more sides, the side ratios must also be checked.

flashcards.front: Scale factor formula
flashcards.back: $k=\dfrac{\text{length in the new shape}}{\text{corresponding length in the original}}$.
$k>1$: enlargement. $0<k<1$: reduction. $k=1$: congruent (identical in shape and size).

flashcards.front: Similar vs. congruent
flashcards.back: Similar: same shape, any size (scale factor $k$). Congruent: same shape AND same size (scale factor exactly $k=1$) — congruent is a special case of similar.

flashcards.front: True or false: in nested similar triangles, a part of a split side (like $DB$) can be used directly as if it were the whole side ($AB$).
flashcards.back: False. Always add up the parts to get the whole side ($AB=AD+DB$) before using it in the scale factor.

flashcards.front: Length, area and volume scale factors, for the same $k$
flashcards.back: Length ratio $=k$. Area ratio (incl. surface area) $=k^2$. Volume ratio $=k^3$.

flashcards.front: Working BACKWARDS from an area or volume ratio to $k$
flashcards.back: From an area ratio $A_1:A_2$: $k=\sqrt{A_2/A_1}$. From a volume ratio $V_1:V_2$: $k=\sqrt[3]{V_2/V_1}$.

flashcards.front: True or false: if a solid's length scale factor is $k$, its mass (same material) also scales by $k$.
flashcards.back: False. Mass (for the same material) scales like volume, by $k^3$, not by $k$.

flashcards.front: Four standard reasons for a pair of equal angles, used to prove similarity
flashcards.back: Common angle; vertically opposite angles; corresponding or alternate angles (parallel lines); a right angle in both triangles.

flashcards.front: Why are two pairs of equal angles enough to prove two triangles similar?
flashcards.back: Because a triangle's angles sum to $180^{\circ}$: once two pairs match, the third pair must match too (each is $180^{\circ}$ minus the same two angles).

flashcards.front: Shadows, parallel-line-in-a-triangle, and crossing-lines configurations — what do they all have in common?
flashcards.back: Each creates a pair of similar triangles from parallel lines (shadows: parallel sun's rays; triangle: a line parallel to one side; crossing lines: two parallel lines cut by a transversal), via corresponding or alternate angles.

flashcards.front: Quick sense-check for any similarity calculation
flashcards.back: Is the shape getting bigger or smaller? Check the calculated answer agrees with whether $k$ is above or below $1$.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: If two shapes have all equal corresponding angles, they must be similar, whatever shape they are.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: For TRIANGLES this statement happens to be true (and is explicitly taught as a shortcut), so it feels natural to extend the same rule to any polygon.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner claims a $2\times6$ rectangle and a $4\times6$ rectangle are similar because both have four right angles, without checking the side ratios.
misconceptions.correct_model: For a general shape, similarity needs BOTH conditions: equal corresponding angles AND all corresponding sides in the same ratio. Only for triangles does equal angles alone force equal side ratios too (because fixing a triangle's three angles fixes its shape completely) — for any shape with more sides, angles alone leave the side lengths free to vary independently.
misconceptions.remediation: Always check which type of shape is being compared before deciding which similarity condition applies; for anything other than a triangle, check the side ratios explicitly, even when the angles already match.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: In a pair of nested similar triangles (one triangle sitting inside a larger one sharing a vertex), the extra segment added on beyond the small triangle (such as $DB$) is the side of the large triangle that corresponds to the small triangle's side (such as $AD$).
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The inner segment and the outer side both start at the same shared vertex and point in the same direction, so without carefully tracking which triangle each length actually belongs to, it is easy to treat the part and the whole as interchangeable.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner pairs $DB=6$ (only the part of $AB$ beyond $D$) with $AD=4$ when setting up the scale factor between triangles $ADE$ and $ABC$, instead of using the full side $AB=10$.
misconceptions.correct_model: The two similar triangles are $ADE$ (the small one: sides $AD$, $DE$, $AE$) and $ABC$ (the large one: sides $AB$, $BC$, $AC$). The scale factor must use the WHOLE corresponding side of each triangle: $AB=AD+DB=4+6=10$\,cm corresponds to $AD=4$\,cm, not $DB=6$\,cm.
misconceptions.remediation: Before calculating, write out explicitly which triangle each labelled point belongs to, and add up any split side (like $AB=AD+DB$) to get the whole length before using it in the scale factor.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Corresponding sides of two similar shapes are the ones drawn in the same position on the page (e.g. both on the left, or both on the top).
misconceptions.why_it_appears: In a simple, non-rotated diagram the position on the page often does line up with the correct correspondence, so position can seem like a reliable shortcut until a rotated or reflected shape breaks the pattern.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner pairs sides by their position in the drawing rather than by the equal angles opposite them, giving a wrong scale factor whenever one triangle is rotated or reflected relative to the other.
misconceptions.correct_model: Corresponding sides are the ones OPPOSITE equal (matching) angles — or equivalently, the sides joining vertices with the same letter under the stated correspondence (e.g. $P\leftrightarrow A$). This works regardless of how the shape has been rotated, reflected or redrawn.
misconceptions.remediation: Always identify corresponding sides by tracking the equal angles (or the stated vertex correspondence), never by the drawn position on the page; redraw the two shapes separately in the same orientation if the original diagram is confusing.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: When a length scale factor is $k$, the area and the volume of a similar shape or solid also scale by $k$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A single number $k$ describes 'how much bigger' the new shape is, and that single number feels like it should apply uniformly to any measurement taken from the shape, whether it is a length, an area or a volume.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner multiplies an $18$\,cm$^2$ area directly by $k=2.5$ to get a 'new area' of $45$\,cm$^2$, instead of by $k^2=6.25$ to get $112.5$\,cm$^2$.
misconceptions.correct_model: Area is built from TWO lengths multiplied together, so it scales by $k^2$; volume is built from THREE lengths multiplied together, so it scales by $k^3$. Only a genuine length (including a perimeter, a height, or a radius) scales by $k$ itself.
misconceptions.remediation: Before scaling any quantity, ask 'is this a length, an area, or a volume?' and apply $k$, $k^2$, or $k^3$ accordingly — never assume $k$ applies by default.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: 'Similar' and 'congruent' describe the same relationship between two shapes — both just mean 'the same shape'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Congruent shapes ARE similar (with scale factor exactly $1$), so the two ideas genuinely overlap at that boundary case, and everyday English uses 'similar' loosely to mean 'alike' without distinguishing size at all.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes two shapes of clearly different sizes as 'congruent' because they have the same shape, or assumes a 'similar' shape must be exactly the same size as the original.
misconceptions.correct_model: Similar shapes have the SAME shape (equal angles, proportional sides) but may be different sizes (scale factor $k\neq1$ allowed). Congruent shapes are a special case of similar shapes where the scale factor is exactly $k=1$: identical in both shape AND size.
misconceptions.remediation: Treat 'congruent' as 'similar with $k=1$', and always check whether a question is asking about shape only (similar) or shape AND size (congruent) before answering.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dividing when the scale factor should be used to multiply (or vice versa).
common_mistakes.why: Both operations appear in the method (one direction for small-to-big, the other for big-to-small), so it is easy to apply the wrong one under time pressure.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before calculating, ask: is the answer expected to be bigger or smaller than the known length? An enlargement must give a bigger answer; use this as an automatic check.

common_mistakes.mistake: Omitting the geometric reason (e.g. 'corresponding angles, $DE\parallel BC$') next to a stated angle equality in a 'show that' proof.
common_mistakes.why: The equality itself can feel like the complete answer, especially once it is visually obvious from a diagram, making the reason feel redundant to write out.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Treat every angle equality in a proof as incomplete without its named reason written immediately next to it; practise writing the reason as part of the same line, not as an afterthought.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to convert units before forming a scale factor (e.g. dividing a length in metres by one in centimetres directly).
common_mistakes.why: The ratio calculation itself still produces a number even with mismatched units, so there is no obvious arithmetic error to signal the mistake.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always convert both lengths to the SAME unit before dividing to find $k$, exactly as for scale-drawing calculations in lesson 4.3.

exam_notes: In 'show that' questions, each statement of equality needs its reason next to it, in words: 'common angle', 'vertically opposite', 'corresponding angles', 'alternate angles'.
Diagrams may not be to scale, so trust the given information and marks (such as arrows for parallel lines), not visual impression.
Give the scale factor as a fraction or exact decimal when possible, and round other answers to $3$ significant figures unless told otherwise.
Core papers only ask for lengths in similar figures; questions on areas, volumes, masses and 'show that' proofs of similarity are Extended only.

summary.big_idea: Similarity is 'same shape, any size': once the single number $k$ (the scale factor) is found from one pair of corresponding lengths, every other length follows by multiplying or dividing by $k$ — and, in Extended work, areas follow by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$, because an area is built from two lengths and a volume from three.
key_points: Similar shapes have equal corresponding angles and all sides in the same ratio $k$; for triangles, equal angles alone are enough.
Find $k$ from a pair of corresponding sides where BOTH lengths are known, then multiply (small to big) or divide (big to small).
Use the WHOLE corresponding side in nested similar triangles, not just a part of a split side.
Lengths scale by $k$, areas (and surface areas) by $k^2$, volumes (and masses, same material) by $k^3$; working backwards, $k=\sqrt{\text{area ratio}}=\sqrt[3]{\text{volume ratio}}$.

To prove two triangles similar, name a geometric reason (common angle, vertically opposite, corresponding/alternate angles, or a shared right angle) for each of two pairs of equal angles; the third pair then follows automatically.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Find $k$ from one trustworthy pair of corresponding lengths, use the WHOLE side (not a part) in nested triangles, and remember that only a genuine length scales by $k$ itself — an area needs $k^2$ and a volume needs $k^3$.

05_Symmetry.json.title: Symmetry
05_Symmetry.json.subject: Mathematics

objectives.statement: Draw all the lines of symmetry of a 2D shape and state how many it has.
State the order of rotational symmetry of a 2D shape, where order $1$ means no (non-trivial) rotational symmetry.
Use symmetry to explain properties of special triangles, quadrilaterals and regular polygons (e.g. equal base angles, perpendicular diagonals).
Identify planes of symmetry and axes of symmetry, with their order, of prisms, cylinders, pyramids and cones.

prerequisites.statement: Name and recognise common 2D shapes: triangle types, special quadrilaterals, and regular polygons (lesson 4.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every statement in this lesson ('a rhombus has 2 lines of symmetry', 'a kite has order 1') refers to these shapes by name; without the vocabulary secure, the statements have nothing to attach to.

prerequisites.statement: Plot coordinate points, find the gradient between two points, and find the distance between two points.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The 'completing a symmetric shape' worked example uses all three skills directly: finding the mirror line's equation from a gradient, reflecting a point in that line, and checking the result with a distance calculation.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise common 3D solids by name: prisms, cylinders, pyramids and cones (lesson 4.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The Extended section names and counts planes/axes for exactly these solids; without the solids already named and pictured correctly, 'a plane parallel to the circular ends' has no solid to attach to.

prerequisites.statement: Know that a full turn is $360^{\circ}$ and a right angle is $90^{\circ}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The order of rotational symmetry is defined directly in terms of $360^{\circ}$ (smallest fitting turn $=360^{\circ}\div n$), and several exercises work backwards from a given angle to find $n$.

diagnostic_items.question: A shape has rotational symmetry of order $6$. What is the smallest angle through which it can be turned to fit onto itself?

common_wrong_answers.answer: $6^{\circ}$, or some other value not derived from dividing $360^{\circ}$ by the order.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Does not connect 'order' to the specific formula smallest angle $=360^{\circ}\div n$, and instead guesses a number loosely related to $6$.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: A direct check of the central formula linking order and angle.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Have the learner state the formula out loud before substituting: 'smallest turn equals a full turn divided by the order'.

diagnostic_items.question: Why is a diagonal of a rectangle (which is not a square) not a line of symmetry?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Folding along the diagonal does not make the two halves coincide: the two corners at the ends of the OTHER diagonal do not land on top of each other, because the other diagonal is not perpendicular to the fold line (the diagonals of a non-square rectangle do not meet at $90^{\circ}$). The diagonal does divide the rectangle into two congruent triangles, but they are related by a half-turn (rotation), not by a reflection.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It should be a line of symmetry, since it splits the rectangle into two identical (congruent) triangles.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Confuses 'splits into two congruent pieces' with 'splits into two mirror-image pieces' — congruence alone does not guarantee the two pieces are related by a REFLECTION rather than a rotation.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This is the single most important conceptual check of the Line symmetry section: congruent pieces are not automatically mirror-image pieces.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Physically fold a rectangle (not a square) along a diagonal and show the overhanging corners directly, then contrast with folding a square along its diagonal, where the corners DO coincide.

diagnostic_items.question: Can a shape have rotational symmetry but no line symmetry? Give an example.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Yes: a parallelogram (rotational symmetry order $2$, no lines of symmetry), or a letter such as S or N drawn in a simple sans-serif form.

common_wrong_answers.answer: No, a shape with rotational symmetry must always have at least one line of symmetry too.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Assumes the two types of symmetry are linked (one implies the other), when in fact they are independent properties that can occur in any combination.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that line symmetry and rotational symmetry are understood as two genuinely INDEPENDENT properties, not as one guaranteeing the other.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Point directly at a parallelogram: rotate it $180^{\circ}$ and show it fits back onto itself (rotational symmetry), then try every candidate fold line and show none of them work (no line symmetry).

diagnostic_items.question: How many lines of symmetry and what order of rotational symmetry does a regular $12$-sided polygon have?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $12$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $12$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Some number other than $12$ for one or both, guessed without applying the 'regular $n$-gon has $n$ lines and order $n$' rule.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Does not apply the general rule for regular polygons directly, perhaps because a $12$-sided shape is harder to visualise than a square or a pentagon.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the general rule for regular polygons (both lines and order equal to $n$) transfers to an unfamiliar, larger value of $n$, not just the small examples seen in the table.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write out the rule explicitly: 'a regular $n$-gon has exactly $n$ lines of symmetry AND rotational symmetry of order $n$', then substitute $n=12$.

diagnostic_items.question: Why does a cone have infinitely many planes of symmetry but a square-based pyramid only four?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: A cone's base is a circle, which has infinitely many lines of symmetry (any diameter), so every plane through the cone's axis is a plane of symmetry — infinitely many. A square-based pyramid's base is a square, which has only $4$ lines of symmetry, so there are only $4$ vertical planes through the apex (one for each line of symmetry of the square base).

common_wrong_answers.answer: Because a cone is a 'rounder' or 'smoother' shape than a pyramid, so it naturally has more symmetry.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Gives a vague visual impression ('rounder', 'smoother') instead of connecting the solid's planes of symmetry directly to the number of lines of symmetry of its base, which is the actual reason.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the central Extended idea that a solid's vertical planes of symmetry come directly from the lines of symmetry of its base — a circle's infinitely many lines of symmetry is the reason a cone has infinitely many planes.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Have the learner state the general rule first ('count the lines of symmetry of the base') and then apply it to both the circle (infinite) and the square ($4$) before comparing.

theory_blocks.title: Symmetry is a movement that leaves the shape exactly where it was
theory_blocks.body:
A symmetry is a movement that leaves the shape *[[blue:exactly where it was]]*. A reflection swaps the two halves of the shape; a rotation carries the shape onto itself before it has turned a full circle.

Symmetry is not only decoration: because the two halves (or positions) are identical, equal sides and equal angles come for free,

and many geometric facts (for example that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal) are simply consequences of symmetry.

theory_blocks.title: Line symmetry
theory_blocks.body:
A 2D shape has **line symmetry** (reflection symmetry) if a straight line, the **line of symmetry** or mirror line, divides it into two parts that are mirror images of each other.

If the shape is folded along this line, the two halves fit exactly on top of each other. Every point of the shape is the same perpendicular distance from the mirror line as its image.

theory_blocks.title: Finding lines of symmetry
theory_blocks.body:
For each candidate line, imagine folding along it and check that every vertex lands on a vertex. In a polygon a mirror line either passes through a vertex or through the midpoint of a side.

Test in turn: lines through opposite vertices (diagonals), lines through midpoints of opposite sides, and lines through a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side.

In the exam, a tracing-paper fold or a quick sketch is acceptable; use a ruler for the mirror lines.

The figure shows the lines of symmetry (dashed) of some common shapes. The parallelogram has none: folding it along a diagonal or through the midpoints of opposite sides does not make the halves match.

assets.caption: Lines of symmetry (dashed) of an equilateral triangle (3), square (4), rectangle (2), regular pentagon (5), isosceles trapezium (1), kite (1), rhombus (2) and parallelogram (0).
assets.purpose: Give one reference gallery of lines of symmetry across the most commonly examined shapes, including the parallelogram as the key zero-lines counterexample.

theory_blocks.title: Line symmetry errors
theory_blocks.body:
- Drawing the diagonals of a rectangle or a parallelogram as lines of symmetry. They are not: [[red:folding along a diagonal of a non-square rectangle leaves the corners overhanging]].
- Counting a line that only *looks* like it splits the shape evenly (for example a diagonal of a parallelogram cuts it into two *congruent* triangles, but the triangles are related by a half-turn, not by a reflection).

theory_blocks.title: Rotational symmetry
theory_blocks.body:
A 2D shape has **rotational symmetry** if it fits exactly onto itself after being rotated about a fixed point (the **centre of rotation**) through an angle less than $360^{\circ}$.

The **order of rotational symmetry** is the number of different positions in which the shape looks exactly the same during one complete turn, counting the starting position.

A shape with no rotational symmetry has order $1$. If the order is $n$, the smallest turn that fits the shape onto itself is $\dfrac{360^{\circ}}{n}$.

Turning a parallelogram through $180^{\circ}$ carries every vertex onto the opposite vertex, so it fits back onto itself after each half-turn: order $2$.

An isosceles trapezium has a line of symmetry but no turn other than a full turn fits it back onto itself, so its order is $1$.

assets.caption: The red dot marks the centre of rotation and the arc shows the smallest fitting turn: parallelogram order $2$ ($180^{\circ}$), equilateral triangle order $3$ ($120^{\circ}$), square order $4$ ($90^{\circ}$), isosceles trapezium order $1$ (none).
assets.purpose: Show the smallest fitting turn explicitly as an arc for several shapes, including the parallelogram as the key example of rotational symmetry without any line symmetry.

theory_blocks.title: Line symmetry and rotational symmetry are independent
theory_blocks.body:
A shape can have line symmetry without rotational symmetry (isosceles trapezium, kite, isosceles triangle), rotational symmetry without line symmetry (parallelogram, the letters S and N), both (rectangle, rhombus, regular polygons) or neither (scalene triangle).

In the exam, 'rotational symmetry of order $1$' and 'no rotational symmetry' mean the same thing.

theory_blocks.title: Symmetry of triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons
theory_blocks.body:
| Shape | Lines | Order | What symmetry tells us |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scalene triangle | $0$ | $1$ | no equal sides or angles |
| Isosceles triangle | $1$ | $1$ | two equal sides, two equal (base) angles |
| Equilateral triangle | $3$ | $3$ | three equal sides and angles ($60^{\circ}$) |
| Kite | $1$ | $1$ | two pairs of adjacent equal sides; diagonals meet at $90^{\circ}$ |
| Isosceles trapezium | $1$ | $1$ | one pair of parallel sides; equal legs; equal diagonals |
| Parallelogram | $0$ | $2$ | opposite sides parallel and equal |
| Rectangle | $2$ | $2$ | four right angles; equal diagonals |
| Rhombus | $2$ | $2$ | four equal sides; diagonals are the mirror lines and meet at $90^{\circ}$ |
| Square | $4$ | $4$ | four equal sides and four right angles |
| Regular polygon with $n$ sides | $n$ | $n$ | all sides and all angles equal |

**Symmetry explains properties.** In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB=AC$ the mirror line passes through $A$ and the midpoint $M$ of $BC$. Reflection swaps $B$ and $C$, so $\angle ABC=\angle ACB$ (base angles) and $AM\perp BC$. In a kite the mirror line is a diagonal, and the other diagonal is bisected at right angles by it. A regular polygon with $n$ sides has $n$ lines of symmetry *and* rotational symmetry of order $n$.

assets.caption: Isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($AB=AC$): the mirror line $AM$ gives $\angle ABC=\angle ACB$. Kite $ABCD$: the mirror line $AC$ gives $BD\perp AC$ with $BX=XD$.
assets.purpose: Show symmetry acting as the actual justification (not just a label) for two standard GCSE facts: equal base angles in an isosceles triangle, and perpendicular bisected diagonal in a kite.

theory_blocks.title: Symmetry of solids
theory_blocks.body:
A **plane of symmetry** of a 3D solid is a plane that cuts the solid into two parts that are mirror images of each other.

An **axis of symmetry** is a straight line through the solid such that the solid fits onto itself after rotation about the line through an angle less than $360^{\circ}$; the **order** of the axis is the number of times this happens in one full turn.

The cuboid (all three edges different) has one plane parallel to each pair of opposite faces (so $3$ planes), and each of its $3$ axes joins the centres of a pair of opposite faces, with order $2$.

A square-based pyramid has two planes through opposite base vertices (containing the apex), two planes through midpoints of opposite base edges ($4$ planes total), and one vertical axis of order $4$.

A cylinder has one horizontal plane (through the middle) and infinitely many vertical planes through its axis; a cone has infinitely many planes, all containing its axis, but no horizontal plane.

assets.caption: Red shaded sections are planes of symmetry; green dashed lines are axes. Cuboid: $3$ planes, $3$ axes of order $2$. Square-based pyramid: $4$ planes, $1$ axis of order $4$. Cylinder: infinitely many planes; any turn about its main axis (shown) fits it onto itself.
assets.purpose: Show the plane and axis of symmetry for three contrasting solids side by side, making the prism/cylinder-vs-pyramid/cone distinction (extra horizontal plane) visually explicit.

theory_blocks.title: Counting planes for a prism or pyramid from its base
theory_blocks.body:
For a prism with a regular polygon as its cross-section, the planes of symmetry are the planes through each line of symmetry of the cross-section, **plus one plane half-way along the prism**.

So an equilateral triangular prism has $3+1=4$ planes, and its main (longitudinal) axis has order $3$. A pyramid or cone has no such extra plane, since its base and its single apex are not identical ends.

theory_blocks.title: Method for counting planes and axes of a solid
theory_blocks.body:
1. Count the lines of symmetry of the solid's base or cross-section.
2. Decide whether the solid also has a horizontal plane (prisms and cylinders do; pyramids and cones do not). If it does, add $1$ to the count from step 1.
3. The order of the main axis of a solid built on a regular $n$-sided polygon is $n$.

Take care when two or more edge lengths are equal: a **cube** has extra diagonal planes, giving $9$ planes of symmetry in total (not $4+1=5$).

assets.caption: A cube has two kinds of plane of symmetry: $3$ planes parallel to a pair of faces and $6$ planes through a pair of opposite edges, giving $9$ altogether.
assets.purpose: Make the cube caveat in the counting rule visible: the six diagonal planes through pairs of opposite edges are the ones the 'lines of symmetry of the base $+1$' rule misses.

keywords.definition: A line (mirror line) that divides a 2D shape into two parts that are mirror images of each other.
A property of a 2D shape that fits exactly onto itself after being rotated about a fixed point through an angle less than $360^{\circ}$.
The number of positions, during one full turn, in which a shape looks exactly the same, counting the starting position; order $1$ means no rotational symmetry.
The fixed point about which a shape with rotational symmetry is turned.
A plane that cuts a 3D solid into two parts that are mirror images of each other.
A straight line through a 3D solid such that the solid fits onto itself after rotation about the line through an angle less than $360^{\circ}$.

worked_examples.statement:
Completing a symmetric shape. The points $A(1,1)$, $B(4,1)$ and $C(3,3)$ are three vertices of a quadrilateral $ABCD$. (a) Find $D$ so that $ABCD$ has $AC$ as a line of symmetry.

(b) The triangle $ABE$ has $E(2.5,4)$; show that it is isosceles and write down the equation of its line of symmetry.
unknowns: $D$; equation of the line of symmetry of triangle $ABE$
reasoning: (a) A mirror line through $A$ and $C$ must swap $B$ and $D$, since $AC$ is the stated line of symmetry; find the line $AC$'s equation, then reflect $B$ in it.
The gradient of $AC$ is $\frac{3-1}{3-1}=1$, so $AC$ is the line $y=x$; reflecting any point in $y=x$ simply swaps its coordinates.
Check the result by computing matching side lengths from both $A$ and $C$ to confirm $ABCD$ really is symmetric about $AC$.
(b) To show a triangle is isosceles from coordinates, compute two candidate equal side lengths using the distance formula (as squared distances, to avoid unnecessary square roots) and compare.
The line of symmetry of an isosceles triangle passes through the apex and the midpoint of the base.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) Reflecting $B(4,1)$ in $y=x$ swaps the coordinates: $D=(1,4)$. Check: $AB=3$ and $AD=3$; $CB=\sqrt{1^2+2^2}=\sqrt5$ and $CD=\sqrt{2^2+1^2}=\sqrt5$, so $ABCD$ is a kite.

(b) $AE^2=1.5^2+3^2=11.25$ and $BE^2=1.5^2+3^2=11.25$, so $AE=BE$: the triangle is isosceles. Its line of symmetry passes through $E$ and the midpoint $(2.5,1)$ of $AB$: the vertical line $x=2.5$.
worked_examples.interpretation:
Reflection in the specific line $y=x$ has the convenient shortcut of simply swapping coordinates, but the GENERAL method — find the mirror line,

then find where each point lands — is what actually proves $D$ is correct, confirmed independently by the distance check.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming any mirror line swaps coordinates the way $y=x$ does; this shortcut only works for $y=x$ (for $y=-x$ the coordinates are swapped AND both signs change), not for a mirror line in general.

worked_examples.statement: Exam decision: identify the transformation, not just the visual balance. A parallelogram has rotational symmetry of order $2$, but does it have a line of symmetry? Compare with a rectangle.
reasoning: Check rotational symmetry first: does a $180^{\circ}$ turn map every vertex to another vertex of the shape?
Separately, and independently, test every candidate fold line for line symmetry — do not assume the answer from the rotational symmetry result.
worked_examples.solution:
A parallelogram has rotational symmetry of order $2$ because a $180^{\circ}$ turn maps every vertex to its opposite vertex, but it has no line of symmetry in general.

A rectangle has the same half-turn (order $2$) and ALSO two reflection lines. To justify an answer, name the angle or mirror line and state where each vertex is sent.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the direct demonstration that line symmetry and rotational symmetry must be checked separately: the parallelogram and the rectangle share the same rotational order, but differ completely in line symmetry.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming that because the parallelogram has SOME symmetry (rotational), it must also have line symmetry, which is exactly the independence misconception this example is designed to correct.

guided_exercises.statement: State the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of (a) a regular octagon; (b) a non-square rhombus; (c) a scalene triangle.
hints: For the regular polygon, use the rule 'regular $n$-gon: $n$ lines and order $n$' directly.
For the rhombus, recall its diagonals are both lines of symmetry, and check what turn (if any) fits it back onto itself.
guided_exercises.answer: (a) $8$ lines, order $8$. (b) $2$ lines, order $2$. (c) $0$ lines, order $1$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) A regular octagon has $n=8$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $8$. (b) A rhombus has $2$ lines of symmetry (its diagonals) and rotational symmetry of order $2$ (a $180^{\circ}$ turn fits it back onto itself). (c) A scalene triangle has no equal sides or angles, so it has $0$ lines of symmetry and order $1$ (no rotational symmetry beyond the trivial full turn).
common_errors: Giving the rhombus order $4$ by confusing it with a square, when only a square (not a general rhombus) has order $4$.

guided_exercises.statement: The points $P(0,0)$, $Q(4,2)$ and $R(0,6)$ are three vertices of a kite $PQRS$ with the line $PR$ (the $y$-axis) as its line of symmetry. Find $S$, and verify your answer using the distance formula.
hints: The mirror line $PR$ is the $y$-axis ($x=0$); reflecting a point in the $y$-axis simply negates its $x$-coordinate and keeps the $y$-coordinate.
Once you have a candidate $S$, check $PQ=PS$ and $RQ=RS$ to confirm the kite property.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Reflecting $Q(4,2)$ in the $y$-axis negates its $x$-coordinate: $S=(-4,2)$. Check: $PQ=\sqrt{4^2+2^2}=\sqrt{20}$ and $PS=\sqrt{(-4)^2+2^2}=\sqrt{20}$; $RQ=\sqrt{4^2+(2-6)^2}=\sqrt{16+16}=\sqrt{32}$ and $RS=\sqrt{(-4)^2+(2-6)^2}=\sqrt{16+16}=\sqrt{32}$. Both pairs match, confirming $PQRS$ is a kite with line of symmetry $PR$.
common_errors: Negating the $y$-coordinate instead of the $x$-coordinate, which would be the correct reflection rule for the $x$-axis, not the $y$-axis.

guided_exercises.statement: A prism has a regular hexagon as its cross-section (a hexagonal prism). How many planes of symmetry does it have, and what is the order of its main (longitudinal) axis of symmetry?
hints: Count the lines of symmetry of a regular hexagon first, using the 'regular $n$-gon has $n$ lines' rule.
A prism has two identical, parallel ends, so remember the extra horizontal plane half-way along its length.
guided_exercises.full_solution: A regular hexagon has $6$ lines of symmetry, giving $6$ vertical planes of symmetry for the prism. Since a prism has two identical ends, there is one extra horizontal plane half-way along its length: $6+1=7$ planes in total. The order of the main longitudinal axis matches the hexagon's rotational symmetry: order $6$.
common_errors: Stopping at $6$ planes and forgetting the extra horizontal plane that a prism (unlike a pyramid) always has.

exercises.statement: Write down the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of (a) an equilateral triangle; (b) a rectangle that is not a square; (c) a rhombus that is not a square; (d) a parallelogram that is not a rectangle or a rhombus; (e) an isosceles trapezium; (f) a regular hexagon.
exercises.full_solution: Each answer follows directly from the shape's standard symmetry (equilateral triangle: $3,3$; non-square rectangle: $2,2$; non-square rhombus: $2,2$; parallelogram: $0,2$; isosceles trapezium: $1,1$; regular hexagon: $6,6$).
common_errors: Giving the parallelogram $0$ lines and order $1$ (forgetting it still has rotational symmetry of order $2$ even with no line symmetry).

exercises.statement: For each capital letter, state the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry (use a simple sans-serif form): (a) H; (b) N; (c) T; (d) Z; (e) E.
exercises.answer: (a) $2$ lines, order $2$. (b) $0$ lines, order $2$. (c) $1$ line, order $1$. (d) $0$ lines, order $2$. (e) $1$ line, order $1$.
exercises.full_solution: H has both a vertical and a horizontal line of symmetry, and also order $2$ rotational symmetry. N and Z each have only a $180^{\circ}$ rotational symmetry (order $2$) and no line of symmetry. T has exactly one line of symmetry (vertical) and E has exactly one line of symmetry (horizontal); neither has rotational symmetry beyond the trivial full turn (order $1$).
common_errors: Giving N or Z a line of symmetry, mistaking their rotational (point) symmetry for reflective symmetry.

exercises.statement: A triangle has vertices $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$ and $(2,3)$. (a) Write down the equation of its line of symmetry. (b) What is the order of its rotational symmetry?
exercises.full_solution: The two sides from $(0,0)$ and $(4,0)$ to $(2,3)$ both have length $\sqrt{2^2+3^2}=\sqrt{13}$, so the triangle is isosceles with its line of symmetry vertical through the midpoint of the base: $x=2$. Since the base ($4$) and the two equal sides ($\sqrt{13}\approx3.61$) are different lengths, the triangle is not equilateral, so its rotational symmetry is order $1$.
common_errors: Assuming any isosceles triangle automatically has rotational symmetry greater than $1$, when only an EQUILATERAL triangle does.

exercises.statement: A convex quadrilateral has exactly one line of symmetry, and its diagonals meet at right angles but are not equal in length. What is the quadrilateral?
exercises.full_solution: Exactly one line of symmetry with perpendicular, unequal diagonals is the defining combination for a kite (a rhombus would have two lines of symmetry, and a square would have both perpendicular AND equal diagonals).
common_errors: Answering 'rhombus', which also has perpendicular diagonals but has TWO lines of symmetry, not one.

exercises.statement: A regular polygon has $9$ lines of symmetry. (a) How many sides does it have? (b) What is its order of rotational symmetry?
exercises.full_solution: A regular $n$-gon always has $n$ lines of symmetry and order $n$ rotational symmetry, so $9$ lines means $n=9$ sides and order $9$.
common_errors: Trying to compute the number of sides from an angle calculation instead of simply using 'lines of symmetry = number of sides' for a regular polygon.

exercises.statement: Name (a) a quadrilateral with rotational symmetry of order $2$ but no line of symmetry; (b) a quadrilateral with rotational symmetry of order $4$; (c) a triangle with rotational symmetry of order $3$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) A parallelogram has order $2$ but no line of symmetry. (b) A square has order $4$. (c) An equilateral triangle has order $3$.
common_errors: Naming a rectangle for part (a), which also has order $2$ but DOES have line symmetry (two lines), failing the 'no line of symmetry' condition.

exercises.statement: A shape has the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis as lines of symmetry. One of its vertices is $(3,2)$ and it is a rectangle. Write down the coordinates of the other three vertices.
exercises.full_solution: Reflecting $(3,2)$ in the $y$-axis gives $(-3,2)$; reflecting in the $x$-axis gives $(3,-2)$; reflecting in both gives $(-3,-2)$. These four points form a rectangle symmetric about both axes.
common_errors: Giving only one or two reflected points instead of all three remaining vertices needed to complete the rectangle.

exercises.statement: A window is in the shape of a regular octagon. Write down its number of lines of symmetry and its order of rotational symmetry.
exercises.full_solution: A regular octagon has $n=8$ sides, so $8$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $8$.
common_errors: Confusing 'octagon' (8 sides) with a different polygon and giving the wrong value of $n$.

exercises.statement: The triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(3,0)$ and $(0,2)$ is reflected in the $y$-axis. Write down the coordinates of the vertices of the image, and name the triangle formed by the two triangles together.
exercises.answer: Image: $(0,0)$, $(-3,0)$, $(0,2)$. Together: an isosceles triangle with vertices $(-3,0)$, $(3,0)$, $(0,2)$.
exercises.full_solution: Reflecting each point in the $y$-axis negates its $x$-coordinate: $(0,0)\to(0,0)$, $(3,0)\to(-3,0)$, $(0,2)\to(0,2)$. The original and image triangles together form the triangle with vertices $(-3,0)$, $(3,0)$, $(0,2)$, which is isosceles (the $y$-axis is its line of symmetry).
common_errors: Negating the $y$-coordinates (reflecting in the $x$-axis) instead of the $x$-coordinates.

exercises.statement: A cuboid has a square base of side $2$\,cm and height $5$\,cm. (a) How many planes of symmetry does it have? (b) State the order of its vertical axis of symmetry.
exercises.full_solution: (a) The square base's $4$ lines of symmetry give $4$ vertical planes, plus $1$ horizontal plane half-way up the height: $4+1=5$. (b) The vertical axis's order matches the square base's rotational symmetry: order $4$.
common_errors: Treating this as a generic cuboid with only $3$ planes (which is true only when ALL three edge lengths are different); here the square base gives extra symmetry.

exercises.statement: For a square-based pyramid, state the number of planes of symmetry and the order of the axis of symmetry.
exercises.full_solution: A square base has $4$ lines of symmetry, giving $4$ vertical planes through the apex; a pyramid has no extra horizontal plane (its apex and base are not identical), so the total stays at $4$. The vertical axis has order $4$, matching the square base.
common_errors: Adding an extra horizontal plane as if this were a prism, when a pyramid's apex and base are never identical ends.

exercises.statement: A prism has ends that are equilateral triangles. How many planes of symmetry does it have, and what is the order of its main (longitudinal) axis of symmetry?
exercises.full_solution: An equilateral triangle has $3$ lines of symmetry, giving $3$ vertical planes, plus $1$ horizontal plane half-way along the prism's length: $3+1=4$ planes. The order of the longitudinal axis matches the triangle's rotational symmetry: order $3$.
common_errors: Forgetting the extra horizontal plane and stopping at $3$.

exercises.statement: Describe all the planes of symmetry of a cylinder.
exercises.answer: One horizontal plane half-way up, and infinitely many vertical planes through the axis.
exercises.full_solution: A cylinder's circular cross-section has infinitely many lines of symmetry (every diameter), giving infinitely many vertical planes, each containing the axis; and since its two circular ends are identical, there is also one horizontal plane half-way up.
common_errors: Naming only a finite number of vertical planes, instead of recognising that a circle's infinitely many diameters give infinitely many planes.

exercises.statement: Explain why a cone has no horizontal plane of symmetry.
exercises.answer: Its top (a point) and its bottom (a flat circular base) are not identical, so no horizontal cut gives two mirror-image halves.
exercises.full_solution: A horizontal plane of symmetry would need to produce a matching mirror image above and below the cut, but a cone comes to a single point at the top and is flat (a full circle) at the bottom, so the two halves are never mirror images of each other, however the horizontal cut is placed.
common_errors: Confusing the cone's infinitely many VERTICAL planes (which it does have, through its axis) with a horizontal plane (which it does not have).

exercises.statement: A solid has a regular pentagon as base and uniform cross-section (a pentagonal prism). How many planes of symmetry does it have?
exercises.full_solution: A regular pentagon has $5$ lines of symmetry, giving $5$ vertical planes, plus $1$ extra horizontal plane half-way along the prism (since both pentagonal ends are identical): $5+1=6$.
common_errors: Stopping at $5$ planes, forgetting the extra horizontal plane half-way along the prism.

exercises.statement: (a) How many planes of symmetry does a solid cube have? (b) State the order of the axis of symmetry that joins the centres of two opposite faces of a cube.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Three of the planes are parallel to a pair of faces, each cutting the cube half-way across; there is one for each of the three directions. Six more planes each pass through a pair of opposite edges, slicing two opposite faces along a diagonal. That gives $3+6=9$ planes. The prism rule ($4$ lines of symmetry in the square base, add $1$ for the horizontal plane) predicts only $5$, because the six diagonal planes exist only when the height equals the side of the square base, as it does in a cube. (b) A quarter turn ($90^{\circ}$) about the line joining the centres of two opposite faces leaves the cube looking exactly the same, so the cube fits onto itself $4$ times in a full turn: the axis has order $4$.
common_errors: Treating the cube as 'just a square prism' and answering $5$ planes ($4$ vertical plus $1$ horizontal), which misses the six diagonal planes through pairs of opposite edges.

exam_questions.statement:
(a) State the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of a regular decagon (10-sided polygon). [2]
(b) A different shape has rotational symmetry of order $5$ but no line of symmetry. State the smallest angle through which it can be turned to fit onto itself, and name a type of object that could have this symmetry. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $10$ lines; order $10$. (b) $72^{\circ}$; e.g. a five-bladed curved propeller or fan.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) A regular $10$-gon has $n=10$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $10$. (b) Smallest angle $=360^{\circ}\div5=72^{\circ}$; a five-bladed curved propeller or similar rotor shape has order $5$ rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry (its blades are not individually mirror-symmetric).
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for $10$ lines; B1 for order $10$
(b) M1 for $360\div5=72^{\circ}$; B1 for a valid example with no line of symmetry
common_errors: In (b), naming a shape that actually DOES have line symmetry (such as a regular pentagon), which fails the 'no line of symmetry' condition even though it has the right order.

exam_questions.statement:
In kite $PQRS$, $PR$ is the line of symmetry, $\angle QPR=35^{\circ}$ and $\angle PRQ=55^{\circ}$.
(a) Write down the value of $\angle QPS$ and $\angle QRS$, giving a reason. [2]
(b) Find $\angle PQR$. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\angle QPS=70^{\circ}$; $\angle QRS=110^{\circ}$ (by symmetry, each is double the given half-angle). (b) $\angle PQR=90^{\circ}$.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Since $PR$ is the line of symmetry, it bisects both $\angle QPS$ and $\angle QRS$: $\angle QPS=2\times35^{\circ}=70^{\circ}$ and $\angle QRS=2\times55^{\circ}=110^{\circ}$ (reason: reflection in $PR$ swaps $Q$ and $S$, so each angle at $P$ and at $R$ is split into two equal halves). (b) Angles of triangle $PQR$ sum to $180^{\circ}$: $\angle PQR=180^{\circ}-35^{\circ}-55^{\circ}=90^{\circ}$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for doubling each given half-angle; A1 for both correct values with the symmetry reason stated
(b) M1 for using the angle sum of triangle $PQR$; A1 for $90^{\circ}$
common_errors: Halving instead of doubling in part (a), treating the given angles as the full angles at $P$ and $R$ rather than as halves split by the mirror line.

exam_questions.statement:
A prism has a regular pentagon as its cross-section.
(a) State the number of planes of symmetry of the prism. [2]
(b) State the order of its main (longitudinal) axis of symmetry. [1]
(c) Would your answer to (a) change if the prism were replaced by a pyramid with the same regular pentagon as its base? If so, state the new number. [1]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) A regular pentagon has $5$ lines of symmetry, giving $5$ vertical planes, plus $1$ extra horizontal plane (the prism has two identical pentagonal ends): $5+1=6$. (b) The axis order matches the pentagon's rotational symmetry: order $5$. (c) Yes: a pyramid has no horizontal plane (its apex and base are not identical ends), so only the $5$ vertical planes remain.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for $5$ vertical planes from the pentagon; A1 for $5+1=6$ including the horizontal plane
(b) B1 for order $5$
(c) B1 for recognising the pyramid loses the horizontal plane, giving $5$
common_errors: In (c), keeping the horizontal plane for the pyramid as well, by analogy with the prism, instead of recognising a pyramid's apex and base are never identical.

challenge_questions.statement: A quadrilateral has exactly two lines of symmetry and they are its diagonals. Explain why it must be a rhombus and not a square.
challenge_questions.answer: The diagonals being mirror lines forces all four sides equal (a rhombus); having only TWO lines (not four) rules out a square.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Reflecting in a diagonal swaps the two neighbours of each end vertex, so adjacent sides are equal. Applying this to both diagonals forces all four sides to be equal, which is a rhombus. A square has four lines of symmetry, not two, so a quadrilateral with EXACTLY two lines (its diagonals) must be a rhombus that is not a square.

challenge_questions.statement: A shape has two perpendicular lines of symmetry. Explain why it must also have rotational symmetry of order at least $2$.
challenge_questions.answer: Reflecting in both lines in turn is equivalent to a single $180^{\circ}$ rotation about their intersection, which fits the shape onto itself.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Reflect the shape in one line, then in the other. The two reflections together make a half-turn about their intersection point ($180^{\circ}$ rotation), which fits the shape onto itself, since each individual reflection does. So the shape has rotational symmetry of order at least $2$.

challenge_questions.statement: The interior angle of a regular polygon is $150^{\circ}$. Find its number of sides, its number of lines of symmetry and its order of rotational symmetry.
challenge_questions.answer: $12$ sides; $12$ lines; order $12$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The exterior angle is $180^{\circ}-150^{\circ}=30^{\circ}$, so $n=360^{\circ}\div30^{\circ}=12$. A regular $12$-gon has $12$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $12$.

challenge_questions.statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=AC$ and $\angle BAC=40^{\circ}$. Use the line of symmetry to find $\angle ABC$, and explain why the line of symmetry through $A$ meets $BC$ at $90^{\circ}$.
challenge_questions.answer: $\angle ABC=70^{\circ}$; the mirror line meets $BC$ at $90^{\circ}$ because it is the perpendicular bisector of $BC$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Since $AB=AC$, the triangle's base angles are equal: $\angle ABC=\angle ACB=(180^{\circ}-40^{\circ})\div2=70^{\circ}$. The mirror line swaps $B$ and $C$ (since they are the two matching vertices under the reflection), so it must be the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, meeting it at exactly $90^{\circ}$.

challenge_questions.statement: Describe a shape that has rotational symmetry of order $4$ but no line of symmetry, and say how many different quarter-turns fit it onto itself.
challenge_questions.answer: For example a windmill or propeller with four identical curved (non-symmetric) blades; $3$ non-trivial quarter-turns ($90^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$, $270^{\circ}$), or $4$ positions counting the start.
challenge_questions.full_solution: A windmill or propeller shape with four identical but curved (not individually symmetric) blades arranged evenly has rotational symmetry of order $4$, since turning it by $90^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$ or $270^{\circ}$ all fit it back onto itself, but no straight fold line makes the two halves match (the curved blades break any potential mirror symmetry). There are $3$ non-trivial turns that work ($90^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$, $270^{\circ}$); including the starting position, there are $4$ positions in total, matching order $4$.

challenge_questions.statement: A solid is a cuboid $4\times4\times10$. It is cut in two by a plane of symmetry parallel to its square ends. Explain why the two halves are identical, and say how many planes of symmetry each half has.
challenge_questions.answer: The two halves are identical because the cutting plane IS a plane of symmetry (reflection maps one half onto the other); each half ($4\times4\times5$) has $5$ planes of symmetry.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The cutting plane is parallel to the two square ends and passes through the middle of the $10$\,cm length, so it is itself a plane of symmetry of the original cuboid: reflecting in it maps one half onto the other exactly, which is precisely what makes them identical. Each half is a $4\times4\times5$ cuboid with a square base, which (exactly as in the related idea) has $5$ planes of symmetry: $4$ vertical ones (two parallel to the faces, two through opposite edges) and one horizontal plane half-way up its own height.

mcq.stem: A rectangle (not a square) has its diagonal drawn in. Is this diagonal a line of symmetry?

options.text: No, because the two corners at the ends of the other diagonal do not coincide when folded along it
Yes, because it divides the rectangle into two congruent triangles
options.why_wrong: Two congruent triangles are not automatically mirror images of each other; here they are related by a half-turn, not a reflection, so the diagonal is not a line of symmetry.

options.text: Yes, because all diagonals of any quadrilateral are lines of symmetry
options.why_wrong: This is a sweeping overgeneralisation; most quadrilaterals' diagonals are not lines of symmetry at all (only specific ones, like a rhombus's or a kite's, are).

options.text: Cannot be determined without knowing the exact side lengths
options.why_wrong: The fact that it is NOT a square is already enough information: for any non-square rectangle, the diagonal fails the fold test, regardless of the specific side lengths.

mcq.explanation: Folding a non-square rectangle along its diagonal leaves the two corners at the ends of the other diagonal un-matched, since the other diagonal is not perpendicular to the fold line (the diagonals of a non-square rectangle do not meet at $90^{\circ}$), so the diagonal is not a line of symmetry.

mcq.stem: A parallelogram's diagonal splits it into two congruent triangles. What transformation relates these two triangles?

options.text: A reflection in the diagonal
options.why_wrong: If this were a reflection, the diagonal would be a line of symmetry — but a parallelogram (that is not also a rhombus or rectangle) has no line of symmetry at all.

options.text: A $180^{\circ}$ rotation about the diagonal's midpoint
A translation along the diagonal
options.why_wrong: A translation would slide the triangle to a different position without rotating or flipping it, which does not match how the two triangles of a parallelogram relate to each other.

options.text: No single transformation relates them; it is a coincidence that they are congruent
options.why_wrong: The congruence is not a coincidence — it follows directly from the parallelogram's rotational symmetry of order $2$, via the $180^{\circ}$ rotation.

mcq.explanation: The parallelogram's rotational symmetry of order $2$ means a $180^{\circ}$ turn about the centre (the diagonal's midpoint) maps the shape onto itself, swapping the two triangles formed by the diagonal.

mcq.stem: A scalene triangle is described as having 'rotational symmetry of order $1$'. What does this mean?

options.text: It has a small amount of genuine rotational symmetry, less than order $2$ shapes
options.why_wrong: There is no 'amount less than order 2' — order $1$ is not a weaker version of rotational symmetry, it is the same statement as having none at all.

options.text: It can be rotated by exactly $1^{\circ}$ and still fit onto itself
options.why_wrong: The 'order' number is a count of fitting positions in a full turn, not an angle measured in degrees.

options.text: It has no rotational symmetry at all, beyond the trivial full turn
It has exactly one line of symmetry
options.why_wrong: This confuses rotational symmetry with line symmetry; 'order 1' describes ROTATIONAL symmetry only, and says nothing about lines of symmetry.

mcq.explanation: 'Rotational symmetry of order $1$' and 'no rotational symmetry' are exactly the same statement: the shape only matches itself after a full $360^{\circ}$ turn.

mcq.stem: A prism has an isosceles triangle (not equilateral) as its cross-section. How many planes of symmetry does it have?

options.text: $1$ (just the vertical plane from the triangle's line of symmetry)
options.why_wrong: This forgets the extra horizontal plane that every prism has, since its two triangular ends are identical and equally spaced from the middle.

options.text: $3$ (as if the triangle had $3$ lines of symmetry)
options.why_wrong: Only an EQUILATERAL triangle has $3$ lines of symmetry; an isosceles (non-equilateral) triangle has only $1$.

options.text: $0$ (since the cross-section is not equilateral)
options.why_wrong: An isosceles triangle still has $1$ line of symmetry even though it is not equilateral, so the prism still has at least one vertical plane.

options.text: $2$ (one vertical plane from the triangle's single line of symmetry, plus one horizontal plane half-way along)

mcq.explanation: The isosceles (non-equilateral) triangle has $1$ line of symmetry, giving $1$ vertical plane; the prism's two identical ends add $1$ more horizontal plane: $1+1=2$.

mcq.stem: A shape has $0$ lines of symmetry. What can be concluded about its order of rotational symmetry?

options.text: Nothing can be concluded without checking separately — it could be order $1$ (like a scalene triangle) or order $2$ or more (like a parallelogram)
It must be order $1$ (no rotational symmetry)
options.why_wrong: This assumes line symmetry and rotational symmetry are linked, but a parallelogram has $0$ lines of symmetry and STILL has rotational symmetry of order $2$.

options.text: It must be order $2$
options.why_wrong: This assumes a FIXED order follows from having zero lines, but a scalene triangle also has $0$ lines yet only order $1$ — the order is not determined by the line count alone.

options.text: It must be greater than $2$
options.why_wrong: There is no such rule; having zero lines of symmetry says nothing at all, by itself, about how large the rotational order must be.

mcq.explanation: Line symmetry and rotational symmetry are independent properties: a shape with $0$ lines of symmetry could have order $1$ (scalene triangle) or order $2$ (parallelogram) or any other order — each must be checked separately.

mcq.stem: Which pair correctly matches a solid to its number of planes of symmetry?

options.text: Square-based pyramid — $5$ planes
options.why_wrong: This wrongly adds a horizontal plane as if the pyramid were a prism; a pyramid's apex and base are not identical, so it has no such extra plane.

options.text: Square-based pyramid — $4$ planes
Cuboid with all edges different — $6$ planes
options.why_wrong: A cuboid with all three edge lengths different has only $3$ planes of symmetry (one parallel to each pair of opposite faces), not $6$.

options.text: Cone — a finite number of planes, equal to its number of 'sides'
options.why_wrong: A cone's base is a circle, which has infinitely many lines of symmetry, so a cone has infinitely many planes of symmetry, not a finite number.

mcq.explanation: A square-based pyramid has exactly $4$ planes of symmetry, matching the square base's $4$ lines of symmetry, with no extra horizontal plane since the apex and base are not identical.

flashcards.front: What is a line of symmetry?
flashcards.back: A line that divides a shape into two parts that are mirror images of each other; folding along it makes the two halves fit exactly.

flashcards.front: True or false: the diagonal of any rectangle is a line of symmetry.
flashcards.back: False, unless the rectangle is a square. For a non-square rectangle, folding along a diagonal leaves the corners overhanging.

flashcards.front: What is the order of rotational symmetry?
flashcards.back: The number of different positions, in one full turn, where the shape looks exactly the same (counting the start). Order $1$ means none.

flashcards.front: Smallest turn that fits a shape onto itself, for order $n$
flashcards.back: $\dfrac{360^{\circ}}{n}$.

flashcards.front: Line symmetry vs. rotational symmetry — are they linked?
flashcards.back: No, they are independent. A parallelogram has $0$ lines but order $2$; an isosceles trapezium has $1$ line but order $1$.

flashcards.front: Regular $n$-gon: lines of symmetry and order of rotational symmetry
flashcards.back: Both equal $n$.

flashcards.front: Why does symmetry prove the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal?
flashcards.back: The mirror line through the apex and the base's midpoint swaps the two base vertices, so it swaps the two base angles too — making them equal.

flashcards.front: Plane of symmetry vs. axis of symmetry (3D)
flashcards.back: A plane of symmetry cuts a solid into two mirror-image halves. An axis of symmetry is a line the solid can be rotated about (through less than $360^{\circ}$) to fit onto itself.

flashcards.front: Counting planes of symmetry of a prism or cylinder
flashcards.back: Count the lines of symmetry of the cross-section, then ADD $1$ for the horizontal plane half-way along (prisms/cylinders only, not pyramids/cones). Exception: a cube has $9$ planes.

flashcards.front: True or false: a square-based pyramid has an extra horizontal plane of symmetry, like a prism does.
flashcards.back: False. A pyramid's apex and base are not identical, so it has NO extra horizontal plane — only the vertical planes from the base's lines of symmetry.

flashcards.front: Why does a cone have infinitely many planes of symmetry?
flashcards.back: Its base is a circle, which has infinitely many lines of symmetry (every diameter), so every plane through the cone's axis is a plane of symmetry.

flashcards.front: Quick check for 'is this candidate line a line of symmetry?'
flashcards.back: Imagine folding along it and check that EVERY vertex lands exactly on another vertex (or itself) — not just that the two halves look similarly sized.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The diagonal of any quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides (such as a rectangle or a parallelogram) is a line of symmetry.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A diagonal of a rectangle or parallelogram genuinely does split the shape into two CONGRUENT triangles, and congruent pieces can look 'symmetric' at a glance without actually checking whether the fold makes every vertex land on a vertex.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner draws a diagonal of a non-square rectangle (or of a parallelogram) and calls it a line of symmetry.
misconceptions.correct_model: A line of symmetry must make every point of the shape land exactly on a matching point when folded — for a rectangle's diagonal, the two corners at the ends of the OTHER diagonal do not coincide after folding, because the other diagonal is not perpendicular to it (the diagonals of a rectangle only meet at $90^{\circ}$ when it is a square). The diagonal only gives two congruent triangles, not two mirror-image halves.
misconceptions.remediation: Before accepting a candidate line, explicitly check where EVERY vertex lands after the fold, not just whether the two resulting pieces look the same size and shape.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Two congruent pieces of a shape are automatically related by a reflection (mirror image), whatever cut produced them.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Reflection is the most familiar way two congruent pieces can relate, so 'congruent' and 'mirror image' can feel like the same idea without a specific counterexample to separate them.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner treats the two triangles formed by a parallelogram's diagonal as mirror images of each other, when they are actually related by a $180^{\circ}$ rotation about the diagonal's midpoint.
misconceptions.correct_model: Congruent pieces can be related by DIFFERENT transformations: a reflection (true mirror image, giving line symmetry), a rotation (as with a parallelogram's diagonal, giving rotational symmetry instead), or a translation. Congruence alone does not say which.
misconceptions.remediation: When two congruent pieces are found, explicitly test whether folding (reflection) or turning (rotation) is the transformation that maps one onto the other, rather than assuming it must be a fold.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: 'Rotational symmetry of order $1$' describes some special, minimal kind of genuine symmetry, distinct from 'no rotational symmetry'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The word 'order' followed by a number sounds like it is always describing a positive property, so 'order 1' can feel like it must mean something more than simply 'none'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner treats a scalene triangle's 'order $1$' rotational symmetry as though it were a meaningfully different (lesser) case from 'no rotational symmetry', rather than the same thing stated two ways.
misconceptions.correct_model: Order $1$ and 'no rotational symmetry' are EXACTLY the same statement: the shape only fits onto itself after a full $360^{\circ}$ turn (which is trivially true of every shape), counted as the one position in the cycle.
misconceptions.remediation: Always read 'order $1$' out loud as 'no rotational symmetry' to reinforce that they are interchangeable, not two different levels of symmetry.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The number of planes of symmetry of a prism or cylinder is exactly the number of lines of symmetry of its cross-section — nothing more.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The vertical planes (one per line of symmetry of the cross-section) are the most visually obvious ones, since they contain the prism's whole length, so the one EXTRA horizontal plane (perpendicular to the length, halfway along) is easy to overlook.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner counts a hexagonal prism as having $6$ planes of symmetry instead of $7$, forgetting the horizontal plane halfway along its length.
misconceptions.correct_model: A prism or cylinder has one plane of symmetry for EACH line of symmetry of its cross-section, PLUS one extra horizontal plane half-way along its length (since the two ends are identical and equally spaced from the middle). A pyramid or cone does NOT get this extra plane, because its two 'ends' (the base and the single apex point) are not identical.
misconceptions.remediation: Always ask, after counting the cross-section's lines of symmetry: 'does this solid have two identical, parallel ends?' If yes (prism, cylinder), add one more plane for the horizontal cut half-way along.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A shape with more lines of symmetry must also have a higher order of rotational symmetry, and vice versa — the two numbers should move together.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: For the most familiar shapes (squares, regular polygons) the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry happen to be EQUAL, which can suggest a general link between the two counts that does not actually exist.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner assumes a parallelogram (zero lines of symmetry) must also have rotational symmetry order $1$ (none), when it actually has order $2$; or assumes an isosceles trapezium ($1$ line of symmetry) must have rotational order greater than $1$.
misconceptions.correct_model: Line symmetry and rotational symmetry are independent properties that must each be checked separately. A parallelogram has $0$ lines but order $2$; an isosceles trapezium has $1$ line but order $1$; a rectangle has $2$ lines AND order $2$ (they happen to agree here, but not because one causes the other).
misconceptions.remediation: Always check lines of symmetry and order of rotational symmetry as two SEPARATE questions about a shape, never inferring one from the other.

common_mistakes.mistake: Drawing a diagonal of a rectangle or parallelogram as a line of symmetry.
common_mistakes.why: The diagonal genuinely splits the shape into two congruent triangles, which can look symmetric without an explicit fold-test check.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always test a candidate line by checking where every vertex actually lands after folding, not by eye alone.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the extra horizontal plane of symmetry when counting a prism's or cylinder's planes.
common_mistakes.why: The vertical planes (matching the cross-section's own lines of symmetry) are the most visually obvious ones, so the one extra horizontal plane is easy to miss.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: After counting the cross-section's lines of symmetry, always ask whether the solid has two identical parallel ends (prism, cylinder) and add $1$ if so.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing 'order 1' as if it meant something different from 'no rotational symmetry'.
common_mistakes.why: A number following the word 'order' can sound like it is always describing a positive, noteworthy property.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always read 'order $1$' out loud as 'no rotational symmetry' to reinforce that the two phrases mean exactly the same thing.

exam_notes: 'Rotational symmetry of order $1$' and 'no rotational symmetry' are accepted as exactly the same answer — either phrasing earns full marks.

For a 'show that' or 'explain why' symmetry question, name the specific transformation (the mirror line, or the angle of rotation) and state explicitly which points or vertices it swaps — a vague visual description does not earn the reasoning mark.

In Extended 'solids' questions, describe a plane or axis in words precisely: 'a plane through the midpoint of the height, parallel to the circular ends' or 'a vertical axis through the apex and the centre of the base', rather than just pointing at a diagram.
Core papers only ask about lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of 2D shapes; questions on planes and axes of symmetry of 3D solids are Extended only.

summary.big_idea: Symmetry is a movement (a reflection or a rotation) that leaves a shape exactly where it was; line symmetry and rotational symmetry are independent properties that must each be checked on their own, and many standard geometric facts (equal base angles, perpendicular diagonals) are simply consequences of a shape's symmetry.
key_points: A line of symmetry must make EVERY vertex land on a vertex when folded — congruent pieces from a cut are not automatically mirror-image pieces.
Order of rotational symmetry $=$ number of fitting positions in a full turn; order $1$ means none; smallest fitting turn $=360^{\circ}\div n$.
Line symmetry and rotational symmetry are independent: a parallelogram has rotational symmetry but no line symmetry, and the reverse combination is also possible.

A regular $n$-gon always has $n$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $n$; symmetry explains properties like equal base angles in an isosceles triangle and perpendicular diagonals in a kite.
Extended: a prism or cylinder has one plane per line of symmetry of its cross-section, PLUS one extra horizontal plane; a pyramid or cone has no such extra plane.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Test a candidate line of symmetry by checking every vertex after folding, check line symmetry and rotational symmetry as two separate questions, and for 3D solids, remember the extra horizontal plane that a prism or cylinder has but a pyramid or cone does not.

epistemic_overrides.note: Method for counting planes and axes of a solid

06_Angle_Properties.json.title: Angle Properties
06_Angle_Properties.json.subject: Mathematics

objectives.statement: Use three-letter angle notation (e.g. $\angle ABC$, vertex as the middle letter) correctly, and apply the basic angle facts (angles on a line add to $180^{\circ}$, angles at a point add to $360^{\circ}$, vertically opposite angles are equal) to find unknown angles, giving reasons.
Find unknown angles in triangles and quadrilaterals (including isosceles and equilateral triangles, and the exterior angle of a triangle), giving reasons.
Find and correctly name angles formed where a transversal crosses two parallel lines (corresponding, alternate, co-interior), giving reasons.
Use the interior and exterior angle facts of REGULAR polygons (sum of interior angles $(n-2)\times180^{\circ}$, each exterior angle $360^{\circ}\div n$) to find angles or the number of sides.
Use the interior and exterior angle SUM facts (which hold for any convex polygon) to find unknown angles in IRREGULAR polygons, including setting up and solving an equation.

prerequisites.statement: Name and recognise triangle types, special quadrilaterals and polygons (lesson 4.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every angle fact in this lesson is stated in terms of a named shape ('isosceles triangle', 'quadrilateral', 'regular polygon'); without the vocabulary secure, the facts cannot even be matched to a diagram.

prerequisites.statement: Set up and solve a simple linear equation, including one with the unknown on both sides (e.g. $3a+10=5a-30$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Nearly every exercise in this lesson ends in an equation like 'angles add up to a known total, find $x$'; without equation-solving secure, the geometry reasoning cannot be converted into a numeric answer.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise the arrowhead marking convention for parallel lines on a diagram.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every parallel-lines angle fact in this lesson depends on first confirming, from the diagram's arrowheads, that the two lines genuinely are marked parallel — these facts are invalid otherwise.

prerequisites.statement: Divide a quantity in a given ratio (e.g. split $180^{\circ}$ in the ratio $2:3:4$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: At least one standard exercise states a triangle's angles as a ratio directly, which needs ratio division (not just an equation) to convert into actual angle sizes.

diagnostic_items.question: Two angles are vertically opposite. One is $63^{\circ}$. What is the other, and why?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $63^{\circ}$, because vertically opposite angles are always equal.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Confuses 'vertically opposite' (equal angles, across the crossing point) with 'angles on a straight line' (supplementary, adjacent angles) — a very common mix-up between two different basic facts.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: The most basic possible check of the vertically-opposite fact, and of NOT confusing it with the straight-line fact.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Draw two crossing lines and physically point to the PAIR of angles that are vertically opposite (diagonally across the crossing point) versus the pair that are adjacent on one line (supplementary), to make the visual distinction explicit.

diagnostic_items.question: In a diagram with two parallel lines and a transversal, which of alternate, corresponding and co-interior angles add up to $180^{\circ}$?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Co-interior angles (they are supplementary).

common_wrong_answers.answer: Alternate angles, or corresponding angles.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Confuses the three parallel-line angle relationships; only co-interior angles sum to $180^{\circ}$, while alternate and corresponding angles are each EQUAL (not summing to anything in particular).

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the THREE different parallel-line relationships are not interchangeable: two give equality, only one gives a sum of $180^{\circ}$.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Have the learner state all three rules side by side: 'corresponding: equal. alternate: equal. co-interior: sum to $180^{\circ}$', emphasising co-interior as the one exception.

diagnostic_items.question: Why can a regular polygon never have an exterior angle of $50^{\circ}$?
