So $\angle ACD=\angle ACB+\angle BCD=90^{\circ}+28^{\circ}=118^{\circ}$. In triangle $ACD$: $\angle CDA=180^{\circ}-28^{\circ}-118^{\circ}=34^{\circ}$ (angles in a triangle add up to $180^{\circ}$).

*Check with the tangent-radius theorem:* $\angle OCD=90^{\circ}$; $OC=OB$, so $\angle OCB=\angle OBC=62^{\circ}$, and $62^{\circ}+28^{\circ}=90^{\circ}$.
worked_examples.interpretation:
This final example chains FOUR different theorems/facts (semicircle, alternate segment, angle addition, triangle sum) into one argument,

and then checks the whole result with a completely independent route using the tangent-radius theorem — exactly the 'check with a second route' advice from the related idea.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Computing $\angle ACD$ as $90^{\circ}-28^{\circ}=62^{\circ}$ (subtracting instead of adding the two parts $\angle ACB$ and $\angle BCD$, which lie on the same side and combine to make the larger angle $\angle ACD$).

guided_exercises.statement: $PT$ is a tangent to a circle with centre $O$, touching at $T$. $OT=7$\,cm and $OP=25$\,cm. (a) State the size of $\angle OTP$, giving a reason. (b) Find $TP$.
hints: The radius $OT$ is drawn to the point of contact $T$, so the tangent-radius theorem applies directly.
Once you know the right angle is at $T$, $OP$ is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle; use Pythagoras' theorem.
guided_exercises.answer: (a) $\angle OTP=90^{\circ}$ (angle between a tangent and a radius is $90^{\circ}$). (b) $TP=24$\,cm.
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) $\angle OTP=90^{\circ}$, since $OT$ is the radius drawn to the point of contact $T$, and a tangent is perpendicular to that radius. (b) Triangle $OTP$ is right-angled at $T$: $TP^2=OP^2-OT^2=25^2-7^2=625-49=576$, so $TP=24$\,cm.
common_errors: Computing $TP^2=OP^2+OT^2$ instead of subtracting, forgetting that $OP$ (not $TP$) is the hypotenuse.

guided_exercises.statement: $A$, $B$, $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$, and $\angle AOB=150^{\circ}$ (the angle at the centre on the arc not containing $C$). (a) Find $\angle ACB$, giving a reason. (b) $D$ is a second point on the circle, on the same side of $AB$ as $C$. State $\angle ADB$, giving a reason.
hints: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc; use this to go from $\angle AOB$ to $\angle ACB$.
$C$ and $D$ are on the same side of chord $AB$, so they are in the same segment.
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) $\angle ACB=\angle AOB\div2=150^{\circ}\div2=75^{\circ}$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, same arc $AB$). (b) $\angle ADB=\angle ACB=75^{\circ}$ (angles in the same segment are equal, since $C$ and $D$ are on the same side of chord $AB$).
common_errors: In part (b), doubling or halving $\angle ACB$ again instead of recognising that the same-segment theorem gives a direct equality, with no further arithmetic needed.

guided_exercises.statement: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral. $\angle ABC=(3x+15)^{\circ}$ and $\angle ADC=(2x+45)^{\circ}$. Find $x$ and the size of each angle.
hints: $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ADC$ are opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral.
Set the sum of the two expressions equal to $180^{\circ}$ and solve for $x$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^{\circ}$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$): $3x+15+2x+45=180$, so $5x+60=180$, $5x=120$, $x=24$. $\angle ABC=3(24)+15=87^{\circ}$; $\angle ADC=2(24)+45=93^{\circ}$ (check: $87+93=180^{\circ}$).
common_errors: Pairing $\angle ABC$ with $\angle BCD$ or $\angle BAD$ (adjacent angles) instead of correctly identifying $\angle ADC$ as the angle OPPOSITE $\angle ABC$ in quadrilateral $ABCD$.

exercises.statement: $AB$ is a diameter of a circle and $C$ is a point on the circle. $\angle CAB=35^{\circ}$. Find $\angle ABC$, giving a reason.
exercises.full_solution: $\angle ACB=90^{\circ}$ (angle in a semicircle), so $\angle ABC=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-35^{\circ}=55^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Forgetting to state the $90^{\circ}$ angle and its reason before using the triangle angle sum.

exercises.statement: $PQR$ is a triangle with all its vertices on a circle and $PR$ is a diameter. $\angle PRQ=62^{\circ}$. Find $\angle QPR$.
exercises.full_solution: $\angle PQR=90^{\circ}$ (angle in a semicircle, $PR$ a diameter), so $\angle QPR=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-62^{\circ}=28^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Placing the $90^{\circ}$ angle at $P$ or $R$ instead of at $Q$, the vertex not on the diameter.

exercises.statement: $PT$ is a tangent to a circle at $T$ and $O$ is the centre. $\angle OPT=25^{\circ}$. Find $\angle TOP$.
exercises.full_solution: $\angle OTP=90^{\circ}$ (angle between tangent and radius), so $\angle TOP=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-25^{\circ}=65^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Confusing which vertex has the right angle, placing it at $P$ or $O$ instead of $T$.

exercises.statement: A tangent from $P$ touches a circle, centre $O$, at $A$. The radius is $5$\,cm and $OP=13$\,cm. Find $AP$.
exercises.full_solution: $AP^2=OP^2-OA^2=13^2-5^2=169-25=144$, so $AP=12$\,cm (the radius $OA$ is perpendicular to the tangent, so triangle $OAP$ is right-angled at $A$).
common_errors: Adding $13^2+5^2$ instead of subtracting, confusing which side is the hypotenuse.

exercises.statement: $AB$ is a diameter of length $10$\,cm. $C$ is on the circle with $AC=6$\,cm. Find $BC$ and state the size of $\angle ACB$.
exercises.full_solution: $\angle ACB=90^{\circ}$ (angle in a semicircle). $BC^2=AB^2-AC^2=10^2-6^2=100-36=64$, so $BC=8$\,cm.
common_errors: Not recognising the $90^{\circ}$ angle first, and attempting to find $BC$ without Pythagoras.

exercises.statement: $O$ is the centre of a circle and $A$, $B$ are points on the circle with $\angle AOB=110^{\circ}$. Find $\angle OAB$, giving a reason.
exercises.full_solution: $OA=OB$ (radii), so triangle $OAB$ is isosceles: $\angle OAB=(180^{\circ}-110^{\circ})\div2=35^{\circ}$ (base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal).
common_errors: Forgetting that $\angle AOB$ is the APEX angle of the isosceles triangle, and instead dividing $110^{\circ}$ directly by $2$ without first subtracting from $180^{\circ}$.

exercises.statement: $AB$ is a diameter of a circle. The tangent at $B$ meets the line $AC$ (extended) at $P$, where $C$ is on the circle and $\angle ABC=40^{\circ}$. Find (a) $\angle BAC$, (b) $\angle ABP$, (c) $\angle APB$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\angle ACB=90^{\circ}$ (semicircle), so $\angle BAC=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-40^{\circ}=50^{\circ}$. (b) $\angle ABP=90^{\circ}$ (tangent perpendicular to the diameter $AB$ at $B$). (c) $\angle APB=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-50^{\circ}=40^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Not recognising that $AB$ itself is the relevant radius/diameter at $B$ for the tangent-radius theorem.

exercises.statement: A circular pond has radius $6$\,m. A straight path touches the edge of the pond at $T$. A post $P$ is on the path, $8$\,m from $T$. Find the distance from $P$ to the centre of the pond.
exercises.full_solution: The radius $OT$ is perpendicular to the path (a tangent), so triangle $OTP$ is right-angled at $T$: $OP^2=OT^2+PT^2=6^2+8^2=36+64=100$, so $OP=10$\,m.
common_errors: Not recognising the path as a tangent, and so missing the right angle at $T$ needed to apply Pythagoras.

exercises.statement: A right-angled triangle has sides $9$\,cm, $12$\,cm and $15$\,cm. It is drawn inside a circle with all three vertices on the circle. Find the radius of the circle.
exercises.full_solution: The hypotenuse ($15$\,cm, opposite the right angle) must be a diameter, by the converse of the angle in a semicircle theorem: a right-angled triangle always fits inside a circle with its hypotenuse as the diameter. So the radius is $15\div2=7.5$\,cm.
common_errors: Using one of the shorter sides ($9$\,cm or $12$\,cm) as the diameter instead of the hypotenuse.

exercises.statement: $XY$ is a diameter of a circle, and $Z$ is on the circle with $XZ=YZ$. Find $\angle ZXY$, giving reasons.
exercises.full_solution: $\angle XZY=90^{\circ}$ (angle in a semicircle). Since $XZ=YZ$, triangle $XYZ$ is isosceles with base angles equal: $\angle ZXY=(180^{\circ}-90^{\circ})\div2=45^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Forgetting to combine the two facts (semicircle giving the apex angle; isosceles giving equal base angles), stopping after finding only $\angle XZY=90^{\circ}$.

exercises.statement: $A$, $B$, $C$ are on a circle with centre $O$. $\angle ACB=48^{\circ}$. Find $\angle AOB$.
exercises.full_solution: $\angle AOB=2\times48^{\circ}=96^{\circ}$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference).
common_errors: Halving instead of doubling, writing $24^{\circ}$.

exercises.statement: $A$, $B$ are on a circle with centre $O$ and $\angle AOB=130^{\circ}$. (a) Find $\angle ACB$ where $C$ is on the major arc. (b) Find $\angle ADB$ where $D$ is on the minor arc.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\angle ACB=130^{\circ}\div2=65^{\circ}$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, $C$ on the major arc sees the $130^{\circ}$ angle directly). (b) $D$, on the minor arc, sees the reflex angle $360^{\circ}-130^{\circ}=230^{\circ}$ at the centre: $\angle ADB=230^{\circ}\div2=115^{\circ}$ (or equivalently, by the cyclic-quadrilateral theorem, $180^{\circ}-65^{\circ}=115^{\circ}$).
common_errors: In part (b), using the non-reflex $130^{\circ}$ angle at the centre again instead of the reflex angle $230^{\circ}$ that $D$ actually stands on.

exercises.statement: $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are on a circle. $\angle ACB=(2x+10)^{\circ}$ and $\angle ADB=(3x-15)^{\circ}$, and $C$ and $D$ are on the same side of $AB$. Find $x$ and the size of each angle.
exercises.full_solution: $C$ and $D$ are on the same side of chord $AB$, so $\angle ACB=\angle ADB$ (angles in the same segment are equal): $2x+10=3x-15$, so $x=25$. Each angle is $2(25)+10=60^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Adding the two expressions to $180^{\circ}$ (the opposite-side rule) instead of setting them equal, when the question states $C$ and $D$ are on the SAME side of $AB$.

exercises.statement: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral with $\angle ABC=108^{\circ}$ and $\angle BAD=95^{\circ}$. Find $\angle ADC$ and $\angle BCD$.
exercises.full_solution: $\angle ADC=180^{\circ}-108^{\circ}=72^{\circ}$ and $\angle BCD=180^{\circ}-95^{\circ}=85^{\circ}$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$).
common_errors: Pairing $\angle ABC$ with $\angle BCD$ (an adjacent pair) instead of correctly pairing opposite vertices $A\leftrightarrow C$ and $B\leftrightarrow D$.

exercises.statement: In the cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, side $AB$ is extended to $E$ and $\angle CBE=74^{\circ}$. Find $\angle ADC$, and explain your answer.
exercises.full_solution: $\angle ABC=180^{\circ}-74^{\circ}=106^{\circ}$ (angles on a straight line), so $\angle ADC=180^{\circ}-106^{\circ}=74^{\circ}$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$). This matches the direct rule: an exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral ($\angle CBE$) equals the interior opposite angle ($\angle ADC$).
common_errors: Setting $\angle ADC=\angle ABC$ directly (treating the exterior angle fact as if it applied to the ADJACENT interior angle rather than the opposite one).

exercises.statement: $PTQ$ is a tangent to a circle at $T$. $A$ and $B$ are points on the circle on opposite sides of $T$, with $\angle PTB=48^{\circ}$ and $\angle QTA=70^{\circ}$. Find $\angle TAB$, $\angle TBA$ and $\angle ATB$.
exercises.full_solution: $\angle TAB=\angle PTB=48^{\circ}$ (alternate segment theorem). $\angle TBA=\angle QTA=70^{\circ}$ (alternate segment theorem). $\angle ATB=180^{\circ}-48^{\circ}-70^{\circ}=62^{\circ}$ (angles in a triangle add up to $180^{\circ}$).
common_errors: Matching $\angle PTB$ to $\angle TBA$ instead of $\angle TAB$, mismatching the tangent side with the wrong triangle vertex.

exercises.statement: $AB$ is a diameter of a circle and the tangent at $C$ meets $AB$ produced at $D$. $\angle CAB=28^{\circ}$. Find $\angle ACD$ and $\angle CDA$.
exercises.full_solution: $\angle ACB=90^{\circ}$ (semicircle); $\angle BCD=\angle CAB=28^{\circ}$ (alternate segment), so $\angle ACD=90^{\circ}+28^{\circ}=118^{\circ}$. In triangle $ACD$: $\angle CDA=180^{\circ}-28^{\circ}-118^{\circ}=34^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Subtracting instead of adding $\angle ACB$ and $\angle BCD$ to get $\angle ACD$.

exercises.statement: In a circle with centre $O$, the chord $AB$ subtends an angle of $84^{\circ}$ at the circumference on the major arc. Find $\angle AOB$ and $\angle OAB$.
exercises.full_solution: $\angle AOB=2\times84^{\circ}=168^{\circ}$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference). $OA=OB$ (radii), so $\angle OAB=(180^{\circ}-168^{\circ})\div2=6^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Not realising the isosceles triangle $OAB$ has a very obtuse apex angle, making both base angles small; estimating $\angle OAB$ by eye instead of calculating it.

exam_questions.statement:
$AB$ is a diameter of a circle, centre $O$. $C$ is a point on the circle with $\angle CAB=37^{\circ}$. The tangent to the circle at $B$ meets the line $AC$ extended beyond $C$ at $D$.
(a) Find $\angle ACB$, giving a reason. [2]
(b) Find $\angle ABD$, giving a reason. [1]
(c) Find $\angle ADB$. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $\angle ACB=90^{\circ}$ (angle in a semicircle). (b) $\angle ABD=90^{\circ}$ (angle between a tangent and a radius is $90^{\circ}$; $AB$ passes through the centre, so it lies along the radius $OB$). (c) In triangle $ABD$: $\angle ABD=90^{\circ}$ and $\angle BAD=\angle BAC=37^{\circ}$ ($D$ lies on line $AC$), so $\angle ADB=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-37^{\circ}=53^{\circ}$ (angles in a triangle add up to $180^{\circ}$). Check: in triangle $ABC$, $\angle ABC=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-37^{\circ}=53^{\circ}$, and $\angle ADB=\angle ABC$ because the right-angled triangles $ACB$ and $ABD$ share the angle at $A$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for $90^{\circ}$; B1 for the reason 'angle in a semicircle'
(b) B1 for $90^{\circ}$ with the tangent-radius reason
(c) M1 for using the triangle angle sum in a correctly identified triangle; A1 for $53^{\circ}$
common_errors: In part (c), forgetting that $\angle BAD=\angle BAC$ (the same angle, since $D$ lies on the extension of line $CA$), and treating it as an unknown separate angle.

exam_questions.statement:
$A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie on a circle with centre $O$, in that order. $\angle AOC=140^{\circ}$ (the non-reflex angle at the centre, standing on the arc $ADC$ that does not contain $B$).
(a) Find $\angle ABC$, giving a reason. [2]
(b) Hence find $\angle ADC$, giving a reason. [2]
(c) $\angle DAB=100^{\circ}$. Find $\angle BCD$. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $\angle ABC=140^{\circ}\div2=70^{\circ}$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, same arc $AC$). (b) $\angle ADC=180^{\circ}-70^{\circ}=110^{\circ}$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ add up to $180^{\circ}$). (c) $\angle BCD=180^{\circ}-100^{\circ}=80^{\circ}$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$: $\angle DAB$ and $\angle BCD$ are opposite).
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for doubling/halving correctly; A1 for $70^{\circ}$
(b) M1 for using $180^{\circ}-\angle ABC$; A1 for $110^{\circ}$ with the cyclic-quadrilateral reason stated
(c) M1 for $180^{\circ}-100^{\circ}$; A1 for $80^{\circ}$
common_errors: In part (b), using the angle-at-the-centre theorem again instead of the cyclic-quadrilateral theorem, since $\angle ADC$ and $\angle AOC$ do not stand on the same arc in the required relationship.

exam_questions.statement:
$A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are points on a circle. $SAT$ is the tangent to the circle at $A$, and $BD$ is drawn. $\angle TAB=58^{\circ}$ and $\angle ADC=94^{\circ}$, as shown in the diagram.
(a) Find $\angle ACB$, giving a reason. [2]
(b) Find $\angle ADB$, giving a reason. [2]
(c) Find $\angle ABC$. [1]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $\angle ACB=58^{\circ}$ (the angle between a tangent and a chord is equal to the angle in the alternate segment: $\angle TAB$ and $\angle ACB$ both stand on the chord $AB$, and $C$ lies in the segment on the other side of $AB$ from $\angle TAB$). (b) $\angle ADB=58^{\circ}$ (angles in the same segment are equal: $\angle ADB$ and $\angle ACB$ both stand on the chord $AB$, with $C$ and $D$ on the same side of it). (c) $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, so $\angle ABC=180^{\circ}-\angle ADC=180^{\circ}-94^{\circ}=86^{\circ}$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$). Check: in triangle $ABC$, $\angle BAC=180^{\circ}-58^{\circ}-86^{\circ}=36^{\circ}$, which agrees with the diagram.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for $58^{\circ}$; B1 for the reason 'the angle between a tangent and a chord is equal to the angle in the alternate segment'
(b) B1 for $58^{\circ}$; B1 for the reason 'angles in the same segment are equal'
(c) B1 for $86^{\circ}$ from $180^{\circ}-94^{\circ}$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral)
common_errors: In (a), matching $\angle TAB$ to $\angle ADB$ or to an angle on the same side of $AB$ as the tangent angle, instead of to the angle in the alternate segment.
In (b), quoting the alternate segment theorem again rather than 'angles in the same segment are equal', which is the reason that earns the mark here.
In (c), pairing $\angle ADC$ with $\angle BCD$ or $\angle DAB$ instead of its opposite angle $\angle ABC$.

assets.caption: $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a circle; $SAT$ is the tangent at $A$. The given angles $\angle TAB=58^{\circ}$ and $\angle ADC=94^{\circ}$ are marked, and $BD$ is shown dashed.
assets.purpose: Give the question the figure an exam paper would print, showing only the two given angles.

challenge_questions.statement: Prove that the angle in a semicircle is $90^{\circ}$, using the fact that the radii $OA$, $OB$ and $OC$ are equal and the angle sum of a triangle (where $AB$ is a diameter and $C$ is any other point on the circle).
challenge_questions.answer: $\angle ACB=90^{\circ}$, proved using two isosceles triangles and the triangle angle sum.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Let $\angle OAC=a$ and $\angle OBC=b$. Since $OA=OC$ (radii), triangle $OAC$ is isosceles, so $\angle OCA=a$. Since $OB=OC$ (radii), triangle $OBC$ is isosceles, so $\angle OCB=b$. In triangle $ABC$: $\angle A+\angle B+\angle C=a+b+(a+b)=180^{\circ}$, so $2(a+b)=180^{\circ}$, giving $a+b=90^{\circ}$. But $\angle ACB=\angle OCA+\angle OCB=a+b=90^{\circ}$, as required.

challenge_questions.statement: Use the angle at the centre theorem to prove that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$.
challenge_questions.answer: $\angle BAD+\angle BCD=180^{\circ}$, proved using the angle-at-the-centre theorem on both sides of chord $BD$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Let $\angle BAD=x$. The angle at the centre $\angle BOD$, on the arc not containing $A$, is $2x$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, same arc). The reflex angle $\angle BOD=360^{\circ}-2x$ (on the other side, the arc not containing $C$) is twice $\angle BCD$ (same theorem, applied to $C$ on that arc), so $\angle BCD=(360^{\circ}-2x)\div2=180^{\circ}-x$. Then $\angle BAD+\angle BCD=x+(180^{\circ}-x)=180^{\circ}$, as required.

challenge_questions.statement: Alternate segment theorem. $T$ is on a circle with centre $O$ and $TA$ is a chord. The angle between the tangent at $T$ and the chord $TA$ is $t$. Show that $\angle TOA=2t$, and deduce that the angle in the alternate segment is $t$.
challenge_questions.answer: $\angle TOA=2t$, and the angle in the alternate segment is $t$, proved using the tangent-radius theorem, the isosceles triangle $OTA$, and the angle-at-the-centre theorem.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The radius $OT$ is perpendicular to the tangent at $T$ (tangent-radius theorem), so the angle between $OT$ and the chord $TA$ is $90^{\circ}-t$. Since $OT=OA$ (radii), triangle $OTA$ is isosceles, so $\angle OAT=90^{\circ}-t$ too. By the triangle angle sum, $\angle TOA=180^{\circ}-2(90^{\circ}-t)=180^{\circ}-180^{\circ}+2t=2t$. The angle in the alternate segment (at the circumference, standing on the same arc $TA$ as $\angle TOA$) is half of $\angle TOA$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference): $2t\div2=t$, matching the original tangent-chord angle.

challenge_questions.statement: $AB$ is a diameter of length $20$\,cm and $C$ is a point on the circle with $\angle ABC=30^{\circ}$. Find $AC$ and $BC$ (to $3$ s.f.).
challenge_questions.full_solution: $\angle ACB=90^{\circ}$ (angle in a semicircle), so triangle $ACB$ is right-angled at $C$ with hypotenuse $AB=20$\,cm. $AC=AB\sin(\angle ABC)=20\sin30^{\circ}=10.0$\,cm (opposite side to $\angle ABC$). $BC=AB\cos(\angle ABC)=20\cos30^{\circ}=17.3$\,cm (3 s.f.) (adjacent side to $\angle ABC$).

challenge_questions.statement: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral with $AB\parallel DC$. Show that $AD=BC$.
challenge_questions.answer: $AD=BC$, proved by showing the trapezium $ABCD$ has equal base angles at $D$ and $C$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $\angle BAD+\angle ADC=180^{\circ}$ (co-interior angles, since $AB\parallel DC$) and $\angle BAD+\angle BCD=180^{\circ}$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$). Subtracting these two equations, $\angle ADC=\angle BCD$. A trapezium ($AB\parallel DC$) whose two angles at the ends of the same parallel side ($DC$) are equal is an isosceles trapezium (it is symmetrical about the perpendicular bisector of $DC$), so its non-parallel sides are equal: $AD=BC$.

challenge_questions.statement: Two lighthouses $A$ and $B$ are on a coast. A boat $P$ sails so that $\angle APB=40^{\circ}$ always. Explain why the boat travels on a circular arc.
challenge_questions.answer: The boat's path is a circular arc through $A$ and $B$, by the converse of the angles-in-the-same-segment theorem.
challenge_questions.full_solution: By the angles-in-the-same-segment theorem, every point on one particular arc of a circle through $A$ and $B$, on one side of $AB$, sees $AB$ at the same fixed angle. The converse is also true: the set (locus) of all points $P$ with a constant angle $\angle APB=40^{\circ}$ is exactly such an arc of a circle through $A$ and $B$. Since the boat maintains $\angle APB=40^{\circ}$ at all times, it must be travelling along this circular arc.

mcq.stem: $A$, $B$, $P$ are three points on a circle, and $AB$ is a chord that does NOT pass through the centre. Is $\angle APB=90^{\circ}$?

options.text: No — the angle in a semicircle theorem gives $90^{\circ}$ only when $AB$ is a diameter
Yes, always, since $P$ is a point on the circle and $AB$ is a chord
options.why_wrong: The $90^{\circ}$ result requires $AB$ specifically to be a DIAMETER (a chord through the centre); an ordinary chord gives no fixed angle at all.

options.text: Yes, but only if $P$ is the midpoint of the major arc
options.why_wrong: The position of $P$ on the circle does not create a fixed $90^{\circ}$ angle unless $AB$ is itself a diameter; the midpoint of the arc is not the relevant condition.

options.text: No, it is always acute
options.why_wrong: If $P$ is on the minor arc, $\angle APB$ is obtuse, so it is not always acute. (For a chord that is not a diameter, $\angle APB$ is acute when $P$ is on the major arc and obtuse when $P$ is on the minor arc — it is never exactly $90^{\circ}$.)

mcq.explanation: The angle in a semicircle theorem requires $AB$ to be a diameter. For a chord that does not pass through the centre, $\angle APB$ is not $90^{\circ}$: it is acute if $P$ is on the major arc and obtuse if $P$ is on the minor arc.

mcq.stem: A tangent touches a circle at $T$. $O$ is the centre, and $M$ is a different point on the circle. Is the angle between the tangent and the radius $OM$ necessarily $90^{\circ}$?

options.text: Yes, any radius is perpendicular to any tangent of the same circle
options.why_wrong: The $90^{\circ}$ fact applies only to the ONE radius drawn to the specific point where the tangent touches the circle, not to a radius drawn to any other point.

options.text: No — only the radius to the actual point of contact, $T$, is perpendicular to the tangent
Yes, because all radii of a circle are equal
options.why_wrong: Radii being equal in length has nothing to do with which one is perpendicular to a given tangent; only the radius to the point of contact has that property.

options.text: Cannot be determined without knowing the circle's radius
options.why_wrong: The radius's length does not decide this; it is the LOCATION of the radius's endpoint (at the point of contact or not) that decides it.

mcq.explanation: A tangent is perpendicular only to the radius drawn to its specific point of contact; a radius to any other point is not guaranteed to meet the tangent at $90^{\circ}$.

mcq.stem: In an exam answer, which of these is an acceptable reason for a 'bow-tie' pair of equal angles made by the same chord on the same side?

options.text: Bow-tie angles
options.why_wrong: 'Bow-tie' is a visual nickname for spotting the configuration, not a proper geometrical theorem statement; it will not earn the reasoning mark.

options.text: Angles in a circle are equal
options.why_wrong: This statement is too vague and is not even generally true (most angle pairs in a circle are NOT equal); the exact condition ('same segment') must be stated.

options.text: Angles in the same segment are equal
The angles look the same size in the diagram
options.why_wrong: A visual impression from a diagram is never a valid geometric reason, and diagrams in exams are often 'not drawn accurately'.

mcq.explanation: The only acceptable written reason is the full, exact theorem statement: 'angles in the same segment are equal'.

mcq.stem: $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie on a circle, with $C$ and $D$ on OPPOSITE sides of chord $AB$. What is true of $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$?

options.text: They are equal, by the angles-in-the-same-segment theorem
options.why_wrong: The same-segment theorem only applies when both angles are on the SAME side of the chord; $C$ and $D$ here are on OPPOSITE sides, so the cyclic-quadrilateral (supplementary) rule applies instead.

options.text: Nothing can be said about the relationship
options.why_wrong: A definite relationship does hold (the two angles add up to $180^{\circ}$), via the cyclic-quadrilateral theorem; it is not an indeterminate case.

options.text: Their difference is always $90^{\circ}$
options.why_wrong: There is no general $90^{\circ}$-difference rule for this configuration; the correct relationship is that the two angles sum to $180^{\circ}$.

options.text: They add up to $180^{\circ}$ (opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral $ACBD$)

mcq.explanation: $C$ and $D$ on opposite sides of $AB$ means $ACBD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, so $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$ (opposite angles) add up to $180^{\circ}$.

mcq.stem: $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are points on a circle with centre $O$. $\angle AOB=80^{\circ}$ (centre angle on the arc not containing $C$ or $D$). Is $\angle ACD$ necessarily $40^{\circ}$?

options.text: No — the $\times2$ relationship only connects $\angle AOB$ to an angle standing on the SAME arc $AB$, not to $\angle ACD$
Yes, since any angle at the centre is always twice any angle at the circumference in the same circle
options.why_wrong: The $\times2$ relationship only holds between an angle at the centre and an angle at the circumference that stand on the SAME arc; $\angle ACD$ is subtended by a different chord ($AD$), not $AB$, so no fixed relationship to $\angle AOB$ exists.

options.text: Yes, because all four points lie on the same circle
options.why_wrong: Lying on the same circle is not sufficient; the specific arc each angle stands on must match for the doubling relationship to apply.

options.text: Only if $ABCD$ happens to be a cyclic quadrilateral
options.why_wrong: $ABCD$ being a cyclic quadrilateral is automatic (all four points are already on the circle); that alone does not create a fixed numeric relationship between $\angle AOB$ and $\angle ACD$, which stand on different arcs.

mcq.explanation: The angle-at-the-centre theorem only relates an angle at the centre to an angle at the circumference standing on the exact same arc; $\angle ACD$ stands on arc $AD$, not arc $AB$, so no fixed relationship to $\angle AOB$ is implied.

mcq.stem: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral with $\angle BAD=92^{\circ}$. What is $\angle BCD$?

options.why_wrong: This treats the opposite angles as equal instead of supplementary; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$, they are not equal in general.
This computes $360^{\circ}-92^{\circ}$ (the sum of the OTHER three angles), not the single opposite angle, which comes from $180^{\circ}-92^{\circ}$.

options.text: Cannot be determined without more information
options.why_wrong: The opposite-angle sum rule for a cyclic quadrilateral fixes $\angle BCD$ exactly, given $\angle BAD$; no further information is needed.

mcq.explanation: $\angle BCD=180^{\circ}-92^{\circ}=88^{\circ}$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$).

flashcards.front: Angle in a semicircle
flashcards.back: If $AB$ is a diameter and $P$ is any other point on the circle, $\angle APB=90^{\circ}$.

flashcards.front: Tangent and radius
flashcards.back: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact: the angle between them is $90^{\circ}$.

flashcards.front: Angle at the centre
flashcards.back: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, standing on the same arc.

flashcards.front: Angles in the same segment
flashcards.back: Angles subtended by the same chord, on the same side of it, are equal.

flashcards.front: Cyclic quadrilateral theorem
flashcards.back: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$.

flashcards.front: Alternate segment theorem
flashcards.back: The angle between a tangent and a chord (from the point of contact) equals the angle in the alternate segment.

flashcards.front: The one step that unlocks most circle problems
flashcards.back: Whenever the centre $O$ and two circle points $A$, $B$ appear, draw radii $OA$, $OB$: $OA=OB$ makes triangle $OAB$ isosceles.

flashcards.front: True or false: the angle in a semicircle is $90^{\circ}$ for ANY chord, not just a diameter.
flashcards.back: False. It only holds when the chord is a DIAMETER (passes through the centre).

flashcards.front: True or false: any radius of a circle is perpendicular to a given tangent.
flashcards.back: False. Only the ONE radius drawn to the actual point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent.

flashcards.front: Same chord, same side vs. opposite sides of it — which rule applies?
flashcards.back: Same side: angles in the same segment are EQUAL. Opposite sides: cyclic quadrilateral, angles ADD TO $180^{\circ}$.

flashcards.front: True or false: 'bow-tie' or 'Z theorem' are acceptable exam reasons.
flashcards.back: False. Nicknames help you spot the configuration, but the written reason must be the exact theorem statement, e.g. 'angles in the same segment are equal'.

flashcards.front: Why is the angle-at-the-centre theorem the 'master theorem' behind the others?
flashcards.back: The semicircle theorem is its special case (straight angle $180^{\circ}$ at the centre gives $90^{\circ}$ at the circumference); the same-segment and cyclic-quadrilateral theorems both follow from applying it on each side of a chord.

flashcards.front: Converse of the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem
flashcards.back: A right-angled triangle can always be drawn inside a circle with its hypotenuse as the diameter.

flashcards.front: How to check a circle-theorem answer
flashcards.back: Ask: is a right angle expected (diameter or tangent)? Is the centre angle bigger than the circumference angle? Do cyclic-quadrilateral/triangle sums check out? Always confirm with a second route.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The angle in a semicircle theorem ($\angle APB=90^{\circ}$) can be used whenever $A$, $B$, $P$ are any three points on a circle, regardless of whether $AB$ is a diameter.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The theorem is simple to state and the diagram often looks similar whether or not $AB$ genuinely passes through the centre, so the crucial condition can be overlooked under time pressure.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes $\angle APB=90^{\circ}$ without first checking (or stating) that $AB$ is a diameter.
misconceptions.correct_model: The angle in a semicircle is $90^{\circ}$ ONLY when the chord is a diameter (marked as such, or explicitly passing through the centre $O$). For any other chord, there is no such fixed angle.
misconceptions.remediation: Before applying the theorem, explicitly check the diagram for a marked diameter or a chord stated to pass through the centre.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any radius drawn in a circle with a tangent is perpendicular to that tangent, not just the radius to the actual point of contact.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The $90^{\circ}$ fact is memorised as 'tangent and radius are perpendicular' without the extra phrase 'at the point of contact', so it is easy to apply it to the wrong radius in a busy diagram with several radii drawn.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner marks a right angle between the tangent and a radius drawn to a point OTHER than where the tangent actually touches the circle.
misconceptions.correct_model: The tangent is perpendicular only to the ONE specific radius drawn to the point of contact (where the tangent actually touches the circle); it is not perpendicular to a radius drawn to any other point.
misconceptions.remediation: Always state the full theorem with its condition: 'a tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact', identifying that exact point before marking any right angle.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A circle theorem can be identified in writing by its visual nickname ('bow-tie', 'Z theorem') or by a vague statement such as 'angles in a circle are equal'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Visual nicknames are a genuinely useful way to SPOT the relevant configuration quickly on a diagram, so it is a natural (but incorrect) next step to also use them as the WRITTEN reason, exactly as with the 'Z angles'/'F angles' nicknames in parallel-line reasoning.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes 'bow-tie' or 'angles in a circle are equal' as the stated reason, instead of the exact theorem name.
misconceptions.correct_model: The exact theorem statement must be given as the written reason, for example 'angles in the same segment are equal' or 'opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$' — nicknames and vague statements do not earn the reasoning mark.
misconceptions.remediation: Practice translating each nickname into its full, exact, mark-scheme wording before writing any final solution.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The 'angles in the same segment are equal' theorem can be applied to two angles subtended by the same chord on OPPOSITE sides of it.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both cases (same side, opposite sides) involve two angles made by the same chord at the circumference, so it is easy to apply the equality rule without first checking which side of the chord each angle is on.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner sets two angles subtended by the same chord, but on opposite sides, EQUAL to each other.
misconceptions.correct_model: Angles subtended by the same chord are equal only when they are on the SAME side of the chord (same segment). On OPPOSITE sides, the four points form a cyclic quadrilateral, and the two angles ADD UP TO $180^{\circ}$ instead.
misconceptions.remediation: Before applying 'angles in the same segment', check explicitly which side of the chord each angle's vertex lies on; opposite sides means the cyclic-quadrilateral (supplementary) rule applies instead.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The angle-at-the-centre theorem (centre angle $=2\times$ circumference angle) can relate ANY angle at the centre to ANY angle at the circumference in the same diagram.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Once the $\times2$ relationship is memorised as a general-purpose fact about circles, it is easy to apply it to a pair of angles that happen to be in the same figure, without checking they stand on the same arc.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner doubles or halves an angle to relate it to a different angle in the diagram that is NOT subtended by the same arc.
misconceptions.correct_model: The angle-at-the-centre theorem only relates the angle at the centre and the angle at the circumference when they are subtended by the SAME arc (or chord). Angles subtended by different arcs have no such fixed relationship.
misconceptions.remediation: Before applying the theorem, trace which arc each angle 'stands on' (is subtended by) and confirm both angles share that exact same arc.

common_mistakes.mistake: Applying the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem to a chord that is not actually a diameter.
common_mistakes.why: The visual impression of 'a chord with a point opposite it' can resemble the semicircle configuration even when the chord does not pass through the centre.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before using the theorem, explicitly check the diagram (or the given information) for a marked diameter or a chord stated to pass through $O$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Marking a right angle between a tangent and a radius that is NOT drawn to the point of contact.
common_mistakes.why: A diagram with several radii drawn can make it unclear which one is the radius specifically to where the tangent touches the circle.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Identify the point of contact first, then draw (or confirm) the one radius to that exact point before marking any right angle.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing a visual nickname ('bow-tie', 'Z theorem') as the exam reason instead of the full theorem statement.
common_mistakes.why: Nicknames are genuinely useful for spotting a configuration quickly, so it is a natural (but incorrect) step to also write them as the final reason.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Use the nickname mentally to spot the pattern, then always translate it into the exact wording (e.g. 'angles in the same segment are equal') before writing the final answer.

exam_notes: Reasons are marked (B marks) separately from the angle itself; 'give a reason for your answer' or 'give a geometrical reason' must be answered with a named theorem, in full, not a nickname.

Give angles exactly if they are whole numbers; otherwise give them to $1$ decimal place. Circle-theorem questions appear on both the non-calculator papers (Papers 1 and 2) and the calculator papers (Papers 3 and 4), so practise the angle reasoning without a calculator.

Only two circle theorems (angle in a semicircle; tangent perpendicular to radius) are examinable on the Core paper; the remaining four (centre, same segment, cyclic quadrilateral, alternate segment) appear only on the Extended paper.
A diagram marked 'not drawn accurately' can never be measured with a protractor or ruler; always find angles by reasoning, and check the final answer with a second, independent route.

summary.big_idea: Most circle theorems in this lesson come from one underlying picture — an arc 'sees' an angle at the centre that is twice the angle it sees at the circumference — and the Core syllabus examines only the two right-angle facts: the angle in a semicircle (a diameter) and the angle between a tangent and the radius at the point of contact.
key_points: Angle in a semicircle $=90^{\circ}$ (chord must be a diameter). Tangent $\perp$ radius at the point of contact.
Two radii always make an isosceles triangle — draw them whenever the centre and two circle points appear together.
Extended: angle at the centre $=2\times$ angle at the circumference (same arc); angles in the same segment (same side of a chord) are equal.
Extended: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$; the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.
Always write the exact theorem name as the reason — nicknames like 'bow-tie' or 'Z theorem' never earn the reasoning mark.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Check the trigger condition before applying any theorem (is it really a diameter? really the radius to the point of contact? really the same arc? really the same side of the chord?), then write the exact theorem name as the reason.
