08_Circle_Theorems_II.json.title: Circle Theorems II
08_Circle_Theorems_II.json.subject: Mathematics

objectives.statement: Use the fact that the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (and its converse, that the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre) to find chord lengths and distances, using Pythagoras' theorem.
Use the fact that equal chords are equidistant from the centre (and its converse) to compare or find chord lengths and distances.
Use the fact that tangents from an external point are equal in length, and the symmetry of the kite this creates, to find lengths and angles.
Combine the chord and tangent-length properties with Pythagoras' theorem, trigonometric ratios and the circle angle theorems (lesson 4.7) in multi-step problems, giving a reason for every step.

prerequisites.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every property in this lesson (chord-distance, equal chords, tangent length) produces a right-angled triangle, and Pythagoras' theorem is the tool that turns that triangle into a numeric answer in almost every exercise.

prerequisites.statement: Use the fact that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact (lesson 4.7).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The tangent-length theorem and every tangent-related right-angled triangle in this lesson depends directly on this one fact from the previous lesson to establish the right angle in the first place.

prerequisites.statement: Use the sine, cosine and tangent ratios in a right-angled triangle (formally taught in the Trigonometry unit).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several problems (finding the angle between two tangents, or a chord's half-angle at the centre) need a trig ratio, not just Pythagoras. Trigonometry is taught formally in its own unit; if you have not met it yet, leave those problems until you have.

prerequisites.statement: Use the fact that base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal (lesson 4.6).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Both the radii-to-a-chord triangle and the tangent kite are built from isosceles triangles (equal radii; equal tangent lengths), and several angle-chasing steps depend on this fact.

diagnostic_items.question: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse $13$\,cm and one of its shorter sides $5$\,cm. Find the length of the third side.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Adds the squares instead of subtracting: the $13$\,cm side is the hypotenuse (it is the longest side), so it is already $c$ in $a^2+b^2=c^2$ and the missing side must be found by subtraction.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner can identify the hypotenuse and subtract to find a missing shorter side. Every property in this lesson (chord-distance, equal chords, tangent length) ends in exactly this calculation.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Practise naming the hypotenuse first (the side opposite the right angle, always the longest), then decide whether to add or subtract the squares, on a short set of right-angled triangles before starting this lesson.

diagnostic_items.question: A chord is at distance $0$ from the centre. What is it?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: A diameter (the chord passes through the centre itself).

common_wrong_answers.answer: A radius, or 'an impossible chord'.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Fails to connect 'distance $0$ from the centre' with 'the chord passes through the centre', which is exactly the definition of a diameter.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the limiting case of the chord-distance relationship, connecting it to the earlier vocabulary (lesson 4.7) that a diameter is a chord through the centre.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Substitute $d=0$ into $c=2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}=2\sqrt{r^2}=2r$ and confirm this is exactly the diameter's length.

diagnostic_items.question: $PT$ is a tangent to a circle with centre $O$, touching the circle at $T$. What is the size of $\angle OTP$, and what is the reason?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $\angle OTP=90^{\circ}$, because the angle between a tangent and the radius drawn to the point of contact is $90^{\circ}$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It depends on where $P$ lies on the tangent, so it cannot be found.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Misses that the right angle is at the point of contact $T$ between $OT$ and the whole tangent line, so it is $90^{\circ}$ for every point $P$ on that tangent.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the one fact from lesson 4.7 that creates the right-angled triangle in every tangent problem in this lesson. Without it, $OT^2+TP^2=OP^2$ cannot be justified.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Have the learner draw a circle, a radius and the tangent at that point, mark the right angle, and state the reason in words, before meeting the tangent-length theorem.

diagnostic_items.question: In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is $10$\,cm and the side opposite the angle $\theta$ is $6$\,cm. Write down $\sin\theta$ and find $\theta$ to $1$ d.p.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{6}{10}=0.6$, so $\theta=36.9^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).

common_wrong_answers.answer: $\cos\theta=0.6$, so $\theta=53.1^{\circ}$.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Picks the wrong ratio: $6$\,cm is *opposite* $\theta$ and $10$\,cm is the hypotenuse, which is the sine ratio. Using cosine finds the other acute angle instead.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner can label a side as opposite, adjacent or hypotenuse relative to a named angle and choose the matching ratio. Problems such as the angle between two tangents need this, not just Pythagoras.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Revise labelling opposite/adjacent/hypotenuse for a named angle and the SOH-CAH-TOA choice in the Trigonometry unit. This prerequisite is not blocking: the chord and tangent-length work that needs only Pythagoras can be done first.

diagnostic_items.question: Why is $OTPT'$ (centre, two points of contact, external point) a kite?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $OT=OT'$ (radii of the same circle) and $PT=PT'$ (tangents from an external point are equal), so it has two pairs of adjacent equal sides, which is the definition of a kite.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Because it looks symmetrical in the diagram.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Relies on a visual impression rather than the two separate equal-length facts (one about radii, one about tangents) that together prove the kite property.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the kite shape is understood as the LOGICAL CONSEQUENCE of combining two separate theorems (equal radii; equal tangents), not just an observed visual pattern.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Have the learner state both equalities separately with their separate reasons (radii; tangent-length theorem) before concluding 'two pairs of adjacent equal sides, so it is a kite'.

diagnostic_items.question: In triangle $OAB$, $OA=OB$ and $\angle AOB=80^{\circ}$. Find $\angle OAB$.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $\angle OAB=50^{\circ}$, since the base angles are equal: $(180^{\circ}-80^{\circ})\div2=50^{\circ}$.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Subtracts $80^{\circ}$ from $180^{\circ}$ but forgets that the remaining $100^{\circ}$ is shared equally between the *two* equal base angles, so it must be halved.

common_wrong_answers.answer: $80^{\circ}$, the same as $\angle AOB$.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Confuses 'two equal angles' with 'all three angles equal'; it is the two base angles opposite the equal sides that are equal, not the apex angle.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the isosceles base-angle fact in the exact shape used throughout this lesson: $O$ is the centre, $OA$ and $OB$ are radii, so every triangle made by two radii and a chord is isosceles. The same step is needed in the tangent kite, where $PT=PT'$ makes triangle $PTT'$ isosceles.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Have the learner mark the two equal sides, then the two equal angles *opposite* them, and use $2x+\text{apex}=180^{\circ}$ on a few isosceles triangles before starting this lesson.

theory_blocks.title: Every property in this lesson is a symmetry argument
theory_blocks.body:
Reflect a circle in any line through its centre and it lands on itself. So the centre must lie on the line of symmetry of every chord (its perpendicular bisector), two chords that are mirror images have the same length and the same distance from the centre, and the two tangents from an outside point are mirror images in the line joining that point to the centre.

Each property in this lesson is [[blue:a symmetry argument]], and each one produces a right-angled triangle where Pythagoras applies.

theory_blocks.title: Chords and the centre
theory_blocks.body:
- The line from the centre of a circle **perpendicular to a chord bisects the chord**.
- The **perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre** of the circle.

The distance from the centre to a chord is the *perpendicular* distance. If a chord has length $c$ and is at distance $d$ from the centre, and the radius is $r$, then by Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle formed by the radius, the distance, and half the chord: $$r^2=d^2+\left(\frac c2\right)^2,\qquad\text{so}\qquad c=2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}\quad\text{and}\quad d=\sqrt{r^2-\left(\tfrac c2\right)^2}.$$

Why is it true? Let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to the chord $AB$. $OA=OB$ (radii), so triangle $OAB$ is isosceles.

In an isosceles triangle the perpendicular from the apex to the base is also the median, so $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Conversely, the centre is equidistant from $A$ and $B$, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

This is why the centre of a circle through three points can be found by drawing the perpendicular bisectors of two chords: the centre is where they intersect.

assets.caption: Left: the perpendicular $OM$ from the centre to chord $AB$ bisects it. Right: the perpendicular bisectors of two chords $AB$ and $BC$ meet at the centre $O$.
assets.purpose: Show both the basic bisection fact and its practical use (locating an unknown centre from two chords) as a single connected pair of figures.

theory_blocks.title: Chord-distance errors
theory_blocks.body:
- Using the full chord instead of half the chord in Pythagoras' theorem: the right-angled triangle has sides $r$, $d$ and [[green:$\tfrac12c$]], never $r$, $d$ and [[red:$c$]].
- Measuring the distance from the centre to the chord along a radius to an endpoint. The distance from a point to a line is the *perpendicular* distance, which is always shorter than a radius to an endpoint (for a diameter it is $0$).

theory_blocks.title: Equal chords
theory_blocks.body:
**Equal chords are equidistant from the centre.** If two chords of a circle have the same length, their perpendicular distances from the centre are equal. Conversely, chords that are the same distance from the centre have equal lengths.

This follows at once from $c=2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}$: the length of a chord depends only on $r$ and $d$, and $r$ is fixed for a given circle. The nearer to the centre a chord is, the longer it is, and the longest possible chord is the diameter ($d=0$).

assets.caption: Equal chords $AB=CD$ are equidistant from the centre: $OM=ON$. The matching tick marks show the equal distances $OM$ and $ON$.
assets.purpose: Show the equal-chords-equal-distance relationship as a single figure with both chords and both perpendicular distances visible together.

theory_blocks.title: Tangents from an external point
theory_blocks.body:
**Tangents from an external point are equal in length.** If $PT$ and $PT'$ are tangents from a point $P$ outside a circle to the circle at $T$ and $T'$, then $PT=PT'$.

Why? The radii $OT$ and $OT'$ are perpendicular to the tangents (angle between a tangent and a radius is $90^{\circ}$), so triangles $OTP$ and $OT'P$ are right-angled, share the hypotenuse $OP$, and have $OT=OT'$.

By Pythagoras, $PT^2=OP^2-r^2=PT'^2$. The figure $OTPT'$ is a **kite** with two right angles at $T$ and $T'$: its line of symmetry $OP$ bisects the angles at $O$ and at $P$, and the angles at $O$ and $P$ add up to $360^{\circ}-2\times90^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$.

Also, $OP$ is the perpendicular bisector of the chord $TT'$.

assets.caption: The kite $OTPT'$: $PT=PT'$ (tangent lengths), with two right angles at $T$ and $T'$, and $OP$ as its line of symmetry.
assets.purpose: Show the kite shape directly, with its two right angles and symmetry line $OP$ visible, making the supplementary relationship between the angles at $O$ and $P$ geometrically obvious rather than a bare formula.

theory_blocks.title: Strategy and exam reasons
theory_blocks.body:
Learn to spot the trigger and write the exact reason:

| You see… | Reason to write |
|---|---|
| A perpendicular from $O$ to a chord (or to its midpoint) | The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord |
| The perpendicular bisector of a chord | The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre |
| Two chords of equal length | Equal chords are equidistant from the centre |
| Two chords at equal distance from $O$ | Chords equidistant from the centre are equal |
| Two tangents from the same point | Tangents from an external point are equal in length |
| A tangent and a radius | Angle between a tangent and a radius is $90^{\circ}$ |

theory_blocks.title: Method for chord and tangent-length problems
theory_blocks.body:
1. Look for a chord and draw the perpendicular from the centre to it (or join the centre to the endpoints).
2. Look for tangents from a common point and draw the radii to the points of contact.
3. You then have right-angled triangles (Pythagoras or trigonometry) and isosceles triangles (equal base angles).
4. Label lengths as you go and keep exact values (fractions, surds) until the last line.

theory_blocks.title: Checking chord and tangent answers
theory_blocks.body:
A chord is never longer than the diameter, so $c\le2r$; the distance $d$ satisfies $0\le d<r$; and a tangent length is always shorter than the distance $OP$ from the external point to the centre.

If you obtain a negative number under the square root (for example $r^2-c^2<0$ because the whole chord was used instead of half of it), then you have used the wrong triangle or forgotten to halve the chord — go back and check before continuing.

theory_blocks.title: Exam precision for lengths and angles
theory_blocks.body:
These symmetry properties are Extended content only, so they appear on Paper 2 (non-calculator) and Paper 4 (calculator); the tangent–radius right angle they rely on is also Core content.

They are often combined with Pythagoras, trigonometry or the angle theorems from lesson 4.7. Give lengths to $3$ significant figures and angles to $1$ decimal place unless the answer is exact.

In 'show that' questions, every reason must be stated explicitly.

keywords.definition: The shortest distance from the centre of a circle to a chord, measured along the line meeting the chord at $90^{\circ}$.
The line that crosses a segment at its midpoint at $90^{\circ}$; for any chord of a circle, this line passes through the centre.
The distance from an external point to a circle, measured along a tangent line to its point of contact; the two tangent lengths from the same external point are always equal.
A quadrilateral with two pairs of adjacent equal sides; the figure $OTPT'$ formed by a centre, two points of tangent contact and an external point is always a kite.

worked_examples.statement: Length of a chord. A circle has radius $13$\,cm and centre $O$. A chord $AB$ has length $24$\,cm. Find the perpendicular distance from $O$ to $AB$.
reasoning: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$; the line $OM$ is perpendicular to $AB$ and bisects it.
Use Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle $OMA$, with half the chord as one side.
worked_examples.solution: Let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to $AB$. Then $AM=24\div2=12$\,cm (the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord). In the right-angled triangle $OMA$: $d^2=OA^2-AM^2=13^2-12^2=169-144=25$, so $d=OM=5$\,cm.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the base-level skill the whole lesson builds on: halving the chord, naming the right-angled triangle $OMA$, and applying Pythagoras — every later chord problem is a variation of exactly this.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing $d^2=13^2-24^2$ (using the full chord instead of half of it), which gives a negative number — exactly the stop-and-check signal from the checking strategy.

worked_examples.statement: Equal chords. A circle has radius $17$\,cm. The chord $AB$ is $30$\,cm long. The chord $CD$ is the same distance from the centre as $AB$. (a) Find the distance of $AB$ from the centre. (b) Write down the length of $CD$, giving a reason.
knowns: radius $=17$\,cm; $AB=30$\,cm; $CD$ equidistant from the centre as $AB$
unknowns: distance of $AB$ from the centre; length of $CD$
reasoning: (a) Halve $AB$ and use Pythagoras to find its distance from the centre.
(b) Use the equal-chords-equidistant theorem directly, with no further calculation needed.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) Half of the chord is $15$\,cm (the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord), so $d^2=17^2-15^2=289-225=64$ and $d=8$\,cm.

(b) $CD=30$\,cm because chords that are equidistant from the centre are equal in length (equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and conversely).
worked_examples.interpretation: Part (b) shows the theorem used in its most efficient form: once two chords are known to be equidistant, their length is shared immediately, with no second Pythagoras calculation needed at all.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Recomputing $CD$ from scratch with Pythagoras in part (b), instead of recognising that the converse of the equal-chords theorem gives the length directly.

worked_examples.statement: Tangent lengths. From a point $P$, two tangents $PT$ and $PT'$ are drawn to a circle with centre $O$ and radius $8$\,cm. $OP=17$\,cm. Find (a) $PT$, (b) $\angle TPT'$ to $1$ d.p.
reasoning: (a) Use the tangent-radius right angle at $T$ and Pythagoras in triangle $OTP$.
(b) Use the sine ratio in the same right-angled triangle to find half of $\angle TPT'$, then double it (since $OP$ bisects the angle, by the kite's symmetry).
worked_examples.solution:
(a) $\angle OTP=90^{\circ}$ (angle between a tangent and a radius), so $PT^2=17^2-8^2=289-64=225$ and $PT=15$\,cm.

(b) In right-angled triangle $OTP$, $\sin\angle TPO=\dfrac{8}{17}$, so $\angle TPO=28.07\ldots^{\circ}$. $OP$ bisects $\angle TPT'$ (symmetry of the kite $OTPT'$; tangents from an external point are equal),

so $\angle TPT'=2\times28.07\ldots^{\circ}=56.1^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
worked_examples.interpretation:
Part (b) shows the kite's symmetry doing real work: rather than finding $\angle TPT'$ directly (which is not a right-angle-triangle angle), the method finds HALF of it in the right-angled triangle $OTP$,

then doubles, using the symmetry line $OP$ as the bridge.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating $\angle TPO$ itself as the final answer, forgetting to double it to get the full angle $\angle TPT'$ between the two tangents.

worked_examples.statement: Using equal tangents with angles. $PT$ and $PT'$ are tangents from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$. $\angle TPT'=50^{\circ}$. Find $\angle PTT'$, $\angle OTT'$ and $\angle TOT'$.
reasoning: Use the tangent-length theorem to identify triangle $PTT'$ as isosceles, then the triangle angle sum for $\angle PTT'$.
Subtract from the tangent-radius right angle to find $\angle OTT'$.
Use the isosceles triangle $OTT'$ (equal radii) and the triangle angle sum to find $\angle TOT'$; check with the kite's supplementary-angles fact.
worked_examples.solution:
$PT=PT'$ (tangents from an external point are equal), so triangle $PTT'$ is isosceles and $\angle PTT'=(180^{\circ}-50^{\circ})\div2=65^{\circ}$ (base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal; angles in a triangle add up to $180^{\circ}$). $\angle OTP=90^{\circ}$ (angle between a tangent and a radius), so $\angle OTT'=90^{\circ}-65^{\circ}=25^{\circ}$. $OT=OT'$ (radii), so $\angle OT'T=25^{\circ}$ and $\angle TOT'=180^{\circ}-2\times25^{\circ}=130^{\circ}$.

Check: $\angle TOT'+\angle TPT'=130^{\circ}+50^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The final check against $\angle TOT'+\angle TPT'=180^{\circ}$ confirms the whole four-step chain at once, and is exactly the supplementary-angles fact from the kite theory block, now verified numerically rather than just stated.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing $\angle TOT'=\angle TPT'=50^{\circ}$ directly (assuming equality, the related idea), instead of working through the isosceles triangle $OTT'$ to find the correct, different value $130^{\circ}$.

worked_examples.statement: A combined exam-style problem. $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from $P$ to a circle of centre $O$ and radius $5$\,cm. $OP=13$\,cm and $OP$ meets the chord $AB$ at $M$. Find $PA$, $AM$ and $AB$ (to $3$ s.f.).
reasoning: Find $PA$ using Pythagoras in right-angled triangle $OAP$.
Use the kite's symmetry to identify $M$ as the midpoint of $AB$, with $OP\perp AB$.
Compare two different expressions for the area of triangle $OAP$ to find $AM$ without first finding the angle.
worked_examples.solution:
$\angle OAP=90^{\circ}$ (angle between a tangent and a radius), so $PA^2=13^2-5^2=144$ and $PA=12$\,cm. $OP$ is the line of symmetry of the kite $OAPB$ (tangents from an external point are equal), so $OP\perp AB$ at $M$ and $AM=MB$ (perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord).

Comparing two expressions for the area of triangle $OAP$: $\tfrac12\times OP\times AM=\tfrac12\times OA\times AP$, so $AM=\dfrac{5\times12}{13}=\dfrac{60}{13}=4.62$\,cm (3 s.f.). So $AB=2\times AM=\dfrac{120}{13}=9.23$\,cm (3 s.f.).
worked_examples.interpretation:
The 'two areas of the same triangle' trick is the most advanced technique in this lesson: it finds $AM$ directly, without ever calculating an angle,

by using the SAME triangle's area computed two different ways (once with base $OP$, once with base $OA$).
worked_examples.common_mistake: Attempting to find $AM$ using an angle and trigonometry (a valid but much longer route) and making an avoidable rounding error, instead of using the shorter area-comparison method.

guided_exercises.statement: A circle has radius $15$\,cm. A chord $AB$ has length $18$\,cm. Find the perpendicular distance from the centre to $AB$.
hints: Halve the chord length first; this half-chord is one side of the right-angled triangle, not the full chord.
Use Pythagoras with the radius as the hypotenuse.
common_errors: Using $18$ (the full chord) instead of $9$ (half the chord) in the Pythagoras calculation.

guided_exercises.statement: A circle has radius $20$\,cm. Chord $AB$ has length $32$\,cm. Chord $CD$ is $16$\,cm from the centre. Find the distance of $AB$ from the centre, the length of $CD$, and state whether $AB$ and $CD$ are the same length.
hints: Find $AB$'s distance from the centre first, using Pythagoras with half of $AB$.
Find $CD$'s length using Pythagoras with $CD$'s given distance, then compare both distances.
guided_exercises.answer: $AB$ is $12$\,cm from the centre; $CD=24$\,cm; $AB$ and $CD$ are NOT the same length (they are at different distances from the centre).
guided_exercises.full_solution: Half of $AB$ is $16$\,cm: $d_{AB}^2=20^2-16^2=400-256=144$, so $d_{AB}=12$\,cm. For $CD$, at distance $16$\,cm: half-chord$^2=20^2-16^2=400-256=144$, so half-chord $=12$\,cm and $CD=24$\,cm. Since $AB$ is $12$\,cm from the centre but $CD$ is $16$\,cm from the centre (different distances), $AB\ne CD$ in length ($32$\,cm vs. $24$\,cm), consistent with 'equal chords are equidistant from the centre' — unequal distances mean unequal lengths.
common_errors: Assuming $AB=CD$ without checking, simply because both chords belong to the same circle.

guided_exercises.statement: $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents to a circle with centre $O$ and radius $6$\,cm, from an external point $P$ with $OP=10$\,cm. Find (a) $PA$, (b) $\angle OPA$ (1 d.p.), (c) $\angle APB$ (1 d.p.).
hints: Use Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle $OAP$ for part (a).
Use the sine ratio ($\sin\angle OPA=\dfrac{OA}{OP}$) for part (b), then double your answer for part (c), since $OP$ bisects $\angle APB$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) $PA^2=10^2-6^2=100-36=64$, so $PA=8$\,cm. (b) $\sin\angle OPA=\dfrac{6}{10}=0.6$, so $\angle OPA=36.87^{\circ}\approx36.9^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.). (c) $OP$ bisects $\angle APB$ (symmetry of the kite $OAPB$), so $\angle APB=2\times36.87^{\circ}=73.7^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
common_errors: Stopping after part (b) and reporting $36.9^{\circ}$ as the final answer to part (c), forgetting to double it.

exercises.statement: A circle has radius $10$\,cm. A chord $AB$ has length $16$\,cm. Find the distance from the centre to $AB$.
common_errors: Using $16$ instead of $8$ in the Pythagoras calculation.

exercises.statement: A circle has radius $25$\,cm. A chord is $24$\,cm from the centre. Find the length of the chord.
exercises.full_solution: Half-chord$^2=25^2-24^2=625-576=49$, so half-chord $=7$\,cm and the chord is $14$\,cm.
common_errors: Reporting the half-chord ($7$\,cm) as the final answer, forgetting to double it.

exercises.statement: A chord of length $20$\,cm is $12$\,cm from the centre of a circle. Find the radius (3 s.f.).
common_errors: Using the full chord ($20$) instead of half of it ($10$) in the Pythagoras calculation.

exercises.statement: Chords $AB$ and $CD$ of a circle of radius $15$\,cm are both $18$\,cm long. Find the distance of $CD$ from the centre, and give a reason.
exercises.full_solution: Half of $AB$ is $9$\,cm, so $d^2=15^2-9^2=225-81=144$, $d=12$\,cm for $AB$. Since $CD=18$\,cm too (equal to $AB$), $CD$ is also $12$\,cm from the centre (equal chords are equidistant from the centre).
common_errors: Recomputing $CD$'s distance from scratch with a separate Pythagoras calculation, instead of using the equal-chords theorem directly, since $CD$'s length was already given as equal to $AB$'s.

exercises.statement: $PT$ is a tangent to a circle of radius $9$\,cm and centre $O$, with $OP=15$\,cm. Find $PT$.
common_errors: Adding $15^2+9^2$ instead of subtracting, confusing which side is the hypotenuse.

exercises.statement: Tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$. $\angle APB=64^{\circ}$. Find $\angle PAB$, $\angle OAB$ and $\angle AOB$.
exercises.full_solution: $PA=PB$ (tangents from an external point), so triangle $PAB$ is isosceles and $\angle PAB=(180^{\circ}-64^{\circ})\div2=58^{\circ}$. $\angle OAB=90^{\circ}-58^{\circ}=32^{\circ}$ (angle between tangent and radius is $90^{\circ}$). $\angle AOB=180^{\circ}-2\times32^{\circ}=116^{\circ}$ (or equivalently $180^{\circ}-64^{\circ}=116^{\circ}$, from the kite's supplementary angles).
common_errors: Writing $\angle AOB=\angle APB=64^{\circ}$ (assuming equality instead of the correct supplementary relationship).

exercises.statement: $PA=(2x+3)$\,cm and $PB=(4x-9)$\,cm are tangents from $P$ to a circle. Find $x$ and $PA$.
exercises.full_solution: $PA=PB$ (tangents from an external point are equal): $2x+3=4x-9$, so $12=2x$, $x=6$; $PA=2(6)+3=15$\,cm.
common_errors: Adding the two expressions to a fixed total instead of setting them EQUAL to each other, confusing this with a different (sum-based) angle fact.

exercises.statement: A circle has radius $25$\,cm. A chord $AB$ is $48$\,cm long. (a) Find the distance of $AB$ from the centre. (b) A second chord $CD$ is $20$\,cm from the centre. Find its length.
common_errors: In part (b), reusing $AB$'s distance ($7$\,cm) instead of the newly given distance ($20$\,cm) for chord $CD$.

exercises.statement: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $8$\,cm. A chord $AB$ makes $\angle AOB=100^{\circ}$. Find the distance from $O$ to $AB$ and the length of $AB$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.full_solution: Triangle $OAB$ is isosceles with apex angle $100^{\circ}$; the perpendicular from $O$ bisects the apex angle, giving $50^{\circ}$ in the right-angled half-triangle. $d=8\cos50^{\circ}=5.14$\,cm (3 s.f.) and half of $AB$ is $8\sin50^{\circ}$, so $AB=2\times8\sin50^{\circ}=12.3$\,cm (3 s.f.).
common_errors: Using the full apex angle $100^{\circ}$ directly in the sine/cosine ratio instead of halving it first, since the right-angled triangle only contains HALF the apex angle.

exercises.statement: A circle passes through $A(0,0)$, $B(8,0)$ and $C(8,6)$. Use perpendicular bisectors to find the centre and the radius.
exercises.full_solution: The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ (horizontal, from $(0,0)$ to $(8,0)$) is the vertical line $x=4$. The perpendicular bisector of $BC$ (vertical, from $(8,0)$ to $(8,6)$) is the horizontal line $y=3$. The centre is where these meet: $(4,3)$. The radius is the distance from the centre to $A$: $\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5$. (Check: $\angle ABC=90^{\circ}$, so $AC$ is a diameter; its midpoint is $(4,3)$ and its length is $\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=10=2\times5$, confirming the radius.)
common_errors: Finding the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ (a diagonal, harder to compute) instead of using the two simpler axis-aligned chords $AB$ and $BC$.

exercises.statement: The cross-section of a circular tunnel has radius $3$\,m. The flat road surface is a chord $4.8$\,m wide. How far below the centre of the circle is the road?
common_errors: Using the full road width ($4.8$\,m) instead of half of it ($2.4$\,m) in the Pythagoras calculation.

exam_questions.statement:
A circle has centre $O$ and radius $26$\,cm. Chord $AB$ has length $48$\,cm.
(a) Find the perpendicular distance from $O$ to $AB$. [2]
(b) Chord $CD$ is $24$\,cm from the centre. Find the length of $CD$. [2]
(c) Is $CD$ equal in length to $AB$? Give a reason. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $d=10$\,cm. (b) $CD=20$\,cm. (c) No, since $AB$ and $CD$ are different distances from the centre ($10$\,cm and $24$\,cm), they cannot be equal in length.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Half of $AB$ is $24$\,cm (the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord): $d^2=26^2-24^2=676-576=100$, so $d=10$\,cm. (b) Half-chord$^2=26^2-24^2=676-576=100$, so half-chord $=10$\,cm and $CD=20$\,cm. (Notice that the numbers $10$ and $24$ simply swap roles compared with part (a).) (c) No. $AB$ is $10$\,cm from the centre but $CD$ is $24$\,cm from the centre; equal chords would be equidistant from the centre, so chords at different distances cannot be equal in length. Indeed $AB=48$\,cm and $CD=20$\,cm.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for halving the chord and using Pythagoras; A1 for $10$\,cm
(b) M1 for using Pythagoras with $d=24$; A1 for $CD=20$\,cm
(c) B1 for 'no', with a reason referring to different distances from the centre
common_errors: In part (c), comparing the two LENGTHS without reference to the underlying distances, instead of using the distance-equals-length relationship as the actual reason.

exam_questions.statement:
$PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from an external point $P$ to a circle with centre $O$ and radius $7$\,cm. $OP=25$\,cm.
(a) Find $PA$. [2]
(b) Find $\angle AOP$ to $1$ d.p. [2]
(c) Hence find $\angle AOB$ to $1$ d.p. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $\angle OAP=90^{\circ}$ (angle between a tangent and a radius is $90^{\circ}$), so $PA^2=25^2-7^2=625-49=576$ and $PA=24$\,cm. (b) In the right-angled triangle $OAP$, $OA$ is adjacent to $\angle AOP$ and $OP$ is the hypotenuse: $\cos\angle AOP=\dfrac{OA}{OP}=\dfrac{7}{25}=0.28$, so $\angle AOP=73.73\ldots^{\circ}=73.7^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.). Check: $\tan\angle AOP=\dfrac{24}{7}$ gives the same angle; it is the large angle of the triangle because it is opposite the longest leg $PA$. (c) $OP$ bisects $\angle AOB$ (symmetry of the kite $OAPB$; tangents from an external point are equal), so $\angle AOB=2\times73.73\ldots^{\circ}=147.5^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for Pythagoras; A1 for $24$\,cm
(b) M1 for a correct trig ratio in triangle $OAP$; A1 for $73.7^{\circ}$
(c) M1 for doubling their $\angle AOP$; A1 for $147.5^{\circ}$ (accept $147.4^{\circ}$ from doubling $73.7^{\circ}$)
common_errors: In part (b), using $\sin\angle AOP=\dfrac{7}{25}$ (mislabelling which angle is opposite which side), which finds $\angle APO$ instead of $\angle AOP$.

exam_questions.statement:
In the diagram, $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from the external point $P$ to the circle with centre $O$. $C$ is a point on the major arc $AB$, and $\angle APB=48^{\circ}$.
(a) Show that $\angle AOB=132^{\circ}$, giving a reason for each step. [3]
(b) Hence find $\angle ACB$, giving a reason. [2]
(c) Find $\angle PAB$, and name the circle theorem that confirms your answer agrees with part (b). [3]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\angle AOB=132^{\circ}$. (b) $\angle ACB=66^{\circ}$. (c) $\angle PAB=66^{\circ}$, confirmed by the alternate segment theorem.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) $\angle OAP=\angle OBP=90^{\circ}$, because the angle between a tangent and the radius drawn to the point of contact is $90^{\circ}$. $OAPB$ is a quadrilateral, and the angles of a quadrilateral add up to $360^{\circ}$, so $$\angle AOB=360^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-48^{\circ}=132^{\circ}.$$

(b) $\angle AOB$ is the angle at the centre and $\angle ACB$ is the angle at the circumference, both standing on the minor arc $AB$. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so $\angle ACB=\tfrac12\times132^{\circ}=66^{\circ}$.

(c) $PA=PB$ (tangents from an external point are equal in length), so triangle $PAB$ is isosceles and its base angles are equal: $\angle PAB=\dfrac{180^{\circ}-48^{\circ}}{2}=66^{\circ}$. This agrees with part (b) because of the alternate segment theorem: the angle between the tangent $PA$ and the chord $AB$ equals the angle $\angle ACB$ in the alternate segment.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for $\angle OAP=\angle OBP=90^{\circ}$ with the reason 'tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact'
(a) M1 for $360^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-48^{\circ}$, using the angle sum of quadrilateral $OAPB$
(a) A1 for the conclusion $\angle AOB=132^{\circ}$
(b) M1 for halving their $\angle AOB$, with the reason 'the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference'
(b) A1 for $66^{\circ}$
(c) M1 for $PA=PB$ (tangents from an external point are equal), so triangle $PAB$ is isosceles
(c) A1 for $\angle PAB=(180^{\circ}-48^{\circ})\div2=66^{\circ}$
(c) B1 for naming the alternate segment theorem as the reason the two answers agree
common_errors: In (a), using the angle sum of a triangle ($180^{\circ}$) on $OAPB$, or forgetting that *both* tangent-radius angles are $90^{\circ}$.
In (b), doubling instead of halving: $\angle ACB$ is the angle at the circumference, so it is the *smaller* of the two.
In (c), quoting 'the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal' without first justifying $PA=PB$ by the tangent-length theorem, which is the mark-earning step.

assets.caption: Tangents $PA$ and $PB$ from $P$ (red), the chord $AB$ (gold) and the angle $\angle ACB$ at a point $C$ on the major arc (green), with $\angle APB=48^{\circ}$ and the two tangent-radius right angles marked.
assets.purpose: Show in one figure how the tangent kite $OAPB$ (E4.8 symmetry properties) and the angle theorems at $C$ (E4.7) describe the same configuration, so students can see why parts (a), (b) and (c) are linked.

challenge_questions.statement: Prove that the line joining the centre of a circle to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.
challenge_questions.answer: $\angle OMA=\angle OMB=90^{\circ}$, proved using congruent triangles $OAM$ and $OBM$ (SSS).
challenge_questions.full_solution: $OA=OB$ (radii), so triangle $OAB$ is isosceles. Triangles $OAM$ and $OBM$ have $OA=OB$, $AM=MB$ (given $M$ is the midpoint), and the common side $OM$, so they are congruent (SSS). Hence $\angle OMA=\angle OMB$. These two angles lie on the straight line $AB$ and add up to $180^{\circ}$, so each is $90^{\circ}$; that is, $OM\perp AB$.

challenge_questions.statement: Two parallel chords $AB$ and $CD$ in a circle of radius $5$\,cm have lengths $6$\,cm and $8$\,cm. Find the possible distances between the chords.
challenge_questions.answer: $1$\,cm (same side of the centre) or $7$\,cm (opposite sides of the centre).
challenge_questions.full_solution: For $AB$ (length $6$\,cm): half-chord $=3$\,cm, $d_1=\sqrt{5^2-3^2}=\sqrt{25-9}=4$\,cm. For $CD$ (length $8$\,cm): half-chord $=4$\,cm, $d_2=\sqrt{5^2-4^2}=\sqrt{25-16}=3$\,cm. If the chords are on the same side of the centre, the distance between them is $4-3=1$\,cm; if on opposite sides, it is $4+3=7$\,cm.

challenge_questions.statement: Prove that equal chords are equidistant from the centre, using Pythagoras' theorem.
challenge_questions.answer: $d_1=d_2$, proved algebraically from the shared relationship $(c/2)^2=r^2-d^2$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: For a chord of length $c$ at distance $d$ from the centre of a circle with radius $r$: $(c/2)^2=r^2-d^2$ (Pythagoras). If two chords have equal lengths $c$ (and the same radius $r$), then $r^2-d_1^2=r^2-d_2^2$, so $d_1^2=d_2^2$, and since distances are positive, $d_1=d_2$.

challenge_questions.statement: A triangle $PQR$ has $PQ=7$\,cm, $QR=8$\,cm and $RP=9$\,cm. A circle inside the triangle touches $PQ$, $QR$ and $RP$ at $X$, $Y$ and $Z$. Find the lengths $PX$, $QY$ and $RZ$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Let $PX=PZ=a$, $QX=QY=b$, $RY=RZ=c$ (tangents from an external point are equal, applied at each of the three vertices). Then $a+b=PQ=7$, $b+c=QR=8$, $c+a=RP=9$. Adding all three: $2(a+b+c)=24$, so $a+b+c=12$. Then $c=12-7=5$, $a=12-8=4$, $b=12-9=3$: $PX=a=4$\,cm, $QY=b=3$\,cm, $RZ=c=5$\,cm.

challenge_questions.statement: A quadrilateral $ABCD$ has a circle inside it that touches all four sides. Show that $AB+CD=BC+AD$.
challenge_questions.answer: $AB+CD=BC+AD$, proved using four separate tangent-length equalities.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Let the circle touch $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ at $W$, $X$, $Y$, $Z$. Tangents from an external point are equal: $AW=AZ=p$, $BW=BX=q$, $CX=CY=r$, $DY=DZ=s$. Then $AB=AW+WB=p+q$, $CD=CY+YD=r+s$, so $AB+CD=(p+q)+(r+s)$. Also $BC=BX+XC=q+r$, $AD=AZ+ZD=p+s$, so $BC+AD=(q+r)+(p+s)$. Both totals equal $p+q+r+s$, so $AB+CD=BC+AD$.

challenge_questions.statement: $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, and $\angle AOB=2\theta$. Show that the length of the chord $AB$ is $2r\sin\theta$, and that $PA=r\tan\theta$.
challenge_questions.answer: $AB=2r\sin\theta$ and $PA=r\tan\theta$, both proved using right-angled triangles formed by the bisected apex angle $2\theta$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Triangle $OAB$ is isosceles with apex angle $2\theta$ (equal radii $OA=OB$). Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$; $OM$ bisects the apex angle into two angles of $\theta$ each. In right-angled triangle $OMA$: $AM=OA\sin\theta=r\sin\theta$, so $AB=2\times AM=2r\sin\theta$. In right-angled triangle $OAP$ (tangent perpendicular to radius at $A$), $OP$ bisects $\angle AOB$ (symmetry of the kite), so $\angle AOP=\theta$: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{PA}{OA}$, so $PA=OA\tan\theta=r\tan\theta$.

mcq.stem: A circle has radius $r$ and a chord of length $c$ is at perpendicular distance $d$ from the centre. Which equation correctly relates them?

options.why_wrong: This uses the FULL chord $c$ as a side of the right-angled triangle, when it is actually HALF the chord ($\tfrac c2$) that forms the triangle with $r$ and $d$.
This treats the chord as the hypotenuse, but the radius $r$ (not the chord) is the hypotenuse of the relevant right-angled triangle.

options.text: $r^2=d^2+\left(\frac c2\right)^2$

options.why_wrong: This adds instead of subtracts, and also uses the full chord instead of half of it; the correct relationship subtracts $d^2$ from $r^2$ to get the half-chord squared.

mcq.explanation: The right-angled triangle formed by the radius, the perpendicular distance, and HALF the chord gives $r^2=d^2+\left(\frac c2\right)^2$.

mcq.stem: What is the correct way to measure the 'distance from the centre to a chord'?

options.text: The length of a radius drawn to one endpoint of the chord
options.why_wrong: A radius to an endpoint is NOT the distance to the chord (as a line); it is always longer than the true perpendicular distance (for a diameter the perpendicular distance is $0$).

options.text: The length of the chord itself
options.why_wrong: The chord's length and its distance from the centre are two different quantities, related by Pythagoras, not the same measurement.

options.text: Half the length of the chord
options.why_wrong: Half the chord length is a different quantity (one side of the right-angled triangle), not the distance from the centre to the chord.

options.text: The perpendicular distance from the centre to the chord

mcq.explanation: The distance from any point to a line is always the perpendicular (shortest) distance; for a chord, this means the specific perpendicular segment from the centre to the chord.

mcq.stem: While calculating $d=\sqrt{r^2-(\tfrac c2)^2}$, a learner finds that $r^2-(\tfrac c2)^2$ is negative. What does this signal?

options.text: An error has been made (likely using the full chord instead of half of it, or the wrong triangle)
The chord is simply longer than the diameter, which is possible for some circles
options.why_wrong: A chord can never be longer than the diameter; a negative value under the square root is never a valid 'longer chord' case, it is always a sign of an error.

options.text: The distance $d$ should be reported as a negative number
options.why_wrong: A distance is always a non-negative quantity; a negative value under a square root instead signals that an earlier value entered the calculation incorrectly.

options.text: The circle described does not have a well-defined radius
options.why_wrong: The radius itself is not in question here; the issue is specifically that the half-chord value used exceeds the radius, which should never happen for a genuine chord.

mcq.explanation: A chord's half-length can never exceed the radius, so a negative result under the square root always signals an error, most often using the full chord instead of half of it.

mcq.stem: $PT=12$\,cm is one tangent from external point $P$ to a circle. $PT'$ is a second tangent from the same point $P$ to the same circle. What is $PT'$?

options.text: It must be calculated separately with Pythagoras, since the two tangents touch the circle at different points
options.why_wrong: The tangent-length theorem guarantees $PT=PT'$ for ANY two tangents from the same external point, regardless of where they touch the circle; no second calculation is needed.

options.text: $12$\,cm, directly, with no further calculation needed
It depends on the radius of the circle
options.why_wrong: While the VALUE of $PT$ does depend on the radius, once $PT$ is known, $PT'$ is automatically equal to it by the theorem — no further radius-dependent calculation is needed for $PT'$ specifically.

options.text: Cannot be determined without more information
options.why_wrong: The tangent-length theorem fully determines $PT'=PT$ with the information already given; no further information is needed.

mcq.explanation: Tangents from an external point are equal in length, so $PT'=PT=12$\,cm directly, with no further calculation required.

mcq.stem: $OTPT'$ is the kite formed by two tangents from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, touching at $T$ and $T'$. Which statement correctly relates $\angle TOT'$ and $\angle TPT'$?

options.text: $\angle TOT'=\angle TPT'$
options.why_wrong: The kite has two right angles (at $T$ and $T'$), so its remaining two angles must sum to $180^{\circ}$ (from the quadrilateral total of $360^{\circ}$); they are supplementary, not equal in general.

options.text: $\angle TOT'+\angle TPT'=360^{\circ}$
options.why_wrong: This would be the sum of ALL FOUR angles of the kite, not just the two non-right angles; the two right angles at $T$ and $T'$ already account for $180^{\circ}$ of the total $360^{\circ}$.

options.text: $\angle TOT'+\angle TPT'=180^{\circ}$
$\angle TOT'-\angle TPT'=90^{\circ}$
options.why_wrong: There is no general fixed-difference relationship between these two angles; the correct relationship is that they sum to $180^{\circ}$.

mcq.explanation: The kite $OTPT'$ has two right angles at $T$ and $T'$ (tangent-radius theorem), so the remaining two angles, at $O$ and at $P$, must add up to $360^{\circ}-180^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$.

mcq.stem: Two chords in the same circle are $3$\,cm and $9$\,cm from the centre respectively. Which chord is longer?

options.text: The chord $9$\,cm from the centre
options.why_wrong: This reverses the relationship: chords CLOSER to the centre are longer, not farther away; the $9$\,cm chord is the shorter one.

options.text: They must be the same length, since they are both chords of the same circle
options.why_wrong: Chords of the same circle can have many different lengths, depending on their distance from the centre; only chords at the SAME distance are guaranteed equal.

options.text: Cannot be determined without knowing the radius
options.why_wrong: While the exact LENGTHS do depend on the radius, which chord is LONGER can already be determined without it: the nearer chord (here, $3$\,cm) is always the longer one.

options.text: The chord $3$\,cm from the centre

mcq.explanation: The nearer a chord is to the centre, the longer it is; since $3\,\text{cm}<9\,\text{cm}$, the chord at $3$\,cm from the centre is the longer one.

flashcards.front: Perpendicular from the centre to a chord
flashcards.back: Bisects the chord; and conversely, the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre.

flashcards.front: Chord-length formula
flashcards.back: $r^2=d^2+\left(\frac c2\right)^2$, so $c=2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}$ and $d=\sqrt{r^2-(\tfrac c2)^2}$.

flashcards.front: Equal chords are equidistant from the centre
flashcards.back: Two chords with the same length are the same distance from the centre, and conversely.

flashcards.front: Tangents from an external point are equal in length
flashcards.back: If $PT$ and $PT'$ are tangents from $P$ to a circle, then $PT=PT'$.

flashcards.front: The kite $OTPT'$
flashcards.back: Has two right angles (at $T$, $T'$, from the tangent-radius theorem); $OP$ is its line of symmetry, bisecting $\angle TOT'$ and $\angle TPT'$.

flashcards.front: Angles of the tangent kite $OTPT'$
flashcards.back: $\angle TOT'+\angle TPT'=180^{\circ}$ (since the other two angles, at $T$ and $T'$, are each $90^{\circ}$).

flashcards.front: True or false: the full chord is a side of the Pythagoras triangle $r,d,\tfrac c2$.
flashcards.back: False. HALF the chord is the side; using the full chord gives a wrong (often impossible, negative-square) result.

flashcards.front: True or false: a radius to a chord's endpoint measures the distance from the centre to the chord.
flashcards.back: False. The distance to a chord is the PERPENDICULAR distance, which is always shorter than a radius to an endpoint (for a diameter it is $0$).

flashcards.front: True or false: $\angle TOT'=\angle TPT'$ in the tangent kite.
flashcards.back: False. They are SUPPLEMENTARY ($\angle TOT'+\angle TPT'=180^{\circ}$), not equal in general.

flashcards.front: Negative value under the Pythagoras square root for a chord
flashcards.back: Always a stop-and-check signal: it means the half-chord exceeds the radius, which is impossible — recheck whether the full chord was used by mistake.

flashcards.front: Nearer vs. farther chord from the centre — which is longer?
flashcards.back: NEARER to the centre means LONGER; the longest possible chord (distance $0$) is the diameter.

flashcards.front: Finding an unknown centre from two chords
flashcards.back: Draw the perpendicular bisector of each of two chords; they meet at the centre.

flashcards.front: The 'two areas of one triangle' trick
flashcards.back: To find a length like $AM$ in a kite without using an angle, compute the SAME triangle's area two different ways (two different base/height pairs) and set them equal.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The FULL chord length (not half of it) is used directly as one side of the right-angled triangle in the Pythagoras relationship $r^2=d^2+(\tfrac c2)^2$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The chord's length is the quantity usually given or asked for, so it is easy to substitute it directly into the triangle without remembering that the perpendicular from the centre bisects it first.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes $r^2=d^2+c^2$ (using the full chord $c$) instead of $r^2=d^2+(\tfrac c2)^2$ (using half the chord).
misconceptions.correct_model: The right-angled triangle formed by the radius, the perpendicular distance, and HALF the chord has sides $r$, $d$ and $\tfrac c2$ — the full chord is the result of doubling the third side at the end, never a side of the triangle itself.
misconceptions.remediation: Before applying Pythagoras, explicitly halve the chord length and label the halved value on the diagram as the triangle's actual side.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The distance from the centre to a chord can be measured along a radius drawn to one of the chord's endpoints.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A radius to an endpoint is a natural line to draw in the diagram, and its length ($r$) can be mistaken for the 'distance to the chord' if the specific PERPENDICULAR line is not drawn.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner uses the full radius length $r$ as if it were the distance $d$ from the centre to the chord.
misconceptions.correct_model: The distance from a point to a line is always the PERPENDICULAR distance — the shortest possible distance, measured along a line meeting the chord at $90^{\circ}$, which is always shorter than a radius to an endpoint (for a diameter it is $0$).
misconceptions.remediation: Always draw and label the specific perpendicular segment from the centre to the chord before reading off or calculating any 'distance from the centre' value.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any numeric values can be substituted into $d=\sqrt{r^2-(\tfrac c2)^2}$ without checking that the half-chord does not exceed the radius.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The formula is applied mechanically once memorised, without pausing to check whether the specific numbers given actually describe a geometrically possible chord.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner computes $r^2-(\tfrac c2)^2$ and obtains a negative number, then either reports a nonsensical negative 'distance' or an error with no diagnosis of what went wrong.
misconceptions.correct_model: A chord can never be longer than the diameter, so the half-chord can never exceed the radius; a negative value under the square root is a signal that the wrong triangle was used, or that the full chord was used instead of half of it — go back and check which value is correct before continuing.
misconceptions.remediation: Treat a negative result under the square root as an automatic stop-and-check signal, specifically checking whether the chord was halved correctly.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Each tangent length from a common external point must be calculated separately with Pythagoras, even when one of the two lengths is already known.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Without recalling the tangent-length theorem by name, it feels safer to re-derive each length independently from the diagram, rather than trusting a single calculated value applies to both tangents.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner sets up and solves a second, separate Pythagoras calculation for the second tangent length, duplicating work already completed for the first.
misconceptions.correct_model: Once ONE tangent length from an external point is found, the OTHER tangent from the same point is automatically equal, by the tangent-length theorem — no second calculation is needed.
misconceptions.remediation: After finding one tangent length, immediately state 'tangents from an external point are equal in length' and write down the second length directly.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: In the kite $OTPT'$ formed by two tangents, the angle at the centre ($\angle TOT'$) and the angle at the external point ($\angle TPT'$) are EQUAL, rather than supplementary.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both angles are 'the angle at the two non-right-angle vertices of the kite', so without checking the actual angle-sum of the quadrilateral, it is easy to assume a symmetric-looking relationship like equality instead of the correct $180^{\circ}$ sum.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes $\angle TOT'=\angle TPT'$ instead of $\angle TOT'+\angle TPT'=180^{\circ}$.
misconceptions.correct_model: The kite $OTPT'$ has two right angles (at $T$ and $T'$), so its remaining two angles (at $O$ and at $P$) must add up to $360^{\circ}-2\times90^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$ — they are supplementary, not equal (except in the special case where both happen to be $90^{\circ}$).
misconceptions.remediation: Recall that a quadrilateral's angles always sum to $360^{\circ}$; with two confirmed right angles already accounted for, the remaining two angles must share the leftover $180^{\circ}$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the full chord length instead of half of it in the Pythagoras chord-distance relationship.
common_mistakes.why: The chord's full length is usually the given or requested quantity, so it is tempting to substitute it directly without halving it first.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always explicitly halve the chord and label this halved value on the diagram before writing the Pythagoras equation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Measuring the distance from the centre to a chord along a radius to an endpoint, instead of along the true perpendicular.
common_mistakes.why: A radius to an endpoint is a natural line to have already drawn, and can be mistaken for 'the distance to the chord' if the specific perpendicular segment is not drawn separately.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always draw and label the specific perpendicular segment from the centre to the chord before reading off any distance value.

common_mistakes.mistake: Recalculating a second tangent length from scratch with Pythagoras, when the tangent-length theorem already gives it for free.
common_mistakes.why: Without recalling the theorem by name, it can feel safer to re-derive each length independently rather than trust a single equality.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: As soon as one tangent length from a given external point is found, state the theorem by name and copy the value directly to the second tangent.

exam_notes: This entire lesson is Extended only (Papers 2 and 4); none of it is examined on the Core papers.
Give lengths to $3$ significant figures and angles to $1$ decimal place unless the answer is exact; keep exact values (fractions, surds) until the final line of working.
In 'show that' questions, every reason must be stated explicitly, in full, using the exact wording from the reasons table.
A negative value appearing under a square root while finding a chord distance is never a valid answer; it always means the full chord was used instead of half of it, or the wrong triangle was chosen.

summary.big_idea: This whole lesson is one symmetry idea applied three times: reflecting a circle in a line through its centre shows that a chord's perpendicular bisector passes through the centre, that equal chords sit at equal distances, and that the two tangents from any external point are mirror images (hence equal) — every property here turns into a right-angled triangle where Pythagoras or trigonometry finishes the job.
key_points: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it: $r^2=d^2+(\tfrac c2)^2$.
Equal chords are equidistant from the centre (and conversely); nearer to the centre always means longer.
Tangents from an external point are equal in length: $PT=PT'$.
The kite $OTPT'$ has two right angles (at the points of contact); the other two angles (at $O$ and $P$) sum to $180^{\circ}$, not equal to each other.
This lesson is Extended only; every result combines with Pythagoras, trigonometry, or the lesson 4.7 angle theorems in multi-step problems.
formulas: PT=PT'\ \text{(tangents from the same external point)}
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Halve the chord, not the radius or distance, before applying Pythagoras; once one tangent length is found, the other from the same point is automatically equal; and the tangent kite's two non-right angles add up to $180^{\circ}$, they are not equal.

exercises.statement:
For each pair below, state whether the two triangles are definitely congruent, and give the reason (SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS).
(a) A right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $8\text{ cm}$ and one of the two shorter sides (next to the right angle) $5\text{ cm}$.
(b) A triangle with angles $50^\circ$ and $35^\circ$ at the two ends of a side of length $10\text{ cm}$.
(c) A triangle with angles $35^\circ$ and $50^\circ$ at the two ends of a side of length $10\text{ cm}$ (same angle pair, opposite order along the labelled side).
(d) A triangle with two sides $8\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$ with an included angle of $120^\circ$.
(e) A triangle with two sides $10\text{ cm}$ and $8\text{ cm}$ with an included angle of $120^\circ$.
(f) A right-angled triangle with a shorter side $5\text{ cm}$ and hypotenuse $8\text{ cm}$ (same measurements as (a)).
exercises.answer: a and f are congruent (RHS); b and c are congruent (ASA); d and e are congruent (SAS).
exercises.full_solution:
(a) and (f): both are right-angled triangles with hypotenuse $8\text{ cm}$ and one side $5\text{ cm}$ $\Rightarrow$ RHS, so a $\cong$ f.
(b) and (c): both have angles $50^\circ$ and $35^\circ$ with the included side $10\text{ cm}$ between them $\Rightarrow$ ASA, so b $\cong$ c (third angle in each $=180-50-35=95^\circ$).
(d) and (e): both have sides $8\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$ with an included angle of $120^\circ$ $\Rightarrow$ SAS, so d $\cong$ e.
No other pairing satisfies a congruence condition (SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS) with the information given.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Draw, on squared paper: (1) two other possible nets of a cube (different from the one shown in the text, a plus-sign/cross arrangement of six squares); (2) the net of a cuboid (rectangular prism); (3) the net of a triangular prism; (4) the net of a cylinder; (5) the net of a square-based pyramid; (6) the net of a tetrahedron.
exercises.answer: Any valid net for each solid (see full_solution for one example of each).
exercises.full_solution:
(1) Two more valid cube nets, e.g. a 'T' shape (a row of three squares with a column of three more squares hanging down from the middle one), or a row of four squares with one extra square attached above the 2nd square and one below the 4th square (there are 11 distinct nets of a cube in total).
(2) A cuboid of dimensions $l\times w\times h$ unfolds into six rectangles: a central strip of four rectangles of size $l\times h$, $w\times h$, $l\times h$, $w\times h$ joined edge to edge, with a $l\times w$ rectangle attached above and below one of the $l\times h$ rectangles.
(3) A triangular prism unfolds into: a central strip of three rectangles (each the prism's length $\times$ the corresponding triangle side), with the two triangular end-faces attached to two of the edges of one of these rectangles.
(4) A cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$ unfolds into: a rectangle of width $2\pi r$ and height $h$ (the curved surface), with one circle of radius $r$ attached to the top edge and another to the bottom edge.
(5) A square-based pyramid unfolds into: a central square (the base) with four congruent isosceles triangles attached, one to each side of the square, folding up to meet at the apex.
(6) A tetrahedron (4 congruent equilateral triangles) unfolds into: one equilateral triangle with a further equilateral triangle attached to each of its three sides, folding up to meet at a single apex.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
Using only a ruler and a pair of compasses, construct the following triangles:
(1) $\triangle ABC$ where $AB=10\text{ cm}$, $AC=7\text{ cm}$ and $BC=9\text{ cm}$.
(2) $\triangle LMN$ where $LM=4\text{ cm}$, $LN=8\text{ cm}$ and $MN=5\text{ cm}$.
(3) $\triangle PQR$, an equilateral triangle of side length $7\text{ cm}$.
(4)(a) $\triangle ABC$ where $AB=8\text{ cm}$, $AC=4\text{ cm}$ and $BC=3\text{ cm}$. (b) Is this triangle possible? Explain your answer.
exercises.answer: (1), (2), (3) are all possible and constructible. (4) The triangle is NOT possible, since $AC+BC=4+3=7\text{ cm} < AB=8\text{ cm}$.
exercises.full_solution:
For (1)-(3): draw the longest given side first with a ruler, then use compasses set to the length of each remaining side, centred at each endpoint of the drawn side, to draw two arcs; their intersection is the third vertex. All three satisfy the triangle inequality, e.g. for (1): $7+9=16>10$, $10+7=17>9$, $10+9=19>7$, so each is constructible.
(4)(a)/(b): For a triangle to exist, the sum of any two sides must exceed the third side (triangle inequality). Here $AC+BC=4+3=7\text{ cm}$, which is less than $AB=8\text{ cm}$. Since $7<8$, the two shorter sides cannot reach each other when the compasses are set to $4\text{ cm}$ (centred at $A$) and $3\text{ cm}$ (centred at $B$) along the $8\text{ cm}$ base — the arcs do not intersect. Therefore this triangle is impossible to construct.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
(1) A map is drawn to the given scale, and the distance between two objects on the map is given. Find the real distance in metres: (a) 1:10 000, 3 cm (b) 1:10 000, 2.5 cm (c) 1:20 000, 1.5 cm (d) 1:8 000, 5.2 cm.
(2) The scale and the TRUE distance between two objects are given. Find the distance on the map in cm: (a) 1:15 000, 1.5 km (b) 1:50 000, 4 km (c) 1:10 000, 600 m (d) 1:25 000, 1.7 km.
(3) A rectangular pool measures $20\text{ m}$ by $36\text{ m}$ ($AB=36\text{ m}$, $AD=20\text{ m}$, rectangle $ABCD$). (a) Construct a scale drawing of the pool, using $1\text{ cm}$ for every $4\text{ m}$. (b) A boy sets off across the pool from $D$ so that his path is in the direction of a point that is $40\text{ m}$ from $D$ and $30\text{ m}$ from $C$. Show, by construction, the path he takes. (c) Work out the distance the boy swam.
(4) A triangular enclosure has sides $8\text{ m}$, $6\text{ m}$ and $10\text{ m}$. (a) Using a scale of $1\text{ cm}$ for each metre, construct a scale drawing of the enclosure. (b) Calculate the true area of the enclosure.
exercises.answer: (1) (a) 300 m (b) 250 m (c) 300 m (d) 416 m. (2) (a) 10 cm (b) 8 cm (c) 6 cm (d) 6.8 cm. (3) Scale drawing at 1 cm : 4 m (9 cm by 5 cm rectangle); the point $X$ ($DX=40\text{ m}$, $CX=30\text{ m}$) lies outside the pool, beyond side $AB$; the boy swims from $D$ towards $X$ until he reaches side $AB$; distance swum $\approx 27.7\text{ m}$ (about 6.9 cm on the drawing; answers of 27–28 m from a careful drawing are acceptable). (4) Scale triangle 8 cm, 6 cm, 10 cm; true area $=24\text{ m}^2$.
exercises.full_solution:
(1) $1:10\,000$ means $1\text{ cm}\to10\,000\text{ cm}=100\text{ m}$. (a) $3\times100=300\text{ m}$. (b) $2.5\times100=250\text{ m}$. (c) $1:20\,000\Rightarrow1\text{ cm}=200\text{ m}$, so $1.5\times200=300\text{ m}$. (d) $1:8000\Rightarrow1\text{ cm}=80\text{ m}$, so $5.2\times80=416\text{ m}$.
(2) Convert real distance to cm, then divide by the scale denominator-in-cm equivalent. (a) $1.5\text{ km}=150\,000\text{ cm}$; map $=150\,000/15\,000=10\text{ cm}$. (b) $4\text{ km}=400\,000\text{ cm}$; map$=400\,000/50\,000=8\text{ cm}$. (c) $600\text{ m}=60\,000\text{ cm}$; map$=60\,000/10\,000=6\text{ cm}$. (d) $1.7\text{ km}=170\,000\text{ cm}$; map$=170\,000/25\,000=6.8\text{ cm}$.
(3) At $1\text{ cm}:4\text{ m}$, draw rectangle $ABCD$ $9\text{ cm}\times5\text{ cm}$ ($36/4=9$, $20/4=5$), with $DC$ the $9\text{ cm}$ side. (b) Set the compasses to $40/4=10\text{ cm}$ and draw an arc centred at $D$; set them to $30/4=7.5\text{ cm}$ and draw an arc centred at $C$. The arcs meet at the point $X$, which lies OUTSIDE the pool, beyond side $AB$. The boy swims along the straight line from $D$ towards $X$, so his path is the part of $DX$ inside the rectangle, ending where $DX$ crosses $AB$. (c) Measuring this path on the drawing gives about $6.9\text{ cm}$, i.e. about $6.9\times4\approx27.7\text{ m}$. (Check by coordinates with $D=(0,0)$, $C=(36,0)$: $X\approx(27.7,\,28.8)$; the line $DX$ reaches $AB$ ($y=20$) at $x\approx19.2$, so the distance is $\sqrt{19.2^2+20^2}\approx27.7\text{ m}$.)
(4) At $1\text{ cm}$ per metre, draw a triangle with sides $8\text{ cm}$, $6\text{ cm}$, $10\text{ cm}$. Since $6^2+8^2=36+64=100=10^2$, this triangle is right-angled, with the right angle between the sides of length $6$ and $8$. Area $=\dfrac{1}{2}\times6\times8=24$, so the true area of the enclosure $=24\text{ m}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two right-angled triangles are shown. The larger triangle has its right angle between sides of $6\text{ cm}$ and $8\text{ cm}$, its hypotenuse is $10\text{ cm}$, and the angle between the $6\text{ cm}$ side and the hypotenuse is $60^\circ$. The smaller triangle has its right angle between sides of $y\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$, its hypotenuse is $x\text{ cm}$, and the angle between the $5\text{ cm}$ side and the hypotenuse is $30^\circ$. (a) Explain why the two triangles are similar. (b) Calculate the scale factor which reduces the larger triangle to the smaller one. (c) Calculate the value of $x$ and the value of $y$.
exercises.answer: (a) Both triangles have angles $90^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$, so they are equiangular and therefore similar. (b) Scale factor $=\dfrac{5}{8}=0.625$. (c) $x=6.25\text{ cm}$, $y=3.75\text{ cm}$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) In the larger triangle the angles are $90^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $180-90-60=30^\circ$; in the smaller triangle they are $90^\circ$, $30^\circ$ and $180-90-30=60^\circ$. The triangles are equiangular, so they are similar.
(b) Match the sides using the angles. In the larger triangle the $30^\circ$ angle lies between the $8\text{ cm}$ side and the hypotenuse; in the smaller triangle the $30^\circ$ angle lies between the $5\text{ cm}$ side and the hypotenuse $x$. So $5\text{ cm}$ corresponds to $8\text{ cm}$, $x$ corresponds to $10\text{ cm}$ and $y$ corresponds to $6\text{ cm}$. Scale factor (large to small) $=\dfrac{5}{8}=0.625$.
(c) $x=10\times0.625=6.25\text{ cm}$ and $y=6\times0.625=3.75\text{ cm}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Which of the triangles A–F below are similar? Two angles of each triangle are given: A: $115^\circ$ and $25^\circ$. B: $50^\circ$ and $105^\circ$. C: $40^\circ$ and $115^\circ$. D: $25^\circ$ and $50^\circ$. E: $115^\circ$ and $50^\circ$. F: $40^\circ$ and $25^\circ$.
exercises.answer: A, C and F are similar (each has angles $115^\circ$, $40^\circ$, $25^\circ$). B and D are similar (each has angles $105^\circ$, $50^\circ$, $25^\circ$). E (angles $115^\circ$, $50^\circ$, $15^\circ$) is not similar to any of the others.
exercises.full_solution: Triangles are similar when they have the same three angles. Use the angle sum $180^\circ$ to find each third angle: A: $180-115-25=40^\circ$, so $\{115^\circ,25^\circ,40^\circ\}$. B: $180-50-105=25^\circ$, so $\{50^\circ,105^\circ,25^\circ\}$. C: $180-40-115=25^\circ$, so $\{40^\circ,115^\circ,25^\circ\}$. D: $180-25-50=105^\circ$, so $\{25^\circ,50^\circ,105^\circ\}$. E: $180-115-50=15^\circ$, so $\{115^\circ,50^\circ,15^\circ\}$. F: $180-40-25=115^\circ$, so $\{40^\circ,25^\circ,115^\circ\}$. Hence A, C and F are similar to one another, B and D are similar to each other, and E is not similar to any other triangle.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Triangles $OMN$ and $ZXY$ are similar, with angle $OMN=$ angle $ZXY$ (marked equal), so $O$ corresponds to $Z$, $N$ to $Y$ and $M$ to $X$. In triangle $OMN$: $ON=6\text{ cm}$, $NM=4\text{ cm}$ and $OM=10\text{ cm}$. In triangle $ZXY$: $ZX=15\text{ cm}$. (a) Calculate the length $XY$. (b) Calculate the length $YZ$.
exercises.full_solution:
Corresponding vertices: $O\leftrightarrow Z$, $M\leftrightarrow X$, $N\leftrightarrow Y$. The side $ZX=15\text{ cm}$ corresponds to $OM=10\text{ cm}$, so the scale factor from the small triangle to the large triangle is $\dfrac{15}{10}=1.5$.
(a) $XY$ corresponds to $MN$: $XY=4\times1.5=6\text{ cm}$.
(b) $YZ$ corresponds to $NO$: $YZ=6\times1.5=9\text{ cm}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In the triangle shown, one side (from the top vertex to the bottom-right vertex) is $12\text{ cm}$ long. A line segment of length $3\text{ cm}$, drawn parallel to the left-hand side $p\text{ cm}$, joins a point on this $12\text{ cm}$ side to a point on the base; it splits the $12\text{ cm}$ side into $q\text{ cm}$ (top part) and $r\text{ cm}$ (lower part), and splits the base into $3\text{ cm}$ (left part) and $5\text{ cm}$ (right part). Calculate the lengths of sides $p$, $q$ and $r$.
exercises.full_solution:
The $3\text{ cm}$ segment is parallel to side $p$, so the small triangle on the right (sides $3\text{ cm}$, $5\text{ cm}$ and $r$) is similar to the whole triangle (sides $p$, $3+5=8\text{ cm}$ and $12\text{ cm}$). Corresponding sides: $3\leftrightarrow p$, $5\leftrightarrow8$, $r\leftrightarrow12$. Scale factor (small to large) $=\dfrac{8}{5}=1.6$.
$p=3\times1.6=4.8\text{ cm}$.
$r=12\div1.6=7.5\text{ cm}$.
$q=12-r=12-7.5=4.5\text{ cm}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In triangle $ABC$, $D$ and $E$ lie on $AB$ and $AC$ with $DE\parallel BC$. The perpendicular distance from $A$ to $DE$ is $6\text{ cm}$ and the perpendicular distance between $DE$ and $BC$ is $4\text{ cm}$. The area of $\triangle ADE$ is $12\text{ cm}^2$. (a) Calculate the area of $\triangle ABC$. (b) Calculate the length $BC$.
exercises.answer: (a) Area of $\triangle ABC = 33\tfrac13\text{ cm}^2$. (b) $BC=6\tfrac23\text{ cm}\approx6.67\text{ cm}$.
exercises.full_solution:
Since $DE\parallel BC$, $\triangle ADE\sim\triangle ABC$. The heights are $6\text{ cm}$ and $6+4=10\text{ cm}$, so the scale factor is $k=\dfrac{10}{6}=\dfrac53$ and the area factor is $k^2=\dfrac{25}{9}$.
(a) Area of $\triangle ABC = 12\times\dfrac{25}{9}=\dfrac{300}{9}=33\tfrac13\text{ cm}^2$.
(b) Area of $\triangle ADE=\tfrac12\times DE\times6=12$, so $DE=4\text{ cm}$. Then $BC=\dfrac53\times4=\dfrac{20}{3}=6\tfrac23\text{ cm}$ (about $6.67\text{ cm}$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: Triangle $ABC$ with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$ and $DE$ parallel to $BC$. The dashed line shows the perpendicular distances: $6$ cm from $A$ to $DE$ and a further $4$ cm from $DE$ to $BC$.
assets.purpose: Show which two distances are the heights of the two similar triangles, so the student uses 6 and 10 (not 6 and 4) as the scale factor.

exercises.statement: Two parallelograms are similar. The smaller has sides $5\text{ cm}$ and $6\text{ cm}$; the larger has corresponding sides $8\text{ cm}$ and $x\text{ cm}$ (with $8\text{ cm}$ corresponding to the $5\text{ cm}$ side). Calculate $x$.
exercises.full_solution: Scale factor $=\dfrac{8}{5}=1.6$. Therefore $x=6\times1.6=9.6\text{ cm}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two rhombuses are shown, one with side $8\text{ cm}$, the other with side $6\text{ cm}$. Explain, giving reasons, whether the two rhombuses are definitely similar.
exercises.answer: Not necessarily — knowing only the side lengths of two rhombuses does not guarantee similarity.
exercises.full_solution: All sides of a rhombus are equal, so each rhombus is equiangular with itself trivially, but the ANGLES of a rhombus can vary (a rhombus can be 'fat' close to a square, or very 'thin'/elongated) while keeping all four sides equal. Since similarity of polygons requires BOTH equal corresponding angles AND proportional sides, and here only the side lengths ($8\text{ cm}$ and $6\text{ cm}$) are given with no information about the angles, the two rhombuses are not necessarily similar — they are similar only if their angles also match (e.g. if both are squares or have the same angle between adjacent sides).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The diagram shows a trapezium within a trapezium (a larger trapezium with sides including $10\text{ cm}$, angles $110^\circ$ and $80^\circ$ at its base, enclosing a smaller, similarly-oriented trapezium with side $5\text{ cm}$ and angles $110^\circ$ and $80^\circ$, with the two parallel sides shown by arrow marks). Explain, giving reasons, whether the two trapezia are definitely similar.
exercises.answer: Not necessarily — equal angles with only the parallel sides known to be proportional (half) does not guarantee that the non-parallel (slanted) sides are also in the same ratio.
exercises.full_solution: Both trapezia have matching angles ($110^\circ,110^\circ,80^\circ,80^\circ$), so they are equiangular. However, equiangular alone is NOT sufficient for similarity of general quadrilaterals (unlike triangles) — all corresponding SIDES must also be in the same ratio. We are only told that one pair of parallel sides is in ratio $5:10=1:2$; nothing is said about the two slanted (non-parallel) sides, which could be of any length consistent with the given angles and still keep both as valid trapezia with those angles. Therefore the trapezia are not necessarily similar unless the slanted sides are also confirmed to be in the ratio $1:2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Hexagon B is an enlargement of hexagon A by a scale factor of $2.5$. If the area of A is $8\text{ cm}^2$, calculate the area of B.
exercises.full_solution: Area factor $=(\text{scale factor})^2=2.5^2=6.25$. Area of B $=8\times6.25=50\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: P and Q are two regular pentagons. Q is an enlargement of P by a scale factor of $3$. If the area of pentagon Q is $90\text{ cm}^2$, calculate the area of P.
exercises.full_solution: Area factor $=3^2=9$. Area of P $=90\div9=10\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Four similar triangles A, B, C, D are shown, each an enlargement of the previous one by a scale factor of $1.5$. (a) If the area of C is $202.5\text{ cm}^2$, calculate the area of (i) triangle D (ii) triangle B (iii) triangle A. (b) If the triangles continue in this sequence, which letter triangle would be the first to have an area greater than $15\,000\text{ cm}^2$?
exercises.answer: (a)(i) Area D $=455.625\text{ cm}^2$ (ii) Area B $=90\text{ cm}^2$ (iii) Area A $=40\text{ cm}^2$. (b) Triangle I (the 9th triangle in the sequence A, B, C, ... I) is the first with area $>15\,000\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A square is enlarged by increasing the length of its sides by $10\%$. If the original side length was $6\text{ cm}$, calculate the area of the enlarged square.
exercises.full_solution: New side length $=6\times1.1=6.6\text{ cm}$. Area $=6.6^2=43.56\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A square of side length $4\text{ cm}$ is enlarged by increasing its sides by $25\%$ and then by a further $50\%$. Calculate the area of the final square.
exercises.full_solution: New side length $=4\times1.25\times1.5=7.5\text{ cm}$. Area $=7.5^2=56.25\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: An equilateral triangle has an area of $25\text{ cm}^2$. If the lengths of its sides are reduced by $15\%$, calculate the area of the reduced triangle.
exercises.full_solution: Linear scale factor $=0.85$, so area factor $=0.85^2=0.7225$. New area $=25\times0.7225=18.0625\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A scale model of a garage has width $5\text{ cm}$, length $10\text{ cm}$ and wall height $6\text{ cm}$, with a pitched roof of (model) slant length $l$. (a) If the real garage has width $4\text{ m}$, calculate (i) the real length (ii) the real wall height. (b) If the apex of the real roof is $2\text{ m}$ above the top of the walls, use Pythagoras' theorem to find the real slant length $l$. (c) What is the area of the (model) roof section (one rectangular slope, length $10\text{ cm}$ by the model slant length)?
exercises.answer: (a)(i) 8 m (ii) 4.8 m. (b) Real slant length $\approx2.83\text{ m}$. (c) Model roof-section area $\approx35.36\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.full_solution:
The real width is $4\text{ m}=400\text{ cm}$ and the model width is $5\text{ cm}$, so the scale factor is $400\div5=80$: every $1\text{ cm}$ on the model represents $0.8\text{ m}$ in real life.
(a)(i) Real length $=10\times0.8=8\text{ m}$. (ii) Real wall height $=6\times0.8=4.8\text{ m}$.
(b) The roof's cross-section is a right triangle with horizontal leg $=$ half the real width $=4/2=2\text{ m}$ and vertical leg $=2\text{ m}$ (apex height above wall top). Real slant length $l=\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt2\approx2.83\text{ m}$.
(c) Model slant length $=l/0.8=2\sqrt2/0.8\approx3.54\text{ cm}$. Model roof-section area (one rectangular slope, $10\text{ cm}$ long) $\approx10\times3.54\approx35.4\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A cuboid has dimensions $10\text{ cm}\times5\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$. If the cuboid is enlarged by a scale factor of $2.5$, calculate: (a) the total surface area of the original cuboid (b) the total surface area of the enlarged cuboid (c) the volume of the original cuboid (d) the volume of the enlarged cuboid.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $SA=2(10\times5+10\times4+5\times4)=2(50+40+20)=2\times110=220\text{ cm}^2$.
(c) $V=10\times5\times4=200\text{ cm}^3$.
(b) Area factor $=2.5^2=6.25$; enlarged $SA=220\times6.25=1375\text{ cm}^2$.
(d) Volume factor $=2.5^3=15.625$; enlarged $V=200\times15.625=3125\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A cube has side length $3\text{ cm}$. (a) Calculate its total surface area. (b) If the cube is enlarged and has a total surface area of $486\text{ cm}^2$, calculate the scale factor of enlargement. (c) Calculate the volume of the enlarged cube.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $SA=6\times3^2=54\text{ cm}^2$.
