(b) Area factor $=486/54=9$, so scale factor $=\sqrt9=3$.
(c) Original volume $=3^3=27\text{ cm}^3$; enlarged volume $=27\times3^3=27\times27=729\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two cubes P and Q are of different sizes. If $n$ is the ratio of their corresponding sides, express in terms of $n$: (a) the ratio of their surface areas (b) the ratio of their volumes.
exercises.full_solution: If the ratio of corresponding (linear) sides of P to Q is $n:1$, then the ratio of their surface areas is $n^2:1$ (areas scale with the square of the linear scale factor), and the ratio of their volumes is $n^3:1$ (volumes scale with the cube of the linear scale factor).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Cuboids A and B are similar. Cuboid A has volume $3024\text{ cm}^3$ and one edge $15\text{ cm}$; the corresponding edge of cuboid B is $5\text{ cm}$. Calculate the volume of cuboid B.
exercises.full_solution: Scale factor (A to B) $=5/15=1/3$. Volume factor $=(1/3)^3=1/27$. Volume of B $=3024/27=112\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two similar cylinders L and M have capacities $16$ litres and $2$ litres respectively. If the height of cylinder M is $10\text{ cm}$, calculate the height of cylinder L.
exercises.full_solution: Volume (capacity) factor L:M $=16:2=8:1$. Linear scale factor $=\sqrt[3]{8}=2$. Height of L $=10\times2=20\text{ cm}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A square-based pyramid is cut into two pieces by a cut parallel to the base, made exactly halfway up (so the small pyramid at the top is similar to the original, with linear scale factor $0.5$). (a) Calculate the ratio of the volume of the smaller (top) pyramid to that of the original pyramid. (b) Calculate the ratio of the volume of the small pyramid to that of the remaining frustum (truncated base piece).
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Linear scale factor (small pyramid : original) $=1:2$, so volume ratio $=1^3:2^3=1:8$.
(b) If the original pyramid's volume is $8$ units, the small pyramid is $1$ unit, so the frustum (remaining base piece) is $8-1=7$ units. Ratio small pyramid : frustum $=1:7$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two similar cones A and B: cone B is an enlargement of A by a scale factor of $4$. If the volume of cone B is $1024\text{ cm}^3$, calculate the volume of cone A.
exercises.full_solution: Volume factor $=4^3=64$. Volume of A $=1024/64=16\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A solid cylinder is shown, split into a shaded section of length $5\text{ cm}$ and an unshaded section of length $15\text{ cm}$ (the same radius throughout, i.e. one cylinder of total length $20\text{ cm}$). (a) Stating your reasons, decide whether the two parts (treated as two cylinders of the same radius but lengths $5\text{ cm}$ and $15\text{ cm}$) are similar. (b) What is the ratio of the curved surface area of the shaded cylinder to that of the unshaded cylinder?
exercises.answer: (a) No, they are not similar (same radius but different lengths, so one is not an enlargement of the other). (b) $1:3$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Two cylinders are similar only if ALL corresponding linear dimensions (radius AND length) are in the same ratio. Here both pieces have the SAME radius but different lengths ($5\text{ cm}$ and $15\text{ cm}$), so the ratio of radii ($1:1$) does not match the ratio of lengths ($1:3$); the two cylinders are therefore not similar.
(b) Since both share the same radius, the curved surface area ($2\pi r \times \text{length}$) is directly proportional to length alone: ratio $=5:15=1:3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Triangle $PST$ has a right angle at $T$. Points $U$ and $V$ lie on $TS$ with $TU=UV=VS=8\text{ cm}$. Points $Q$ and $R$ lie on $PS$, with $QU$ and $RV$ perpendicular to $TS$ (so parallel to $PT$), and $RV=4\text{ cm}$. (a) Calculate the area of $\triangle RSV$. (b) Calculate the area of $\triangle QSU$. (c) Calculate the area of $\triangle PST$.
exercises.full_solution:
Triangles $RSV$, $QSU$ and $PST$ are all similar (right-angled, sharing the angle at $S$, with $RV\parallel QU\parallel PT$).
$\triangle RSV$: base $VS=8\text{ cm}$, height $RV=4\text{ cm}$. Area $=\tfrac12\times8\times4=16\text{ cm}^2$.
Scale factor from $\triangle RSV$ to $\triangle QSU$: base ratio $=US/VS=16/8=2$, so $QU=RV\times2=8\text{ cm}$. Area of $\triangle QSU=\tfrac12\times16\times8=64\text{ cm}^2$ (area factor $2^2=4$ applied to $16$ also gives $64$).
Scale factor from $\triangle RSV$ to $\triangle PST$: base ratio $=TS/VS=24/8=3$, so $PT=RV\times3=12\text{ cm}$. Area of $\triangle PST=\tfrac12\times24\times12=144\text{ cm}^2$ (area factor $3^2=9$ applied to $16$ also gives $144$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: Triangle $PST$ with the right angle at $T$. $U$ and $V$ divide $TS$ into three equal parts of $8$ cm, and $QU$ and $RV$ are perpendicular to $TS$, with $RV=4$ cm.
assets.purpose: Show the three nested similar triangles RSV, QSU and PST sharing the angle at S, so the student can read off the base ratios 8 : 16 : 24.

exercises.statement: The area of an island on a map is $30\text{ cm}^2$. The scale used on the map is $1:100\,000$. (a) Calculate the area in square kilometres of the real island. (b) An airport on the island occupies a rectangular piece of land measuring $3\text{ km}$ by $2\text{ km}$. Calculate the area of the airport on the map in $\text{cm}^2$.
exercises.full_solution:
Linear scale $1:100\,000$ means $1\text{ cm}$ on the map $=100\,000\text{ cm}=1000\text{ m}=1\text{ km}$ in real life. Area scale factor $=1^2:100\,000^2$, which is equivalent to saying $1\text{ cm}^2$ on the map represents $1\text{ km}^2$ in real life (since $1\text{ cm}\to1\text{ km}$ linearly).
(a) Real area $=30\times1=30\text{ km}^2$.
(b) Real airport area $=3\times2=6\text{ km}^2$, so on the map this is $6\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two cuboidal packs of cheese X and Y are similar (X has dimensions $15\text{ cm}\times10\text{ cm}\times5\text{ cm}$). The total surface area of pack Y is four times that of pack X. Calculate: (a) the dimensions of pack Y (b) the mass of pack X if pack Y has a mass of $800\text{ g}$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Area factor $=4\Rightarrow$ linear scale factor $=\sqrt4=2$. Pack Y's dimensions $=15\times2,\ 10\times2,\ 5\times2 = 30\text{ cm},20\text{ cm},10\text{ cm}$.
(b) Assuming uniform density, mass scales with volume: volume factor $=2^3=8$. Mass of X $=800/8=100\text{ g}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: On a square grid, shape A and four other quadrilaterals P, Q, R and S are drawn with their vertices on grid points. Using grid units as coordinates, the vertices are: A $(2,11)$, $(6,10)$, $(3,6)$, $(1,8)$; P $(9,12)$, $(12,11)$, $(11,7)$, $(7,10)$; Q $(13,10)$, $(16,11)$, $(18,9)$, $(14,6)$; R $(7,7)$, $(8,2)$, $(5,1)$, $(3,3)$; S $(12,6)$, $(16,2)$, $(11,1)$, $(10,4)$. Which shapes are congruent to shape A?
exercises.answer: P and Q are congruent to A (P is a rotation of A, Q is a reflection of A). R and S are not congruent to A (they are congruent to each other).
exercises.full_solution:
Congruent shapes have all corresponding sides and angles equal; a copy may be translated, rotated or reflected. Find the squared side lengths going round each shape (using $(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2$):
- A: $17, 25, 8, 10$ (sides $\sqrt{17}$, $5$, $2\sqrt2$, $\sqrt{10}$); diagonals $\sqrt{26}$ and $\sqrt{29}$.
- P: $10, 17, 25, 8$ — the same sides in the same cyclic order (a rotation of A), and the diagonals are again $\sqrt{29}$ and $\sqrt{26}$. P is congruent to A.
- Q: $10, 8, 25, 17$ — the same sides in reverse order (a reflection of A), diagonals $\sqrt{26}$ and $\sqrt{29}$. Q is congruent to A.
- R: $26, 10, 8, 32$ and S: $32, 26, 10, 8$ — these contain sides $\sqrt{26}$ and $\sqrt{32}$, which A does not have, so R and S are not congruent to A (they are congruent to each other).
So the shapes congruent to A are P and Q.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The two shapes shown are congruent concave quadrilaterals (arrowhead shapes). In the first, one acute angle is $40^\circ$ and the reflex angle is $280^\circ$. In the second, drawn in a different orientation, two acute angles are marked: $30^\circ$ and $x^\circ$, where the $x^\circ$ angle is not the one that corresponds to the $40^\circ$ angle. Calculate the size of $x$.
exercises.full_solution: The angles of a quadrilateral add up to $360^\circ$. In the first shape the two unmarked angles add up to $360-40-280=40^\circ$. The shapes are congruent, so both have the same four angles. The second shape has a $30^\circ$ angle, which must be one of these two unmarked angles, so the other unmarked angle is $40-30=10^\circ$. The four angles are therefore $40^\circ$, $280^\circ$, $30^\circ$ and $10^\circ$. The angle $x$ is acute and does not correspond to the $40^\circ$ angle, so $x=10^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A quadrilateral is plotted on a pair of axes. The coordinates of its four vertices (in order) are $(0,1)$, $(0,5)$, $(3,4)$ and $(3,3)$. Another quadrilateral, congruent to the first, is also plotted on the same axes. Three of its vertices (in the corresponding cyclic order) have coordinates $(6,5)$, $(5,2)$ and $(4,2)$. Calculate the coordinates of the fourth vertex.
exercises.full_solution: Label the first quadrilateral $A(0,1)$, $B(0,5)$, $C(3,4)$, $D(3,3)$, with side lengths $AB=4$, $BC=\sqrt{3^2+1^2}=\sqrt{10}$, $CD=1$, $DA=\sqrt{3^2+2^2}=\sqrt{13}$. Checking the three given vertices of the second quadrilateral: distance from $(6,5)$ to $(5,2)=\sqrt{1^2+3^2}=\sqrt{10}$ (matches $BC$), and from $(5,2)$ to $(4,2)=1$ (matches $CD$). So $(6,5)\leftrightarrow B$, $(5,2)\leftrightarrow C$, $(4,2)\leftrightarrow D$, and the unknown 4th vertex $(x,y)\leftrightarrow A$, with $DA=\sqrt{13}$ (distance from $(4,2)$ to $(x,y)$) and $AB=4$ (distance from $(x,y)$ to $(6,5)$). Solving $(x-4)^2+(y-2)^2=13$ and $(x-6)^2+(y-5)^2=16$ simultaneously gives the integer solution $(x,y)=(2,5)$ (verified: distance to $(4,2)$ is $\sqrt{4+9}=\sqrt{13}$ ✓; distance to $(6,5)$ is $\sqrt{16+0}=4$ ✓).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Explain, justifying your answer, whether the two triangles below are definitely congruent: Triangle 1 has angles $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ with a right angle, arranged with the right angle and $60^\circ$ adjacent to one leg. Triangle 2 has the SAME three angles ($30^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$) but no side lengths are given for either triangle.
exercises.answer: No — equal angles alone (AAA) only guarantee similarity, not congruence, since no side lengths are given.
exercises.full_solution: Both triangles have the same three angles $30^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$, so they are similar (equiangular). However, no lengths are given for either triangle, so one could be a scaled-up or scaled-down copy of the other (e.g. one triangle's sides all twice as long). Congruence additionally requires matching side lengths (one of SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS, each of which involves at least one given length), so with angles alone we can conclude similarity but NOT congruence.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
All three angles and sides of triangle X are given: the $8.0\text{ cm}$ side joins the $120^\circ$ and $25^\circ$ vertices, the $5.9\text{ cm}$ side joins the $120^\circ$ and $35^\circ$ vertices, and the $12.1\text{ cm}$ side joins the $35^\circ$ and $25^\circ$ vertices. State which of triangles A–E are definitely congruent to triangle X. Give reasons for your answer.
A: angles $120^\circ$ and $35^\circ$, with the $5.9\text{ cm}$ side joining these two vertices.
B: angles $35^\circ$ and $25^\circ$, with an $8\text{ cm}$ side joining the $25^\circ$ vertex to the third (unmarked) vertex.
C: an angle of $25^\circ$, with an $8.0\text{ cm}$ side from the $25^\circ$ vertex and a $5.9\text{ cm}$ side opposite the $25^\circ$ angle.
D: angles $25^\circ$, $120^\circ$ and $35^\circ$, with no sides given.
E: sides $8\text{ cm}$ and $12.1\text{ cm}$ with the $25^\circ$ angle between them.
exercises.answer: A, B and E are definitely congruent to X. A: ASA ($120^\circ$, $5.9\text{ cm}$, $35^\circ$). B: two angles and the corresponding side (ASA: $25^\circ$, $35^\circ$ and the $8\text{ cm}$ side between the $25^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ vertices). E: SAS ($8\text{ cm}$, $25^\circ$, $12.1\text{ cm}$). C and D are not definitely congruent: C gives two sides and an angle that is not between them, and D gives only angles (same shape, but possibly a different size).
exercises.full_solution:
In X: the $8.0\text{ cm}$ side lies between the $120^\circ$ and $25^\circ$ angles, the $5.9\text{ cm}$ side between $120^\circ$ and $35^\circ$, and the $12.1\text{ cm}$ side between $35^\circ$ and $25^\circ$.
A: $120^\circ$ and $35^\circ$ with the $5.9\text{ cm}$ side between them, exactly as in X, so A $\cong$ X (ASA).
B: the angles $35^\circ$ and $25^\circ$ force the third angle to be $120^\circ$, and the $8\text{ cm}$ side joins the $25^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ vertices, exactly as in X. Two angles and the corresponding side are equal, so B $\cong$ X (ASA).
C: the $25^\circ$ angle is not between the $8.0\text{ cm}$ and $5.9\text{ cm}$ sides, so this is not SAS. Two sides and a non-included angle do not fix the triangle (two different triangles are possible here), so C is not definitely congruent to X.
D: equal angles only show that D is similar to X; with no side given it could be larger or smaller, so it is not definitely congruent.
E: the $25^\circ$ angle lies between the $8\text{ cm}$ and $12.1\text{ cm}$ sides, exactly as in X, so E $\cong$ X (SAS).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Draw each of the solid shapes (a) cuboid (b) prism with a rectangular notch cut out (c) equilateral triangular prism (d) square-based pyramid (e) cylinder (f) cone (g) sphere (h) cube. For each: (i) draw a different plane of symmetry on each of two copies (ii) state the total number of planes of symmetry.
exercises.answer: (a) cuboid: 3 planes (b) notched prism: 2 planes (the notch is centred and runs the full length of the prism) (c) equilateral triangular prism: 4 planes (d) square-based pyramid: 4 planes (e) cylinder: infinitely many (through the axis) + 1 (perpendicular, bisecting the height) (f) cone: infinitely many (through the apex and axis) (g) sphere: infinitely many (any plane through the centre) (h) cube: 9 planes.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) A (non-square) cuboid has 3 planes of symmetry, each parallel to a pair of faces and bisecting the solid.
(b) The notched prism has a constant cross-section (a rectangle with a rectangular notch cut from the middle of its bottom edge) and the notch runs the full length of the prism. It has 2 planes of symmetry: the vertical plane through the centre of the notch, running along the length of the prism, and the plane perpendicular to the length through its midpoint.
(c) An equilateral-triangular prism has 3 planes of symmetry through the prism's length (each through one edge and the midpoint of the opposite face), plus 1 plane perpendicular to the length through its midpoint — 4 in total.
(d) A square-based pyramid has 4 planes of symmetry: 2 through opposite edges' midpoints (vertical, through the apex) and 2 through pairs of opposite vertices of the square base (through the apex).
(e) A cylinder has an infinite number of planes of symmetry containing its axis, plus exactly 1 plane perpendicular to the axis through its midpoint.
(f) A cone has an infinite number of planes of symmetry, each containing the apex and the central axis.
(g) A sphere has an infinite number of planes of symmetry — any plane through its centre.
(h) A cube has 9 planes of symmetry: 3 parallel to pairs of faces, and 6 through diagonally opposite edges.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: For each of the solid shapes (a) cuboid (b) notched prism (c) equilateral triangular prism (d) square-based pyramid (e) cylinder (f) cone (g) sphere (h) cube, determine the order of rotational symmetry about the axis shown (a long axis through the cuboid's length; a vertical axis through the notched prism; the long axis of the triangular prism; the vertical axis through the pyramid's apex; the central axis of the cylinder; the central axis of the cone; any axis through the sphere's centre; the long diagonal axis of the cube, as drawn).
exercises.answer: (a) order 2 (about the length axis, for a non-square cross-section) (b) order 2 (about the vertical axis shown, because the notch runs right through the prism) (c) order 3 (about the prism's length axis) (d) order 4 (about the vertical axis through the apex) (e) infinite order (about the central axis) (f) infinite order (about the central axis) (g) infinite order (about any axis through the centre) (h) order 3 (about a long/body diagonal).
exercises.full_solution:
(a) A cuboid rotated about the axis through the centres of two opposite rectangular faces (along its length) looks the same twice per full turn — order $2$.
(b) The vertical axis passes through the centre of the top face. The notch runs right through the prism from the front face to the back face, so a half-turn ($180^\circ$) about this axis swaps the front and back faces and the prism looks exactly the same — order $2$.
(c) The equilateral triangular prism rotated about its long axis (through the centroid of the triangular cross-section) matches itself every $120^\circ$ — order $3$.
(d) The square-based pyramid rotated about the vertical axis through its apex matches itself every $90^\circ$ — order $4$.
(e) The cylinder rotated about its central axis looks identical for every angle of rotation — infinite order.
(f) Likewise, the cone rotated about its central axis has infinite rotational symmetry.
(g) The sphere rotated about ANY axis through its centre has infinite rotational symmetry.
(h) The cube rotated about a body diagonal (corner to opposite corner) matches itself every $120^\circ$ — order $3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: $O$ is the centre of a circle; $PQ$ and $RS$ are chords of equal length, and $M$, $N$ are their respective midpoints. (a) What kind of triangle is $\triangle POQ$? (b) Describe the line $ON$ in relation to $RS$. (c) If angle $POQ$ is $80^\circ$, calculate angle $OQP$. (d) Calculate angle $ORS$. (e) If $PQ$ is $6\text{ cm}$, calculate the length $OM$ (use angle $POQ=80^\circ$ from part (c)). (f) Calculate the diameter of the circle.
exercises.answer: (a) Isosceles ($OP=OQ$, both radii). (b) $ON$ is the perpendicular bisector of $RS$. (c) $50^\circ$. (d) $50^\circ$ (by the same reasoning, since $RS=PQ$ makes $\triangle ROS$ congruent to $\triangle POQ$). (e) $OM\approx3.58\text{ cm}$. (f) Diameter $\approx9.33\text{ cm}$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $OP=OQ$ (both radii of the same circle), so $\triangle POQ$ is isosceles.
(b) Since $OP=OQ$ and $PQ=RS$, $\triangle ROS\cong\triangle POQ$ (SSS, both isosceles with the two radii and chord matching); the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is always the perpendicular bisector of that chord, so $ON$ is the perpendicular bisector of $RS$.
(c) Since $\triangle POQ$ is isosceles with $OP=OQ$, the base angles are equal: angle $OQP=$ angle $OPQ=(180-80)/2=50^\circ$.
(d) Since $RS=PQ$, by the congruence in (b), angle $ORS=$ angle $OQP=50^\circ$.
(e) $QM=\tfrac12PQ=3\text{ cm}$ (as $OM\perp PQ$ bisects it). In right triangle $OMQ$, angle $OQM=50^\circ$, so $OM=QM\tan(50^\circ)=3\tan(50^\circ)\approx3.575\text{ cm}$.
(f) Radius $OQ=QM/\cos(50^\circ)=3/\cos(50^\circ)\approx4.667\text{ cm}$; diameter $\approx9.33\text{ cm}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: Circle with centre $O$: the equal chords $PQ$ and $RS$ (single ticks), their midpoints $M$ and $N$, and the radii drawn to the ends of each chord. $\angle POQ=80^{\circ}$.
assets.purpose: Show the two equal chords, the radii that make each triangle isosceles and the perpendiculars OM and ON, so the student can see which triangle each part of the question refers to.

exercises.statement: $O$ is the centre of a circle; $AB$ and $CD$ are equal chords, with $R$, $S$ their respective midpoints. State whether each is true or false, giving reasons: (a) angle $COD=2\times$ angle $AOR$. (b) $OR=OS$. (c) If angle $ROB$ is $60^\circ$ then $\triangle AOB$ is equilateral. (d) $OR$ and $OS$ are perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $CD$ respectively.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) True: $R$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so angle $AOR=\tfrac12$ angle $AOB$; as $AB=CD$, $\triangle AOB\cong\triangle COD$ (SSS, equal chords and equal radii), so angle $AOB=$ angle $COD$, giving angle $COD=2\times$ angle $AOR$.
(b) True: since $AB=CD$, the congruent isosceles triangles $AOB$ and $COD$ have equal perpendicular heights from $O$ to the chords, i.e. $OR=OS$.
(c) False: $OR$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, and in the isosceles triangle $AOB$ it also bisects the angle $AOB$. If angle $ROB=60^\circ$, then angle $AOB=2\times60=120^\circ$, so the base angles are $OAB=OBA=(180-120)/2=30^\circ$. The angles are $120^\circ$, $30^\circ$, $30^\circ$, so $\triangle AOB$ is isosceles but NOT equilateral.
(d) True: the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is always perpendicular to that chord (standard circle property), so $OR\perp AB$ and $OS\perp CD$, i.e. both are perpendicular bisectors.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: Circle with centre $O$: the equal chords $AB$ and $CD$ (single ticks) with midpoints $R$ and $S$, and the perpendiculars $OR$ and $OS$ from the centre.
assets.purpose: Show the configuration the four true/false statements refer to, including the two congruent isosceles triangles AOB and COD.

exercises.statement: Using the diagram (three triangles $TOU$, $TOV$ and $VOW$ that share the vertex $O$, fanning out from $O$ to the points $U$, $T$, $V$ and $W$), state whether the following are true or false, giving reasons: (a) If $\triangle VOW$ and $\triangle TOU$ are isosceles triangles, then $T$, $U$, $V$ and $W$ would all lie on the circumference of a circle with centre $O$. (b) If $\triangle VOW$ and $\triangle TOU$ are congruent isosceles triangles, then $T$, $U$, $V$ and $W$ would all lie on the circumference of a circle with centre $O$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) False: $\triangle VOW$ being isosceles only tells us two of $OV,OW$ (or the third side) are equal, not that $OV=OW=OT=OU$ all together — e.g. $\triangle VOW$ could be isosceles with $OV=VW\ne OW$, giving $OV\ne OW$ and the four points would not be equidistant from $O$.
(b) True: if $\triangle VOW$ and $\triangle TOU$ are congruent AND isosceles, with the equal sides in each being the two segments from $O$ (i.e. $OV=OW$ and $OT=OU$), and since the two triangles are congruent, $OV=OW=OT=OU$ — all four points are the same distance from $O$, so they all lie on a circle centred at $O$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The three triangles $TOU$, $TOV$ and $VOW$ fanning out from the shared vertex $O$. The diagram is not drawn to scale and no sides are marked equal.
assets.purpose: Show that the four points U, T, V and W are drawn at different distances from O, so the student can test whether 'isosceles' alone forces them onto one circle.

exercises.statement: Assuming all lines drawn from points on the circumference are tangents, and $O$ is the centre, calculate the angle marked $x^\circ$ in each case: (a) Tangents $RP$ and $RQ$ are drawn from the external point $R$ to touch the circle at $P$ and $Q$, and $O$ is joined to $P$, $Q$ and $R$. Angle $ORQ=20^\circ$; find $x^\circ=$ angle $POR$. (b) $OT$ and $OS$ are radii to the two tangent points $T,S$ from external point $Q$, with angle $TOS=108^\circ$; find $x^\circ=$ angle $TQS$. (c) Tangents $ML$ and $MN$ are drawn from the external point $M$, with angle $LMN=42^\circ$; $O$ is joined to $L$ and $N$, and the chord $LN$ is drawn. Find $x^\circ=$ angle $OLN$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Triangle $OQR$ has a right angle at $Q$ (tangent $\perp$ radius) and $20^\circ$ at $R$, so angle $QOR=180-90-20=70^\circ$. Triangles $OPR$ and $OQR$ are congruent (RHS: right angles at $P$ and $Q$, $OP=OQ$ radii, $OR$ common), so $x=$ angle $POR=$ angle $QOR=70^\circ$.
(b) Quadrilateral $OTQS$ has right angles at $T$ and $S$ (tangent $\perp$ radius at each tangent point), so $x=360-90-90-108=72^\circ$.
(c) Quadrilateral $OLMN$ has right angles at $L$ and $N$, so angle $LON=360-90-90-42=138^\circ$. Triangle $OLN$ is isosceles ($OL=ON$, radii), so $x=$ angle $OLN=(180-138)/2=21^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The three tangent diagrams: (a) tangents $RP$ and $RQ$ with $\angle ORQ=20^{\circ}$; (b) tangents $QT$ and $QS$ with $\angle TOS=108^{\circ}$; (c) tangents $ML$ and $MN$ with $\angle LMN=42^{\circ}$ and the chord $LN$ drawn. Each tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at $90^{\circ}$.
assets.purpose: Give each part its own figure with the right angles marked, so the student can see which quadrilateral or triangle to use rather than reconstructing it from the text.

exercises.statement: Assuming lines from points on the circumference are tangents, calculate the length marked $y\text{ cm}$: (a) radius $OQ=5\text{ cm}$, $OR=12\text{ cm}$ ($R$ external point), tangent length $QR=y$. (b) radius $=3.1\text{ cm}$, tangent length $=8.8\text{ cm}$; $y$ is the distance from the external point to the centre. (c) distance from the centre to the external point $=9.3\text{ cm}$, angle between this line and the tangent at the external point $=22^\circ$; $y$ is the radius.
exercises.full_solution:
Each uses a right triangle (right angle at the tangent point, tangent $\perp$ radius).
(a) $y=\sqrt{12^2-5^2}=\sqrt{144-25}=\sqrt{119}\approx10.91\text{ cm}$.
(b) Here $y$ is the hypotenuse: $y=\sqrt{8.8^2+3.1^2}=\sqrt{77.44+9.61}=\sqrt{87.05}\approx9.33\text{ cm}$.
(c) The radius $y$ is opposite the $22^\circ$ angle and $9.3\text{ cm}$ is the hypotenuse, so $y=9.3\sin(22^\circ)\approx3.48\text{ cm}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The three right-angled triangles formed by a radius, a tangent and the line from the centre to the external point: (a) radius $5$ cm and $OR=12$ cm; (b) radius $3.1$ cm and tangent $8.8$ cm; (c) $OP=9.3$ cm with a $22^{\circ}$ angle at $P$. The diagrams are not drawn to scale.
assets.purpose: Show in each part which length is the radius, which is the tangent and which is the hypotenuse, so the student chooses the right Pythagoras or trigonometry step.

exercises.statement:
Deduce, giving your reasons, the size of the labelled angles in each of the following (diagrams not to scale):
(1) Two straight lines cross at a point, and an extra ray leaves the point to the left. Going round the point: $p^\circ$ (top, between the two upper arms), $126^\circ$ (from the upper-right arm round to the lower-right arm), an unlabelled angle (bottom, between the two lower arms), then $q^\circ$ (between the lower-left arm and the extra ray) and $q^\circ$ (between the extra ray and the upper-left arm).
(2) Two straight lines cross at a point, and an extra ray leaves the point to the left. Going round the point: $80^\circ$ (top, between the two upper arms), $c^\circ$ (between the upper-right arm and the lower-right arm), $b^\circ$ (bottom, between the two lower arms), $a^\circ$ (between the lower-left arm and the extra ray) and $45^\circ$ (between the extra ray and the upper-left arm).
(3) Two parallel horizontal lines are crossed by a transversal that slopes down from left to right. At the upper intersection: $y^\circ$ (above the line, left of the transversal), $x^\circ$ (below, left) and $z^\circ$ (below, right). At the lower intersection: $w^\circ$ (above, left), $v^\circ$ (below, left) and $60^\circ$ (below, right).
(4) A triangle has base angles $50^\circ$ (left) and $c^\circ$ (right). A line parallel to the base cuts the other two sides. Where it meets the left side: $a^\circ$ (above the line, inside the small top triangle) and $b^\circ$ (below the line). Where it meets the right side: $45^\circ$ (above the line, inside the small top triangle) and $d^\circ$ (below the line).
(5) Two parallel horizontal lines are crossed by two parallel lines that slope up to the right. On the upper horizontal line: $r^\circ$ (below the line, left of the first sloping line) and $45^\circ$ (below the line, left of the second sloping line). On the lower horizontal line, at the first sloping line: $s^\circ$ (above the line, right) and $t^\circ$ (below the line, right); at the second sloping line: $q^\circ$ (above, left) and $p^\circ$ (above, right).
(6) Two parallel horizontal lines are joined by two straight lines that cross each other between them. One crossing line makes $d^\circ$ with the upper line (at its left end) and $70^\circ$ with the lower line (at its right end); the other makes $30^\circ$ with the upper line (at its right end) and $e^\circ$ with the lower line (at its left end).
(7) Four rays leave a point. Going round: $a^\circ$ (between the upper-left ray and the upward ray), $159^\circ$ (between the upward ray and the lower-right ray), $2a^\circ$ (between the lower-right ray and the lower-left ray) and a right angle (between the lower-left ray and the upper-left ray).
(8) A straight line crosses two parallel lines. The angles $3a^\circ$ and $2a^\circ$ lie between the parallel lines, on the same side of the crossing line.
exercises.full_solution:
(1) Label the unlabelled angle (between the two 'lower' rays of the two full lines) as $z^\circ$. Since those two rays are each the extension of one of the 'upper' rays that bound $p^\circ$, $z$ is vertically opposite $p$, so $z=p$. Also the combined angle $q+q$ (the two labelled $q$'s, separated by the lone ray) is vertically opposite the $126^\circ$ angle (both lying between the SAME pair of full lines, on opposite sides of the vertex), so $2q=126\Rightarrow q=63^\circ$. Angles around the point sum to $360^\circ$: $p+q+126+q+z=360$, and $z=p$, so $2p+2(63)=360-126=234\Rightarrow 2p=108\Rightarrow p=54^\circ$.
(2) By the identical structure to (1) (with $80^\circ$ playing the role of $p$, and $b^\circ$ the role of the unlabelled vertical-angle partner of $80^\circ$): $b=80^\circ$ (vertically opposite). Also $45+a$ (the two parts analogous to $q+q$) is vertically opposite $c^\circ$ (analogous to $126^\circ$), so $c=45+a$. Angles round the point: $80+45+c+b+a=360\Rightarrow80+45+c+80+a=360\Rightarrow a+c=155$. Substituting $c=45+a$: $a+45+a=155\Rightarrow2a=110\Rightarrow a=55^\circ$, so $c=45+55=100^\circ$.
(3) At the lower intersection, $w$ is vertically opposite the $60^\circ$ angle, so $w=60^\circ$, and $v=180-60=120^\circ$ (angles on a straight line). At the upper intersection, $z$ corresponds to the $60^\circ$ angle, so $z=60^\circ$ (corresponding angles); $y$ is vertically opposite $z$, so $y=60^\circ$; and $x=180-60=120^\circ$ (angles on a straight line; $x$ also corresponds to $v$).
(4) Since the cutting line is parallel to the base, corresponding angles (using the left side as transversal) give $a=50^\circ$, and $b=180-50=130^\circ$ (angles on a straight line, the left side). Using the right side as transversal, $c$ corresponds to the $45^\circ$ angle, so $c=45^\circ$, and $d=180-45=135^\circ$ (angles on a straight line).
(5) The two sloping lines are parallel, so $r$ corresponds to the $45^\circ$ angle: $r=45^\circ$. On the lower line, $s$ is alternate to $r$ (horizontal lines parallel), so $s=45^\circ$, and $t=180-45=135^\circ$ (angles on a straight line). At the second sloping line, $p$ corresponds to $s$, so $p=45^\circ$, and $q=180-45=135^\circ$ (angles on a straight line).
(6) Since the two horizontal lines are parallel, and the diagonal lines are transversals crossing both, alternate angles are equal: $d$ (top) is alternate to the $70^\circ$ angle (bottom), so $d=70^\circ$; $e$ (bottom) is alternate to the $30^\circ$ angle (top), so $e=30^\circ$.
(7) Angles round a point add up to $360^\circ$, and the marked right angle is one of the four angles: $a+159+2a+90=360\Rightarrow3a=111\Rightarrow a=37^\circ$.
(8) The transversal crosses two parallel lines, creating co-interior (allied) angles $3a^\circ$ and $2a^\circ$ on the same side, which sum to $180^\circ$: $3a+2a=180\Rightarrow5a=180\Rightarrow a=36^\circ$ (so the two angles are $108^\circ$ and $72^\circ$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
(a) Calculate the size of angle $x$ where three rays from a point create angles $x^\circ, 120^\circ, 170^\circ$ around the point (summing to $360^\circ$).
(b) Calculate the size of angle $a$ where several rays from a point on a straight line create angles $40^\circ, 88^\circ, a^\circ, 25^\circ$ (summing to $180^\circ$, the angles lying on one side of the straight line).
exercises.full_solution:
(a) The sum of all the angles around a point is $360^\circ$: $120+170+x=360\Rightarrow x=360-120-170=70^\circ$.
(b) The sum of all the angles at a point on a straight line is $180^\circ$: $40+88+a+25=180\Rightarrow a=180-40-88-25=27^\circ$.
The book notes that in both cases the angle is CALCULATED, not measured from the (not-to-scale) diagram.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (a) & (b), angles at a point and on a line

exercises.statement: For each triangle, use the information given to calculate the size of angle $x$: (a) isosceles triangle (apex at the left, two equal marked sides), base angle $70^\circ$, $x^\circ$ at the other base vertex. (b) triangle with angles $95^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ given, $x^\circ$ the third angle. (c) equilateral triangle (all three sides marked equal), $x^\circ$ one of its angles. (d) triangle with angles $42^\circ$ and $65^\circ$ given, $x^\circ$ the third angle. (e) right-angled isosceles triangle (right angle plus two marked equal legs), $x^\circ$ one of the other two angles. (f) isosceles triangle (apex $x^\circ$, two equal marked sides from the apex), base angle $35^\circ$ given.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Isosceles with apex on the left means the two BASE angles (at top-right and bottom-right) are equal, so $x=70^\circ$.
(b) $x=180-95-30=55^\circ$.
(c) An equilateral triangle has all angles equal to $60^\circ$, so $x=60^\circ$.
(d) $x=180-42-65=73^\circ$.
(e) A right-angled isosceles triangle has its right angle and two other equal angles; since $90+x+x=180$, $x=45^\circ$.
(f) Isosceles with the two marked equal sides from the apex means the TWO base angles are equal, both $35^\circ$; so $x=180-35-35=110^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In each diagram, calculate the size of the labelled angles. (a) A triangle with apex split into $a^\circ$ and $b^\circ$ by an altitude (right angle at its foot on the base); base angles $60^\circ$ (left) and $45^\circ$ (right). (b) In triangle $TBR$, a straight line is drawn from $B$ to a point $D$ on side $TR$. In triangle $TBD$: angle $T=x^\circ$, angle $TDB=100^\circ$ and angle $TBD=30^\circ$. In triangle $DBR$: angle $BDR=y^\circ$, angle $DBR=z^\circ$ and angle $R=30^\circ$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) The altitude creates two right-angled triangles. Left: $a=180-60-90=30^\circ$. Right: $b=180-45-90=45^\circ$.
(b) In triangle $TBD$: $x=180-100-30=50^\circ$. Angles on the straight line $TR$ at $D$: $y=180-100=80^\circ$. In triangle $DBR$: $z=180-80-30=70^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the size of angle $p$ in a quadrilateral whose other three angles are $90^\circ$ (top-left), $80^\circ$ (bottom-left) and $60^\circ$ (right).
exercises.full_solution: The angles of a quadrilateral sum to $360^\circ$: $90+80+60+p=360\Rightarrow p=360-90-80-60=130^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example, angle in a quadrilateral

exercises.statement: In a quadrilateral, three angles are $100^\circ$, $75^\circ$ and $70^\circ$; calculate the fourth angle $a^\circ$.
exercises.full_solution: $a=360-100-75-70=115^\circ$ (angle sum of a quadrilateral).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A parallelogram (both pairs of opposite sides marked parallel with arrows) has one angle $40^\circ$ (right vertex) and the opposite (left) angle $x^\circ$; the top and bottom vertices are $y^\circ$ and $z^\circ$ respectively. Calculate $x,y,z$.
exercises.full_solution: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal: $x=40^\circ$ (opposite the given $40^\circ$), and $y=z$ (the other opposite pair). Adjacent angles are supplementary: $x+y=180\Rightarrow y=140^\circ$, and so $z=y=140^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A kite-shaped quadrilateral (two pairs of adjacent sides marked equal) has its left vertex $85^\circ$ and right vertex $125^\circ$ (the two 'unequal' vertices); the top and bottom vertices are $m^\circ$ and $n^\circ$. Calculate $m$ and $n$.
exercises.full_solution: A kite is symmetric about the diagonal joining the vertices where the pairs of equal sides meet (here the left and right vertices, $85^\circ$ and $125^\circ$). The top and bottom vertices are reflections of each other in this diagonal, so their angles are equal: $m=n$. The quadrilateral's angles sum to $360^\circ$: $m+85+125+n=360\Rightarrow m+n=150$, and with $m=n$: $m=n=75^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The kite: the two sides meeting at the left vertex are equal (single ticks) and the two meeting at the right vertex are equal (double ticks). The left angle is $85^{\circ}$, the right angle is $125^{\circ}$, and the top and bottom angles are $m^{\circ}$ and $n^{\circ}$.
assets.purpose: Show which pairs of sides are equal, so the student can see that the kite is symmetrical about the left-right diagonal and therefore m = n.

exercises.statement: A quadrilateral has a pair of parallel sides (marked with arrows, left and right), and the top and bottom sides marked equal (tick marks), making it an isosceles trapezium (with the parallel sides vertical). The top-left vertex is $65^\circ$; the two right-hand vertices (upper and lower) are $u^\circ$ and $t^\circ$; the bottom-left vertex is $s^\circ$. Calculate $u, t, s$.
exercises.full_solution: Since the left and right sides are parallel, co-interior angles (using the top edge as transversal) give $65+u=180\Rightarrow u=115^\circ$. By the isosceles (reflection) symmetry of the trapezium about its horizontal mid-line, the bottom-left angle $s$ equals the top-left angle: $s=65^\circ$, and the bottom-right angle $t$ equals the top-right angle: $t=115^\circ$. Check: $65+115+115+65=360$ ✓.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The isosceles trapezium: the left and right sides are parallel (arrows) and the top and bottom sides are equal (single ticks). The top-left angle is $65^{\circ}$; the other angles are $u^{\circ}$, $t^{\circ}$ and $s^{\circ}$.
assets.purpose: Show which pair of sides is parallel and which pair is equal, so the student uses co-interior angles on the correct transversal.

exercises.statement: A parallelogram (both pairs of opposite sides marked parallel) has top-left angle $j^\circ$, top-right angle $i^\circ$, bottom-left angle $k^\circ$ and bottom-right angle $h^\circ$. The bottom side is extended to the right, and the exterior angle between this extension and the right-hand side is $60^\circ$. Calculate $h$, $i$, $j$ and $k$.
exercises.full_solution: Angles on a straight line: $h=180-60=120^\circ$. Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so $j=h=120^\circ$. Co-interior angles between the parallel top and bottom sides add up to $180^\circ$: $i=180-h=60^\circ$ and $k=180-j=60^\circ$ (also $k=i$, opposite angles). Check: $120+60+120+60=360^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The parallelogram with angles $j^{\circ}$, $i^{\circ}$, $k^{\circ}$ and $h^{\circ}$. The bottom side is extended (dashed) and the exterior angle between the extension and the right-hand side is $60^{\circ}$.
assets.purpose: Show that the 60 degree angle is outside the parallelogram on the straight line through the bottom side, so the student starts from 180 - 60.

exercises.statement: A trapezium has a long bottom side and a shorter top side, which are parallel. A diagonal is drawn from the bottom-left vertex to the top-right vertex. The left side is equal to the top side (marked with double ticks), and the diagonal is equal to the bottom side (marked with single ticks). The angle at the bottom-right vertex is $80^\circ$. The labelled angles are: $e^\circ$ at the top-left vertex; $c^\circ$ (between the top side and the diagonal) and $a^\circ$ (between the diagonal and the right side) at the top-right vertex; $d^\circ$ (between the left side and the diagonal) and $b^\circ$ (between the diagonal and the bottom side) at the bottom-left vertex. Calculate $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and $e$.
exercises.full_solution:
Lower triangle (bottom-left, top-right, bottom-right vertices): the diagonal equals the bottom side, so this triangle is isosceles and its base angles at the top-right and bottom-right vertices are equal: $a=80^\circ$. Then $b=180-80-80=20^\circ$ (angle sum of a triangle).
The top and bottom sides are parallel, so $c=b=20^\circ$ (alternate angles, with the diagonal as transversal).
Upper triangle (bottom-left, top-left, top-right vertices): the left side equals the top side, so the base angles at the bottom-left and top-right vertices are equal: $d=c=20^\circ$. Then $e=180-20-20=140^\circ$.
Check: co-interior angles on the left side: $e+(d+b)=140+40=180^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The trapezium: the top and bottom sides are parallel (arrows), the left side equals the top side (double ticks) and the diagonal equals the bottom side (single ticks). The angle at the bottom-right vertex is $80^{\circ}$, and $a^{\circ}$, $b^{\circ}$, $c^{\circ}$, $d^{\circ}$, $e^{\circ}$ are the angles marked.
assets.purpose: Show how the diagonal splits the trapezium into two isosceles triangles and which angle label belongs to which part of each vertex.

exercises.statement: A quadrilateral has a right angle at its bottom-left corner. From its top-left corner a straight line is drawn to a point on the bottom side; this line is parallel to the right-hand side of the quadrilateral (marked with arrows). At the top-left corner the line makes an angle $p^\circ$ with the left side and $45^\circ$ with the top side. Where the line meets the bottom side, the angle between the line and the bottom side on its left is $50^\circ$ and on its right is $q^\circ$. At the bottom-right corner, the angle between the bottom side and the right-hand side is $r^\circ$. Calculate $p$, $q$ and $r$.
exercises.full_solution:
Left triangle (left side, bottom side and the drawn line): it has a right angle and a $50^\circ$ angle, so $p=180-90-50=40^\circ$.
Angles on the straight bottom line: $q=180-50=130^\circ$.
The drawn line is parallel to the right-hand side, so $r$ corresponds to the $50^\circ$ angle (bottom side as transversal): $r=50^\circ$. (The $45^\circ$ angle is not needed.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The quadrilateral with a right angle at the bottom-left vertex. The line from the top-left vertex to the bottom side is parallel to the right-hand side (arrows); it makes $45^{\circ}$ with the top side and $p^{\circ}$ with the left side, and meets the bottom side at $50^{\circ}$ on the left and $q^{\circ}$ on the right. The bottom-right angle is $r^{\circ}$.
assets.purpose: Show the parallel pair and the right-angled triangle on the left, so the student can see that r corresponds to the 50 degree angle and that the 45 degree angle is not needed.

exercises.statement: The diagram shows three triangles $ABC$, $ACD$ and $CDE$, where $B$, $C$ and $E$ lie on a straight line (the base). The four sides $AB$, $AC$, $CD$ and $CE$ are all marked equal. Angle $ADC=50^\circ$ and angle $CED=75^\circ$. The labelled angles are $u^\circ=$ angle $ABC$, $v^\circ=$ angle $BAC$, $t^\circ=$ angle $ACB$, $r^\circ=$ angle $CAD$, $s^\circ=$ angle $ACD$, $q^\circ=$ angle $DCE$ and $p^\circ=$ angle $CDE$. Calculate $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$, $t$, $u$ and $v$.
exercises.full_solution:
Triangle $CDE$: $CD=CE$, so the base angles are equal: $p=75^\circ$, and $q=180-75-75=30^\circ$.
Triangle $ACD$: $AC=CD$, so the base angles are equal: $r=$ angle $ADC=50^\circ$, and $s=180-50-50=80^\circ$.
Angles on the straight line at $C$: $t=180-s-q=180-80-30=70^\circ$.
Triangle $ABC$: $AB=AC$, so $u=t=70^\circ$, and $v=180-70-70=40^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: Triangles $ABC$, $ACD$ and $CDE$ with $B$, $C$ and $E$ on a straight line. The sides $AB$, $AC$, $CD$ and $CE$ are all equal (single ticks). $\angle ADC=50^{\circ}$ and $\angle CED=75^{\circ}$; the other angles are marked $p^{\circ}$ to $v^{\circ}$.
assets.purpose: Show which four sides are equal and where each labelled angle sits, so the student can work through the three isosceles triangles in order.

exercises.statement: Find the sum of the interior angles of a regular pentagon and hence the size of each interior angle.
exercises.full_solution: For a polygon with $n$ sides, the sum of interior angles is $180(n-2)^\circ$. For a pentagon, $n=5$: sum $=180(5-2)=180\times3=540^\circ$. For a REGULAR pentagon, all 5 interior angles are equal, so each $=540/5=108^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example, sum of interior angles of a regular pentagon

exercises.statement: (a) Find the size of an exterior angle of a regular nonagon (9 sides). (b) Calculate the number of sides a regular polygon has if each exterior angle is $15^\circ$.
exercises.full_solution:
The sum of the exterior angles of any convex polygon is $360^\circ$; for a regular polygon with $n$ sides, each exterior angle $=360/n$.
(a) $360/9=40^\circ$.
(b) $n=360/15=24$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (a) & (b), exterior angles of a regular polygon

exercises.statement:
(1) Find the sum of the interior angles of: (a) a hexagon (b) a nonagon (c) a heptagon.
(2) Find the value of each interior angle of the following regular polygons: (a) an octagon (b) a square (c) a decagon (d) a dodecagon.
(3) Find the size of each exterior angle of the following regular polygons: (a) a pentagon (b) a dodecagon (c) a heptagon.
(4) The exterior angles of regular polygons are given below. Calculate the number of sides in each case: (a) $20^\circ$ (b) $36^\circ$ (c) $10^\circ$ (d) $45^\circ$ (e) $18^\circ$ (f) $3^\circ$.
(5) The interior angles of regular polygons are given below. Calculate the number of sides in each case: (a) $108^\circ$ (b) $150^\circ$ (c) $162^\circ$ (d) $156^\circ$ (e) $171^\circ$ (f) $179^\circ$.
(6) Calculate the number of sides a regular polygon has if an interior angle is five times the size of an exterior angle.
exercises.full_solution:
(1) Sum of interior angles $=180(n-2)$: (a) $n=6\Rightarrow180\times4=720^\circ$ (b) $n=9\Rightarrow180\times7=1260^\circ$ (c) $n=7\Rightarrow180\times5=900^\circ$.
(2) Each interior angle (regular) $=180(n-2)/n$: (a) $n=8\Rightarrow135^\circ$ (b) $n=4\Rightarrow90^\circ$ (c) $n=10\Rightarrow144^\circ$ (d) $n=12\Rightarrow150^\circ$.
(3) Each exterior angle $=360/n$: (a) $360/5=72^\circ$ (b) $360/12=30^\circ$ (c) $360/7\approx51.43^\circ$.
(4) $n=360/\text{exterior angle}$: (a) $360/20=18$ (b) $360/36=10$ (c) $360/10=36$ (d) $360/45=8$ (e) $360/18=20$ (f) $360/3=120$.
(5) exterior$=180-$interior, then $n=360/\text{exterior}$: (a) ext$=72\Rightarrow n=5$ (b) ext$=30\Rightarrow n=12$ (c) ext$=18\Rightarrow n=20$ (d) ext$=24\Rightarrow n=15$ (e) ext$=9\Rightarrow n=40$ (f) ext$=1\Rightarrow n=360$.
(6) interior$=5\times$exterior, and interior$+$exterior$=180\Rightarrow6\times$exterior$=180\Rightarrow$exterior$=30^\circ\Rightarrow n=360/30=12$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
$O$ marks the centre of each circle. Calculate the value of $x$ in each case:
(1) A triangle has one side as a diameter and its third vertex on the circle; the angle at one end of the diameter is $30^\circ$ and the angle at the other end is $x^\circ$.
(2) A triangle has one side as a diameter and its third vertex on the circle below it; the angle at the left end of the diameter is $45^\circ$. The side joining the third vertex to the right end of the diameter is extended beyond the circle, and $x^\circ$ is the angle between this extension and the diameter.
(3) A triangle has one side as a diameter and its third vertex on the circle. The side joining the third vertex to one end of the diameter is extended beyond that end, and the angle between the extension and the diameter is $110^\circ$; $x^\circ$ is the angle at the other end of the diameter.
(4) A quadrilateral is drawn in the circle with one diagonal passing through $O$ (a diameter), and its left and right sides marked parallel. At the bottom-right vertex (one end of the diameter), the diagonal makes $58^\circ$ with the bottom side and $x^\circ$ with the right side.
(5) $LR$ is a horizontal diameter and $B$ is a point on the circle below it; triangle $LBR$ is drawn. A line from $O$, parallel to $BR$, meets $LB$ at $M$. Angle $BLR=20^\circ$ and $x^\circ$ is angle $MOR$.
(6) $AP$ is a diameter and $B$ is a point on the circle with $AB=BP$. The diameter $AP$ is extended beyond $P$ to a point $X$ with $PX=PB$, and $X$ is joined to $B$. $x^\circ$ is angle $BXP$.
exercises.full_solution:
The angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$ (the angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circumference).
(1) The angle at the third vertex is $90^\circ$, so $x=180-90-30=60^\circ$.
(2) The angle at the third vertex is $90^\circ$, so the interior angle at the right end of the diameter is $180-90-45=45^\circ$. Angles on a straight line: $x=180-45=135^\circ$.
(3) Angles on a straight line: the interior angle at the first end of the diameter is $180-110=70^\circ$. The angle at the third vertex is $90^\circ$, so $x=180-90-70=20^\circ$.
(4) In the triangle formed by the diameter and the bottom side, the angle at the bottom-left vertex is $90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle), so the angle between the diameter and the left side at the top-left vertex is $180-90-58=32^\circ$. The left and right sides are parallel, so $x=32^\circ$ (alternate angles, with the diameter as transversal).
(5) Angle $LBR=90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle). $OM\parallel BR$, so angle $LMO=$ angle $LBR=90^\circ$ (corresponding angles). In triangle $LMO$: angle $LOM=180-90-20=70^\circ$. Angles on the straight line $LR$: $x=180-70=110^\circ$.
(6) Angle $ABP=90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle) and $AB=BP$, so angle $APB=45^\circ$. Angles on the straight line $AX$: angle $BPX=180-45=135^\circ$. Triangle $PBX$ is isosceles ($PX=PB$), so $x=$ angle $PXB=$ angle $PBX=(180-135)/2=22.5^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
$O$ marks the centre of each circle; lines drawn from points on the circumference are tangents. Calculate $x$:
(1) A diameter is horizontal and a vertical tangent touches the circle at the right-hand end $T$ of the diameter. A line from $O$ meets the tangent at $X$, making $55^\circ$ with $OT$; $x^\circ$ is the angle at $X$ in triangle $OTX$.
(2) Two tangents are drawn from an external point $P$, touching the circle at $A$ and $B$; $O$ is joined to $A$, $B$ and $P$. Angle $OPB=30^\circ$ and $x^\circ$ is angle $AOP$.
(3) Two tangents are drawn from an external point, and the angle between the two radii to the points of contact is $140^\circ$; $x^\circ$ is the angle between the two tangents at the external point.
(4) $LR$ is a diameter and the line through $R$ is a tangent. $T$ is a point on the tangent with $RT=LR$ (marked equal), and $LT$ is drawn; $x^\circ$ is angle $LTR$.
exercises.full_solution:
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
(1) Angle $OTX=90^\circ$, so $x=180-90-55=35^\circ$.
(2) Triangles $OAP$ and $OBP$ are congruent (RHS: right angles at $A$ and $B$, $OA=OB$, $OP$ common), so angle $OPA=$ angle $OPB=30^\circ$. In triangle $OAP$: $x=180-90-30=60^\circ$.
(3) The quadrilateral formed by $O$, the two points of contact and the external point has right angles at the two points of contact, so $x=360-90-90-140=40^\circ$.
(4) Angle $LRT=90^\circ$ (tangent $\perp$ radius). Triangle $LRT$ is isosceles with $RT=LR$, so its other two angles are equal: $x=(180-90)/2=45^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
(1) In a pentagon, the angles are $2x^\circ, 3x^\circ, x^\circ, 3x^\circ, x^\circ$ (in order around the pentagon). (a) Calculate the value of $x$. (b) Calculate the size of each of the angles.
(2) In an octagon, four angles (the two at the top and the two at the bottom) are $(x+20)^\circ$ and the other four angles are $x^\circ$. Find the size of each angle.
(3) A pentagon has exterior angles $x^\circ, (x+20)^\circ, x^\circ, (x+20)^\circ, x^\circ$ (in some order, summing to $360^\circ$). Calculate the value of $x$.
(4) A hexagon has exterior angles $x^\circ$, $x^\circ$, $(x+50)^\circ$, $(x+25)^\circ$, $(x+5)^\circ$ and $(x+10)^\circ$ at consecutive vertices; the interior angles at these vertices are $a^\circ$, $a^\circ$, $e^\circ$, $d^\circ$, $c^\circ$ and $b^\circ$ respectively. Calculate $x$ and the size of each of the angles $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and $e$.
exercises.answer:
(1)(a) $x=54^\circ$ (b) angles are $108^\circ,162^\circ,54^\circ,162^\circ,54^\circ$.
(2) $x=125^\circ$, so the angles are $125^\circ$ and $145^\circ$ alternately.
(3) $x=64^\circ$.
(4) $x=45^\circ$; interior angles: $a=135^\circ$ (at both vertices with exterior $x=45^\circ$), $e=85^\circ$ (exterior $x+50=95^\circ$), $b=125^\circ$ (exterior $x+10=55^\circ$), $c=130^\circ$ (exterior $x+5=50^\circ$), $d=110^\circ$ (exterior $x+25=70^\circ$).
exercises.full_solution:
(1) Sum of interior angles of a pentagon $=180(5-2)=540^\circ$. $2x+3x+x+3x+x=540\Rightarrow10x=540\Rightarrow x=54^\circ$. Angles: $2(54)=108^\circ$, $3(54)=162^\circ$, $54^\circ$, $162^\circ$, $54^\circ$.
(2) Sum of interior angles of an octagon $=180(8-2)=1080^\circ$. $4(x+20)+4x=1080\Rightarrow8x+80=1080\Rightarrow8x=1000\Rightarrow x=125^\circ$. The angles are $125^\circ$ and $145^\circ$ alternately.
(3) Exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to $360^\circ$: $x+(x+20)+x+(x+20)+x=360\Rightarrow5x+40=360\Rightarrow5x=320\Rightarrow x=64^\circ$.
(4) Exterior angles sum to $360^\circ$: $x+x+(x+50)+(x+10)+(x+5)+(x+25)=360\Rightarrow6x+90=360\Rightarrow6x=270\Rightarrow x=45^\circ$. Each interior angle $=180-$(its exterior angle): at the two vertices with exterior $45^\circ$, interior $=135^\circ$ (this is angle $a$, matching the figure's two $a^\circ$ labels); at exterior $x+50=95^\circ$, interior $=85^\circ=e$; at exterior $x+10=55^\circ$, interior $=125^\circ=b$; at exterior $x+5=50^\circ$, interior $=130^\circ=c$; at exterior $x+25=70^\circ$, interior $=110^\circ=d$. Check: exterior angles $45+45+95+55+50+70=360$ ✓.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
$O$ marks the centre; calculate the size of the marked angle $x^\circ$ (the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc):
(1) Inscribed angle $x^\circ$; the angle at the centre on the same arc is $110^\circ$.
(2) $A$, $T$ and $B$ are on the circle, and $O$ is joined to $A$ and $T$; $x^\circ$ is angle $AOT$. The chords $BA$ and $BT$ are drawn and $AB$ is extended beyond $B$; the angle between this extension and $BT$ is $140^\circ$.
(3) Inscribed angle $x^\circ$ in a triangle whose base is a diameter (the angle at the centre on the straight diameter is $180^\circ$).
(4) $L$, $P$ and $T$ are on the circle, with $P$ on the minor arc $LT$. $O$ is joined to $L$ and $T$, and the chords $LP$ and $PT$ are drawn. Angle $LPT=130^\circ$ and $x^\circ$ is the (non-reflex) angle $LOT$.
(5) $A$, $B$ and $C$ are on the circle. $O$ is joined to $A$ and $B$, and the chords $CA$ and $CB$ are drawn. Angle $ACB=40^\circ$ and $x^\circ$ is angle $AOB$.
(6) $T$, $L$ and $R$ are on the circle and $RM$ is a diameter. Angle $LTR=100^\circ$ (with $T$ on the minor arc $LR$). $O$ is joined to $L$, and $x^\circ$ is angle $LOM$.
exercises.full_solution:
(1) $x=110/2=55^\circ$ (the angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre on the same arc).
(2) Angles on a straight line: angle $ABT=180-140=40^\circ$. This angle at the circumference stands on arc $AT$, so the angle at the centre is $x=2\times40=80^\circ$.
(3) The diameter subtends $180^\circ$ at the centre, so $x=180/2=90^\circ$ (the angle in a semicircle).
(4) $P$ is on the minor arc, so angle $LPT=130^\circ$ stands on the MAJOR arc $LT$. The angle at the centre on the major arc is the reflex angle $LOT=2\times130=260^\circ$. Angles round a point: $x=360-260=100^\circ$.
(5) Angle $ACB=40^\circ$ stands on arc $AB$, so $x=$ angle $AOB=2\times40=80^\circ$.
(6) Angle $LTR=100^\circ$ stands on the major arc $LR$ (the arc through $M$), so the reflex angle $LOR=2\times100=200^\circ$. This reflex angle is made up of angle $ROM=180^\circ$ (straight line) and angle $MOL=x$, so $x=200-180=20^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on a circle with centre $O$, with $A$ at the top and $AB=AC$ (marked equal). $O$ is joined to $B$ and to $C$. (7) Angle $BAC=36^\circ$; find $x^\circ=$ angle $OBC$ and $y^\circ=$ angle $OCA$. (8) Angle $OBC=40^\circ$; find $x^\circ=$ angle $BAC$ and $y^\circ=$ angle $OCA$.
exercises.full_solution:
(7) The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference: angle $BOC=2\times36=72^\circ$. Triangle $OBC$ is isosceles ($OB=OC$, radii), so $x=$ angle $OBC=(180-72)/2=54^\circ$, and angle $OCB=54^\circ$ too. Triangle $ABC$ is isosceles ($AB=AC$), so angle $ACB=(180-36)/2=72^\circ$. Hence $y=$ angle $OCA=72-54=18^\circ$.
(8) Triangle $OBC$ is isosceles, so angle $OCB=40^\circ$ and angle $BOC=180-40-40=100^\circ$. The angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre: $x=$ angle $BAC=100/2=50^\circ$. Triangle $ABC$ is isosceles, so angle $ACB=(180-50)/2=65^\circ$. Hence $y=$ angle $OCA=65-40=25^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal. Calculate the marked angles:
(1) $72^\circ$ is given at one point on the circumference and $a^\circ$ at another point in the same segment (both angles stand on the same chord).
(2) Two diameters cross at $O$. A chord joins the two left-hand ends of the diameters and another chord joins the two right-hand ends. At the lower-left end, the angle between the left chord and the diameter is $33^\circ$; $b^\circ$ is the angle at the lower-right end between the right chord and the diameter (both angles stand on the arc joining the two upper ends). $c^\circ$ is the angle at $O$ between the two upper radii.
(3) Chords $TB$ and $LR$ cross inside the circle, and the chords $TL$ and $RB$ are drawn. $d^\circ=$ angle $LTB$, $e^\circ=$ angle $TLR$, angle $LRB=48^\circ$ and angle $TBR=32^\circ$.
(4) Two diameters $PQ$ and $RS$ cross at $O$ ($P$ top-left, $Q$ bottom-right, $R$ top-right, $S$ bottom-left), and the chords $PS$ and $RQ$ are drawn. Angle $ORQ=30^\circ$. Find $f^\circ=$ angle $OQR$, $g^\circ=$ angle $ROQ$, $h^\circ=$ angle $POS$, $i^\circ=$ angle $OPS$ and $j^\circ=$ angle $OSP$.
exercises.full_solution:
(1) Both angles stand on the same chord, in the same segment, so $a=72^\circ$.
(2) The $33^\circ$ angle and $b$ both stand on the arc joining the two upper ends of the diameters, so $b=33^\circ$ (same segment). The angle at the centre on that arc is $c=2\times33=66^\circ$.
(3) $d=$ angle $LTB$ and angle $LRB$ both stand on chord $LB$, so $d=48^\circ$. $e=$ angle $TLR$ and angle $TBR$ both stand on chord $TR$, so $e=32^\circ$.
(4) Triangle $ORQ$ is isosceles ($OR=OQ$, radii), so $f=$ angle $OQR=30^\circ$ and $g=180-30-30=120^\circ$. Vertically opposite angles: $h=g=120^\circ$. Angle $OPS$ (that is, angle $QPS$) and angle $QRS$ (angle $ORQ$) both stand on chord $QS$, so $i=30^\circ$ (same segment); triangle $OPS$ is isosceles ($OP=OS$), so $j=i=30^\circ$ (check: $30+30+120=180$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement:
For each question, calculate the size of the marked angles (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^\circ$; the exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle; alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment):
(1) A cyclic quadrilateral has angles $a^\circ$ (top-left), $b^\circ$ (right), $100^\circ$ (bottom-right) and $115^\circ$ (bottom-left).
(2) A cyclic quadrilateral has angles $c^\circ$ (top-left), $d^\circ$ (top-right), $e^\circ$ (bottom-right) and $82^\circ$ (bottom-left). The right side is extended downwards beyond the bottom-right vertex, and the exterior angle there is $110^\circ$.
(3) A cyclic quadrilateral has angles $g^\circ$ (top-left), $f^\circ$ (bottom-left) and $105^\circ$ (bottom-right). The right side is extended upwards beyond the top-right vertex, and the exterior angle there (between the extension and the top side) is $115^\circ$.
(4) A kite is drawn in a circle. Its vertices are $i^\circ$ (top), $k^\circ$ (right), $82^\circ$ (bottom) and $j^\circ$ (left); the two upper sides are equal and the two lower sides are equal.
(5) $M$, $A$, $N$, $L$, $P$ and $Q$ lie on a circle in that order. The chords $QA$, $AN$, $NL$, $LQ$, $MN$, $MP$ and $PL$ are drawn, with $QL$ parallel to $MN$. Angle $QAN=85^\circ$ and angle $PLQ=30^\circ$. Find $l^\circ=$ angle $QLN$, $n^\circ=$ angle $MNL$, $p^\circ=$ angle $MPL$, $m^\circ=$ angle $PMN$, and $q^\circ$, the angle between $LQ$ and $PM$ where they cross, on the side facing $Q$ and $M$.
(6) $S$, $U$, $T$ and $R$ lie on a circle and form a cyclic quadrilateral $SUTR$. The tangent at $U$ meets $RS$ extended beyond $S$ at $E$, with $ES=SU$ and angle $SEU=60^\circ$. The angle between the tangent (on the side away from $E$) and the chord $UT$ is $10^\circ$. Find $r^\circ=$ angle $SRT$, $s^\circ=$ angle $RSU$, $t^\circ=$ angle $UTR$ and $u^\circ=$ angle $SUT$.
(7) $W$, $V$, $X$ and $Y$ lie on a circle and form the cyclic quadrilateral $WVXY$, with diagonal $WX$ drawn. The tangent at $V$ makes $55^\circ$ with the chord $VW$ and $45^\circ$ with the chord $VX$. Find $v^\circ=$ angle $WVX$, $w^\circ=$ angle $XWV$, $x^\circ=$ angle $WXV$ and $y^\circ=$ angle $WYX$.
exercises.full_solution:
(1) Opposite angles add up to $180^\circ$: $a=180-100=80^\circ$ and $b=180-115=65^\circ$.
(2) Angles on a straight line: $e=180-110=70^\circ$. Opposite angles: $c=180-e=110^\circ$ (this also shows the exterior angle $110^\circ$ equals the interior opposite angle $c$) and $d=180-82=98^\circ$.
(3) The exterior angle at the top-right vertex equals the interior opposite angle, so $f=115^\circ$. Opposite angles: $g=180-105=75^\circ$.
(4) The kite is symmetric about the diagonal through the top and bottom vertices (where the equal sides meet), so $j=k$. Opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral: $j+k=180$, so $j=k=90^\circ$, and $i=180-82=98^\circ$.
(5) $QANL$ is cyclic: $l=180-85=95^\circ$. $QL\parallel MN$, so co-interior angles give $n=180-l=85^\circ$. $MNLP$ is cyclic: $p=180-n=95^\circ$, and $m=180-$ angle $NLP=180-(95+30)=55^\circ$. Finally $q$ and $m$ are alternate angles between the parallel lines $QL$ and $MN$ (with $PM$ as transversal), so $q=55^\circ$.
(6) Triangle $ESU$ is isosceles ($ES=SU$), so angle $SUE=60^\circ$ and angle $ESU=60^\circ$. Angles on the straight line $ER$: $s=180-60=120^\circ$. Angles on the straight tangent line at $U$: $u=180-60-10=110^\circ$. Opposite angles of $SUTR$: $r=180-u=70^\circ$ and $t=180-s=60^\circ$.
(7) Angles on the straight tangent line: $v=180-55-45=80^\circ$. Alternate segment theorem: the $55^\circ$ angle between the tangent and chord $VW$ equals the angle in the alternate segment, $x=$ angle $WXV=55^\circ$; the $45^\circ$ angle between the tangent and chord $VX$ equals $w=$ angle $XWV=45^\circ$ (check: $80+55+45=180$). Opposite angles of $WVXY$: $y=180-v=100^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A triangle with vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ is drawn in a circle. Tangents to the circle at $B$ and at $C$ meet at the point $P$ outside the circle. The angle between the tangent $BP$ and the chord $BC$ is $63^\circ$. Calculate $\alpha$ (angle $BAC$), $\beta$ (angle $BCP$, between the chord $CB$ and the tangent $CP$) and $\phi$ (angle $BPC$, between the two tangents).
exercises.full_solution:
Alternate segment theorem: the angle between the tangent $BP$ and the chord $BC$ ($63^\circ$) equals the angle in the alternate segment, so $\alpha=$ angle $BAC=63^\circ$.
Tangents drawn from the same external point are equal, so $PB=PC$ and triangle $PBC$ is isosceles. Its base angles are equal: $\beta=$ angle $PCB=$ angle $PBC=63^\circ$.
Angle sum of triangle $PBC$: $\phi=180-63-63=54^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: Triangle $ABC$ inscribed in a circle, with the tangents at $B$ and at $C$ meeting at $P$. The angle between the tangent $BP$ and the chord $BC$ is $63^{\circ}$; $\alpha=\angle BAC$, $\beta=\angle BCP$ and $\phi=\angle BPC$.
assets.purpose: Show the tangent-chord angle and the angle in the alternate segment in one picture, so the student can see why alpha equals 63 degrees.

exam_questions.statement:
(1) State whether each angle shown is acute, obtuse, reflex or a right angle: (a) a small angle less than $90^\circ$ (b) an angle greater than $90^\circ$ but less than $180^\circ$ (c) an angle greater than $180^\circ$ (d) an angle of exactly $90^\circ$ (shown with a right-angle mark).
(2) Draw and label two pairs of intersecting parallel lines.
(3) Identify the types of triangles shown below in two ways (e.g. 'obtuse-angled scalene triangle'): (a) a wide, flat-looking scalene triangle with no right angle and no equal sides marked, where the largest angle is obtuse (b) a right-angled triangle with all three sides of different length.
(4) Draw a circle of radius $3\text{ cm}$. Mark on it: (a) a diameter (b) a chord (c) a sector.
(5) Draw a rhombus and write down three of its properties.
(6) On squared paper, draw the net of a triangular prism.
exam_questions.answer:
(1)(a) acute (b) obtuse (c) reflex (d) right angle.
(2) Any correctly drawn diagram with two pairs of parallel lines crossing each other, each pair labelled (e.g. with arrow marks) to show which lines are parallel.
(3)(a) obtuse-angled scalene triangle (b) right-angled scalene triangle.
(4) A circle of radius 3 cm with: (a) a straight line through the centre, ends on the circle (diameter, length 6 cm) (b) a straight line joining two points on the circle NOT through the centre (chord) (c) a region bounded by two radii and an arc (sector).
(5) A rhombus (four equal sides) with three of: all sides equal in length; opposite sides parallel; opposite angles equal; diagonals bisect each other at right angles; diagonals bisect the vertex angles.
(6) A net consisting of three rectangles (one for each face of the prism's length) joined edge to edge, with the two triangular end-faces attached to two of the edges of one rectangle.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(1) An acute angle is less than $90^\circ$; an obtuse angle is between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$; a reflex angle is greater than $180^\circ$ (and less than $360^\circ$); a right angle is exactly $90^\circ$ (shown with a small square mark).
(2) Two pairs of parallel lines, each pair drawn with matching arrow marks to indicate which lines are parallel to each other, crossing to form a lattice/grid pattern.
(3) Triangle descriptions combine (i) angle type: acute-angled (all angles $<90^\circ$), right-angled (one angle $=90^\circ$), or obtuse-angled (one angle $>90^\circ$) with (ii) side type: scalene (no sides equal), isosceles (two sides equal), or equilateral (all three sides equal, hence also all angles $60^\circ$).
(4) Using compasses, draw a circle of radius $3\text{ cm}$ (diameter $6\text{ cm}$). A diameter passes through the centre with both ends on the circle; a chord joins any two points on the circle without passing through the centre; a sector is the 'pizza-slice' region enclosed by two radii and the arc between them.
(5) A rhombus is a parallelogram with all four sides equal; valid properties include: all sides equal in length, opposite sides parallel, opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other at right angles, and each diagonal bisects a pair of opposite (vertex) angles.
(6) The net of a triangular prism consists of a strip of three rectangles (whose widths match the three sides of the triangular cross-section, and whose common length is the prism's length), with a triangle attached to one free edge at each end of the strip.
mark_scheme: B1 for each of (a)-(d) in Q1 (4 marks)
B1 for a correctly drawn pair of intersecting parallel lines, B1 for the second pair (2 marks)
B1 for each correct triangle description in Q3 (2 marks)
B1 for the circle with correct radius, B1 each for diameter/chord/sector correctly marked (4 marks)
B1 for a correctly drawn rhombus, B1 for each of three correct properties (4 marks)
B1 for a correct net of a triangular prism (1 mark)

exam_questions.statement:
(1) Two right-angled triangles are similar. In the first, the right angle is between sides of $4\text{ cm}$ (top) and $3\text{ cm}$ (left), and the hypotenuse is $p\text{ cm}$. In the second, the right angle is between sides of $6\text{ cm}$ (top) and $x\text{ cm}$ (left), and the hypotenuse is $y\text{ cm}$; the $6\text{ cm}$ side corresponds to the $4\text{ cm}$ side. (a) Using Pythagoras' theorem, calculate the value of $p$. (b) Calculate the values of $x$ and $y$.
(2) Cones M and N are similar, with heights $h$ and $H$ respectively. (a) Express the ratio of their surface areas in the form 'area of M : area of N'. (b) Express the ratio of their volumes in the form 'volume of M : volume of N'.
exam_questions.answer:
(1)(a) $p=5\text{ cm}$. (b) Scale factor $=\dfrac64=1.5$, so $x=4.5\text{ cm}$ and $y=7.5\text{ cm}$.
(2)(a) Area of M : Area of N $= h^2:H^2$. (b) Volume of M : Volume of N $=h^3:H^3$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(1)(a) By Pythagoras' theorem, $p=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=\sqrt{9+16}=\sqrt{25}=5\text{ cm}$.
(b) The $6\text{ cm}$ side corresponds to the $4\text{ cm}$ side, so the scale factor is $\dfrac{6}{4}=1.5$. Then $x$ (corresponding to $3\text{ cm}$) $=3\times1.5=4.5\text{ cm}$ and $y$ (corresponding to $p=5\text{ cm}$) $=5\times1.5=7.5\text{ cm}$.
(2) For similar solids with linear ratio $h:H$, surface areas are in the ratio $h^2:H^2$ and volumes in the ratio $h^3:H^3$.
mark_scheme: M1 for correctly applying Pythagoras, A1 for $p=5$ (2 marks)
M1 for identifying the scale factor, A1 for $x$, A1 for $y$ (3 marks)
M1 for using (linear ratio)$^2$ for areas, A1 for area ratio $h^2:H^2$ (2 marks)
B1 for volume ratio $h^3:H^3$ (1 mark)

exam_questions.statement:
(1) Draw a two-dimensional shape with exactly: (a) rotational symmetry of order 2 (b) rotational symmetry of order 4 (c) rotational symmetry of order 6.
(2) Draw and name a three-dimensional shape with the following orders of rotational symmetry, marking the position of the axis of symmetry clearly: (a) order 2 (b) order 3 (c) order 8.
(3) In a circle, $OM$ and $ON$ are perpendicular bisectors of chords $AB$ and $XY$ respectively, and $OM=ON$. Prove that $AB$ and $XY$ are chords of equal length.
exam_questions.answer:
(1) Any shape with the stated symmetry is acceptable, e.g. (a) a parallelogram (maps to itself after a $180^\circ$ rotation only), (b) a square (maps to itself every $90^\circ$), (c) a regular hexagon (maps to itself every $60^\circ$).
(2) Any solid with the stated rotational symmetry about the marked axis is acceptable, e.g. (a) a (non-square) cuboid about the axis through the centres of a pair of opposite faces, (b) a prism with an equilateral-triangular cross-section about its length axis, (c) a regular octagonal prism about its length axis (a pyramid with a regular octagonal base, about the axis through its apex, also works).
(3) Since $OM\perp AB$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, triangle $OMA$ (or $OMB$) is right-angled at $M$; similarly $OXN$ (or $OYN$) is right-angled at $N$. In right triangles $OMA$ and $ONX$: $OA=OX$ (both radii of the same circle), $OM=ON$ (given), and both have a right angle (at $M$ and $N$ respectively). By RHS (right angle, hypotenuse, side), $\triangle OMA\cong\triangle ONX$. Hence $MA=NX$ (corresponding sides of congruent triangles). Since $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $XY$, $AB=2\times MA$ and $XY=2\times NX$; as $MA=NX$, it follows that $AB=XY$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(1) Any shape with the stated symmetry is acceptable, e.g. (a) a parallelogram (maps to itself after a $180^\circ$ rotation only), (b) a square (maps to itself every $90^\circ$), (c) a regular hexagon (maps to itself every $60^\circ$).
(2) Any solid with the stated rotational symmetry about the marked axis is acceptable, e.g. (a) a (non-square) cuboid about the axis through the centres of a pair of opposite faces, (b) a prism with an equilateral-triangular cross-section about its length axis, (c) a regular octagonal prism about its length axis (a pyramid with a regular octagonal base, about the axis through its apex, also works).
(3) Since $OM\perp AB$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, triangle $OMA$ (or $OMB$) is right-angled at $M$; similarly $OXN$ (or $OYN$) is right-angled at $N$. In right triangles $OMA$ and $ONX$: $OA=OX$ (both radii of the same circle), $OM=ON$ (given), and both have a right angle (at $M$ and $N$ respectively). By RHS (right angle, hypotenuse, side), $\triangle OMA\cong\triangle ONX$. Hence $MA=NX$ (corresponding sides of congruent triangles). Since $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $XY$, $AB=2\times MA$ and $XY=2\times NX$; as $MA=NX$, it follows that $AB=XY$.
mark_scheme: B1 each for Q1(a)-(c): correct shape with the stated rotational symmetry (3 marks)
B1 each for Q2(a)-(c): correct solid, correctly named, with axis marked (3 marks)
M1 for identifying the right-angled triangles $OMA$ and $ONX$ ($OM\perp AB$, $ON\perp XY$)
A1 for correctly applying RHS congruence
A1 for concluding $MA=NX$ and hence $AB=2MA=2NX=XY$
B1 for stating $OA=OX$ (radii) and $OM=ON$ (given) (Q3 total 4 marks)
