exam_questions.statement:
(1) For the diagrams below, calculate the size of the labelled angles. (a) Two parallel horizontal lines are crossed by a transversal that slopes down from left to right (at $45^\circ$ to the lines). At the upper intersection: $q^\circ$ (below the line, left of the transversal) and $r^\circ$ (below the line, right of the transversal). At the lower intersection: $45^\circ$ (above the line, left of the transversal) and $p^\circ$ (above the line, right of the transversal). (b) Two parallel horizontal lines are crossed by two parallel lines that slope up to the right. At the upper crossing of the first sloping line: $a^\circ$ (above the line, left), $b^\circ$ (above the line, right) and $120^\circ$ (below the line, right). At the lower horizontal line: $c^\circ$ (above the line, right of the first sloping line) and $d^\circ$ (above the line, right of the second sloping line).
(2) For the diagrams below, calculate the size of the labelled angles. (a) A right-angled triangle has its right angle at the bottom-left, $40^\circ$ at the bottom-right and $m^\circ$ at the top. A line parallel to the base joins the left side to the hypotenuse. At the left side, $n^\circ$ is the angle above this line; at the hypotenuse, $p^\circ$ is the angle above the line and $q^\circ$ the angle below it. (b) Two triangles meet at a single point, one above the other (an hourglass shape), and the top side of the upper triangle is parallel to the bottom side of the lower triangle. The upper triangle has angles $55^\circ$ (top-left), $w^\circ$ (top-right) and $70^\circ$ (at the meeting point); the lower triangle has angles $x^\circ$ (at the meeting point), $y^\circ$ (bottom-left) and $z^\circ$ (bottom-right). (c) A trapezium has its top side parallel to its bottom side. A line is drawn from the bottom-left vertex to a point on the top side; this line is equal in length to the right-hand side (marked). In the small triangle on the left, the angle at the top-left vertex is $80^\circ$, the angle at the top is $d^\circ$ and the angle at the bottom-left vertex is $e^\circ$. In the larger shape on the right, the angles are $c^\circ$ (top-left, next to $d^\circ$), $b^\circ$ (top-right), $a^\circ$ (bottom-right) and $70^\circ$ (bottom-left).
(3) Find the size of each interior angle of a twenty-sided regular polygon.
(4) What is the sum of the interior angles of a nonagon?
exam_questions.full_solution:
(1)(a) $r$ and the $45^\circ$ angle are alternate angles, so $r=45^\circ$. Angles on a straight line: $q=180-45=135^\circ$. $p$ and $q$ are alternate angles, so $p=135^\circ$ (or: $p=180-45$, angles on a straight line).
(b) $a$ is vertically opposite the $120^\circ$ angle, so $a=120^\circ$; $b=180-120=60^\circ$ (angles on a straight line). $c$ corresponds to $b$ (horizontal lines parallel), so $c=60^\circ$. $d$ corresponds to $c$ (sloping lines parallel), so $d=60^\circ$.
(2)(a) Angle sum of the large triangle: $m=180-90-40=50^\circ$. The line is parallel to the base, so $n=90^\circ$ and $p=40^\circ$ (corresponding angles). Angles on a straight line: $q=180-40=140^\circ$.
(b) Upper triangle: $w=180-55-70=55^\circ$. Vertically opposite angles: $x=70^\circ$. The top and bottom sides are parallel, so $y=w=55^\circ$ and $z=55^\circ$ (alternate angles).
(c) The right-hand part is a trapezium whose two non-parallel sides are equal, so it is an isosceles trapezium: $a=70^\circ$ (equal base angles) and, by co-interior angles, $c=180-70=110^\circ$ and $b=180-a=110^\circ$. Angles on the straight top side: $d=180-c=70^\circ$. Small triangle: $e=180-80-70=30^\circ$. (Check: co-interior angles on the left side, $80+(e+70)=180$.)
(3) Interior angle of a regular $n$-gon $=\dfrac{180(n-2)}{n}$. For $n=20$: $\dfrac{180\times18}{20}=162^\circ$.
(4) Sum of interior angles $=180(n-2)$. For a nonagon, $n=9$: $180\times7=1260^\circ$.
mark_scheme: B1 each for Q1(a) $q,r,p$ and Q1(b) $a,b,c,d$ (up to 7 marks)
B1 each for Q2(a) $m,n,p,q$ (4 marks)
B1 each for Q2(b) $w$, $x$, $y$, $z$ and Q2(c) $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $e$ (9 marks)
M1A1 for Q3: correct formula and $x=162^\circ$ (2 marks)
B1 for Q4: $1260^\circ$ (1 mark)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: $XY$ is a tangent to a circle at $A$; $O$ is the centre of the circle; $B$ and $C$ are also points on the circumference. The angle between the tangent $AX$ and the chord $AB$ is $67^\circ$ (angle $BAX=67^\circ$). Calculate each of the following angles, justifying each answer: (a) angle $ACB$ (b) the reflex angle $AOB$ (c) angle $ABO$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) Alternate segment theorem: the angle between the tangent $AX$ and the chord $AB$ ($67^\circ$) equals the angle in the alternate segment, so angle $ACB=67^\circ$.
(b) The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc: the non-reflex angle $AOB=2\times67=134^\circ$. So the reflex angle $AOB=360-134=226^\circ$.
(c) Triangle $OAB$ is isosceles ($OA=OB$, radii) with angle $AOB=134^\circ$, so angle $ABO=(180-134)/2=23^\circ$.
mark_scheme: M1A1 for angle $ACB=67^\circ$ (alternate segment theorem) (2 marks)
M1A1 for the central angle ($134^\circ$) and hence the reflex angle $=226^\circ$ (2 marks)
M1A1 for recognising triangle $OAB$ is isosceles and calculating angle $ABO=23^\circ$ (2 marks)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: In each of the following diagrams, $O$ marks the centre of the circle. Identify which angles are: (i) supplementary angles, (ii) right angles, (iii) equal. (a) Points $A,B,C$ lie on a vertical line, with $B$ on the circle and $O$ joined to $B$ by a horizontal radius (so the vertical line $AC$ is tangent to the circle at $B$). (b) A general cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ (no further marks). (c) $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on the circle, and the chords $AD$, $DB$, $AC$ and $CB$ are drawn, so that $AC$ and $DB$ cross inside the circle (neither passes through $O$). (d) An isosceles triangle $ABC$ inscribed with $AB=AC$ (tick marks) and $BC$ a diameter through $O$.
exam_questions.answer:
(a) angle $OBA$ and angle $OBC$ are both right angles (tangent $\perp$ radius); they are also supplementary (they lie on the straight line $AC$, summing to $180^\circ$) and equal (each $90^\circ$).
(b) angle $DAB$ and angle $BCD$ are supplementary (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to $180^\circ$); likewise angle $ABC$ and angle $CDA$ are supplementary. No angles are necessarily right angles or equal from the information given alone.
(c) Angle $DAC=$ angle $DBC$ (both stand on chord $DC$) and angle $ADB=$ angle $ACB$ (both stand on chord $AB$) — angles in the same segment are equal; the vertically opposite angles where $AC$ crosses $DB$ are also equal, and adjacent angles at that crossing point are supplementary. No angles are necessarily right angles.
(d) Since $BC$ is a diameter, angle $BAC=90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle); since $AB=AC$, triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with the two base angles equal: angle $ABC=$ angle $ACB=45^\circ$ each.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) The radius $OB$ is perpendicular to the tangent $AC$ at the point of contact $B$ (tangent $\perp$ radius), so both angle $OBA$ and angle $OBC$ equal $90^\circ$. As $A,B,C$ are collinear, these two angles lie on a straight line and so are supplementary (sum $180^\circ$); being both exactly $90^\circ$, they are also equal to each other.
(b) For ANY cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles sum to $180^\circ$ (supplementary) — this follows from the 'angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference' theorem applied to each pair of opposite vertices. With no further markings, no angles are guaranteed to be right angles or equal.
(c) Angles $DAC$ and $DBC$ both stand on the chord $DC$ and lie in the same segment, so they are equal; similarly angles $ADB$ and $ACB$ both stand on chord $AB$, so they are equal. Where $AC$ and $DB$ cross, vertically opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles add up to $180^\circ$ (supplementary). Neither chord is a diameter, so no angle is necessarily $90^\circ$.
(d) $BC$ is a diameter, so angle $BAC=90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle). With $AB=AC$ given (isosceles), the remaining two angles of the triangle are equal: angle $ABC=$angle $ACB=(180-90)/2=45^\circ$.
mark_scheme: B1 for identifying (a)'s two right angles, B1 for noting they are also supplementary and equal (2 marks)
B1 for correctly stating the supplementary opposite-angle pairs in (b) (1 mark)
B1 for each correct pair of equal angles in the same segment in (c) (2 marks)
M1 for using the semicircle angle in (d), A1 for $45^\circ$ base angles (2 marks)
(1 mark for overall clear justification/reasoning throughout)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
$A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a circle, centre $O$. $AC$ is a diameter of the circle. $\angle BAC=32^{\circ}$ and $\angle ACD=25^{\circ}$.
(a) Write down the size of $\angle ABC$. Give a reason for your answer. [2]
(b) Calculate $\angle BCA$. [2]
(c) Find $\angle ABD$. Give a reason for your answer. [2]
(d) Show that $\angle BAD=97^{\circ}$, giving a reason for each step. [3]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\angle ABC=90^{\circ}$ (angle in a semicircle). (b) $\angle BCA=58^{\circ}$. (c) $\angle ABD=25^{\circ}$ (angles in the same segment). (d) $\angle BCD=83^{\circ}$, so $\angle BAD=180^{\circ}-83^{\circ}=97^{\circ}$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) $AC$ is a diameter, so $\angle ABC=90^{\circ}$ (the angle in a semicircle is $90^{\circ}$).

(b) In triangle $ABC$ the angles add up to $180^{\circ}$, so $\angle BCA=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-32^{\circ}=58^{\circ}$.

(c) $\angle ABD$ and $\angle ACD$ both stand on the chord $AD$, and $B$ and $C$ are in the same segment, so $\angle ABD=\angle ACD=25^{\circ}$ (angles in the same segment are equal).

(d) $\angle BCD=\angle BCA+\angle ACD=58^{\circ}+25^{\circ}=83^{\circ}$. $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, so its opposite angles add up to $180^{\circ}$: $\angle BAD=180^{\circ}-83^{\circ}=97^{\circ}$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for $90^{\circ}$; B1 for the reason 'angle in a semicircle'
(b) M1 for $180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-32^{\circ}$ (angle sum of a triangle); A1 for $58^{\circ}$
(c) B1 for $25^{\circ}$; B1 for the reason 'angles in the same segment are equal'
(d) M1 for $\angle BCD=58^{\circ}+25^{\circ}=83^{\circ}$; M1 for using 'opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^{\circ}$'; A1 for the conclusion $\angle BAD=97^{\circ}$
common_errors: In (c), using $\angle ACD$ as an angle at the centre and halving or doubling it, instead of recognising two angles in the same segment.
In (d), forgetting to add $\angle BCA$ and $\angle ACD$ first, and subtracting only $25^{\circ}$ from $180^{\circ}$.

exam_questions.statement:
A company makes conical paper cups in three sizes. All three cups are mathematically similar.
The small cup has height $8$ cm and holds $90$ ml.
(a) The medium cup has height $12$ cm. Calculate how much it holds. [3]
(b) The curved surface area of the small cup is $95\ \mathrm{cm^2}$. Calculate the curved surface area of the medium cup. [2]
(c) The large cup holds $720$ ml. Calculate its height. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) The linear scale factor is $k=\dfrac{12}{8}=1.5$. Volumes scale by $k^3$, so the medium cup holds $90\times1.5^3=90\times3.375=303.75$ ml.

(b) Areas scale by $k^2=1.5^2=2.25$, so the curved surface area is $95\times2.25=213.75\ \mathrm{cm^2}$.

(c) The volume scale factor from the small cup to the large cup is $\dfrac{720}{90}=8$, so the linear scale factor is $\sqrt[3]{8}=2$ and the height is $8\times2=16$ cm.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for the linear scale factor $12\div8=1.5$; M1 for $90\times1.5^3$; A1 for $303.75$ ml (accept $304$)
(b) M1 for $95\times1.5^2$; A1 for $213.75\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ (accept $214$)
(c) M1 for $\sqrt[3]{720\div90}=2$; A1 for $16$ cm
common_errors: Using the linear scale factor $1.5$ for the volume ($90\times1.5=135$ ml) or for the area, instead of $k^3$ and $k^2$.
In (c), dividing the volumes and then taking the square root instead of the cube root.

exam_questions.statement:
Each interior angle of a regular polygon is $156^{\circ}$.
(a) Calculate the number of sides of the polygon. [3]
(b) Write down the order of rotational symmetry of the polygon. [1]
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) Each exterior angle $=180^{\circ}-156^{\circ}=24^{\circ}$ (angles on a straight line). The exterior angles of any polygon add up to $360^{\circ}$, so the number of sides is $\dfrac{360^{\circ}}{24^{\circ}}=15$.

(b) A regular polygon with $15$ sides maps onto itself after a rotation of $\dfrac{360^{\circ}}{15}=24^{\circ}$, so its order of rotational symmetry is $15$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for the exterior angle $180^{\circ}-156^{\circ}=24^{\circ}$
(a) M1 for $360^{\circ}\div24^{\circ}$
(a) A1 for $15$
(b) B1 for $15$, following through from their number of sides
common_errors: Dividing $360^{\circ}$ by the interior angle $156^{\circ}$ instead of by the exterior angle.
Using $\dfrac{180(n-2)}{n}=156$ and then making an algebraic slip; the exterior-angle route is shorter and safer.
